s: John 15:25. — “They hated me for no reason.”
Our Lord Jesus Christ spoke these words.
In my last two sermons, I spoke about total depravity—how completely sinful people are. In them I tried to prove that all sinners who have not turned from their sin hate God more than anything else.
I believe I proved this teaching beyond any argument by pointing to the facts. So now we face a very serious and important question. Why do sinners hate God?

If sinners have a good reason to hate God, then they are not to blame for it. But what if they have no good reason? What if they hate him when they should love him? Then their hostility toward God makes them very guilty.
As I speak about this subject, I plan to show three things:
First, what is not the reason they hate him.
Second, what the reason really is.
Third, that they hate him for the very reasons they should love him.

blocks.x: I. First, I will show what is not the reason sinners hate God.

s: First, it is not because God made them in such a way that they have a built-in dislike of him, as part of their body or their basic makeup.
Our text says that sinners have hated God without a cause.
This does not mean there is no reason at all why they hate him. It means there is no good reason.
Strictly speaking, their hatred does have a cause, because everything that happens must have some cause. But it has no fair and right cause.
Suppose God had made human beings so that they could not help hating their Maker. Then that would not only be a cause for hating him. It would be a fair cause.

Suppose God had built a natural dislike of himself into the very stuff a person is made of. Then that would be reason enough for the sinner to hate him. In fact, it would be a good reason for every other being to hate him too.
Second, the sinner’s hatred of God is not caused by some leaning toward hating him that is inherited or passed down from parents.
Being inclined to hate God is already hatred.
An inclination like this is something the mind does. It is not a part of the mind itself.
So it makes no sense to talk about inheriting an inclination to love or hate God, or anything else, or having it passed down to us.
A state of mind that we choose cannot be inherited. It cannot be handed down from one generation to the next.

But some of you may mean something else by “inclination.” You may mean a tendency or temper that is not an action, and so not a state of mind we choose. You may mean a quality or feature that is part of the mind itself. If so, I say this:
Third, the sinner’s hatred is not caused by any such feature that is part of the mind and that, all by itself, naturally and unavoidably dislikes God.
Fourth, there is nothing in the way our nature is made that gives us a fair reason to oppose God.
Human nature is just as it should be.
Its abilities are just the way God made them.
He made them in the best way that his unlimited power, goodness, and wisdom could make them.

They are perfectly fitted for serving the One who made us. Look at all the amazing workings and delicate design of the body. Study all the qualities, powers, and abilities of the mind. We can find no fair reason to complain. Instead, we find endless reasons to love and worship the great Designer, and to cry out with the psalm writer, “I am made in an awesome and wonderful way.”

Fifth, the sinner has no fair reason to hate God because of the wise and kind plan by which all people come from one common ancestor. Under this plan from God, we are naturally influenced (but not forced) by the circumstances we live in, and those circumstances shape our characters.

We are made so that we naturally influence each other. We play a big part in shaping each other’s character. This is a wise and kind arrangement, and it is extremely important for the whole universe. But like every other good thing, it can be badly misused. The more power we have to encourage goodness when we do right, the more power we have to encourage evil when we do wrong.
Sixth, the sinner has no reason to hate God because of the way God rules people through his moral law.

His commands are not hard and heavy. They are not impossible to obey. They are not designed to make us miserable when we obey them. Just the opposite: “his yoke is easy to carry, and his load is light.”
His commands are easy to obey, and obeying them naturally leads to happiness.

Suppose God had set up a government that demanded so much that it was extremely hard to obey his laws. Suppose his laws were so unclear, complicated, and hard to understand that even an honest person could easily get wrong what he really wanted. Or suppose his laws were random, pointless, and based on whims. Or suppose they were backed up by unfair and cruel punishments. If any of these things were true, sinners would have a fair reason to hate God.
But not one of these things is true.
Also, sinners have no fair reason to hate God because of what the Gospel asks of them.

Suppose the conditions for salvation offered in the Gospel were random, based on whims, or unfair. Suppose it were impossible to meet them. Suppose the terms were set so high that people did not have the natural ability to obey them and meet the conditions their salvation depends on. Suppose God commanded people to repent when they had no power to repent. Suppose he required them to believe when they had no power to believe, and then threatened to send them to hell for not repenting and believing. In any of these cases, and in all of them, sinners would have a fair reason to hate God.
But none of this is true.

The conditions of the Gospel are not random at all. By their very nature, no one can be saved without them. And they are not set so high that they are impossible or even hard to meet. They have been brought down as low as they can possibly go without making the sinner’s salvation impossible.

Repentance and faith are absolutely needed to prepare the soul to enjoy heaven. If God dropped these conditions and agreed to let the sinner stay in his sins, that would make it certain that the sinner is damned.
Also, the conditions of salvation are not only necessary by their very nature. They are also easy to meet.
It is much easier to meet them than to reject them.
Our minds are just as able to accept the Gospel as to reject it.
The reasons to accept God’s offer of mercy are infinitely greater than the reasons to reject it.
In fact, the reasons to meet the Gospel’s conditions are so strong that sinners often find them hard to resist. They have to work almost nonstop to keep themselves from repenting and believing.
Also, there is no fair reason to hate God because of the way he guides and controls what happens in the world.
There is no reason to doubt that God guides the events of the world in the way that, overall, does the most good possible to encourage holiness.
It is clear that his moral laws are backed up by the strongest possible rewards and penalties. Everything a perfect moral government could do to make the whole world holy has been done.
In the same way, it is true beyond all reasonable doubt that he runs the physical world and all its events in the wisest possible way.
No doubt he runs it only to help and support his moral government.
It is set up to have the greatest moral influence that such a government can possibly have.

Many sinners talk as if God could have run both of his governments, the moral one and the one over events, much more wisely. They think he could have done it in a way far better suited to make his subjects behave perfectly.
They seem to think that because God is all-powerful, he can do anything you can imagine, even things that are absurd or that contradict themselves.

They think he can make moral beings perfect just by using his physical power. They also think the fact that sin exists in our world proves something. It proves, they say, that although God is against sin in some ways, overall he would rather have sin than holiness in its place.

They seem to assume that God could have run his two governments over the universe, moral and physical, in a way that would make everyone everywhere holy. But this idea has no basis at all, and it is a very wicked thing to assume.

You cannot fairly draw this conclusion from the fact that God is all-powerful and all-knowing. This idea is based on a wrong view of what it means to be a moral being who makes choices, and of what moral government is.
Also, there is nothing in God’s character that gives a fair reason to hate him.
However you look at the character of Jehovah, you will find nothing hateful or offensive to any fair-minded person.
Just the opposite: his character includes every good quality anyone could imagine, every good quality that could possibly exist.
Also, there is no fair reason to hate God because of the way he acts.
What he does always matches what he says.

Some people seem to picture God as sly, tricky, and two-faced. They picture him saying one thing and meaning another. They think he claims to hate sin, yet runs himself and his kingdom in a way that is sure to produce sin, and on purpose. They think he commands people to keep his law or face eternal death, but in the end would rather they break it. They think he commands everyone to repent and believe the Gospel, yet made atonement only for the elect, the ones he chose. They think he requires people to repent, yet made them in such a way that he knows they cannot repent. They think he says he wants very much for everyone to be saved, and yet has made their salvation depend on conditions no one can meet.
In fact, many seem to describe what God does and what God says as always at war with each other. They make it all into a tangled web of contradictions, nonsense, and hypocrisy.
But every description like this is a slander against the way he acts, which is infinitely fair and honest.
Also, God does nothing unkind or needlessly harsh to the people of this world.
Sinners have complained a lot about the way God acts. They have often said he treats them unfairly. Sometimes they have asked what they did to deserve such harsh punishment from him.
But all this complaining only proves how stubborn and twisted they are. It can never give anyone a fair reason to suspect that God has done wrong.
II. Sinners really do hate God because selfishness rules them above everything else. And God, as he should be, is infinitely against the thing they chase above all else.
The first thing we see in the behavior of little children is the desire to please themselves.
We cannot say at what point in their lives this desire turns into selfishness.
It is clear that it is not sinful to have a proper desire to satisfy our hunger and thirst, and all the other natural appetites we are made with.
These appetites are neither good nor bad in themselves. Satisfying them in the right way is not sinful.

But sometimes we satisfy them too much. Sometimes satisfying our appetites clashes with what God requires. Whenever and wherever we give in to our natural desires when we are supposed to hold back, we sin in every such case. That is because in all these cases we are selfish. We make our own pleasure the rule for what we ought to do, instead of what God requires.
We agree to please ourselves at the cost of everyone else, in a way that goes against God’s glory and the highest good of his universe.
This is what all sin really is, and this is the story of all sin.

At some point in our lives, we first choose pleasing ourselves over our duty to God. We first make pleasing ourselves the thing we choose above everything else. At some moment, pleasing ourselves becomes the rule that controls how we act and the highest goal of our lives. But it is probably impossible for us to know exactly when that happens.
But whenever it happens, that is where our depravity begins.
It is our first moral choice.
It gives us our first moral character.
Nothing that came before it was morally good or bad at all.
The Bible tells us this happens so early in our lives that it can be said, “The wicked turn away from God from the womb;
they wander off as soon as they are born, telling lies.”
Of course, we should not take these words literally, because we cannot talk at all when we are first born. But the wicked tell lies as soon as they can talk.
The psalm writer says, “Look, I was formed in wickedness, and my mother conceived me in sin.”
These words are also clearly a figure of speech. After all, the actual material of an unborn baby cannot possibly be sin!
That would go against God’s own definition of sin.
He says, “sin is breaking the law.” But the law gives us a rule for how to act. It is not a rule about what we are made of.
If the material of an unborn child is sin, if the child itself is a sin before it is born, then God is the one who committed that sin.

This verse and others like it can mean only one thing, unless we want to turn God’s word into complete nonsense and set different passages against each other forever. They mean that we have been sinners from the very start of our life as moral beings, from the first moment we began making moral choices.
Insisting that passages like these must be taken literally is the most dangerous way to twist the Bible.

Take the rule that says these passages must be read literally, and use it to explain the whole Bible. Then you will prove not only that sin and holiness are physical substances, but also that God is made of physical matter.
In fact, this has been the great mistake people have made about depravity.

There is an important rule for understanding language: words must be understood according to the kind of thing they are describing. People have ignored this rule. They have often given a word the same meaning whether it was used about physical things or about the mind.

For example, God defines sin as nothing but breaking the law. Some people set this definition aside. Instead they bring in figures of speech which, if God’s own definition does not explain them, might seem to say that sin is something other than choosing to break the law. Doing this makes Scripture contradict itself in a way that can never be fixed. It ignores one of the most important rules for understanding the Bible.
It is playing games with God’s word.
It is putting the Holy Spirit to the test.
It is a foolish twisting of God’s truth, if not a deliberate one.
So the main reason sinners are against God is not that something is wrong with their nature that forces them to oppose him. It is because he will never make peace with their selfishness.
He is infinitely against the main goal they are chasing. That goal is to get happiness for themselves in a way that goes against HIS glory and the happiness of others.
Their highest goal is to increase their own happiness in a way that goes against the good of everyone.
God is infinitely against this.
Since their goal is unholy, the ways they use to reach it are, of course, just as wicked as the goal.
So God is just as much against the ways they use as he is against the goal they are trying to reach by them.
These ways make up the whole story of their lives.
All of them are meant, directly or indirectly, to reach the one goal that fills the sinner’s whole mind: making himself happy.
So God is against everything they do or say as long as they refuse to repent. He is against it sincerely, with a clear conscience, and without limit, just as he should be.
They want to make everything serve their own private interests.
God insists that they look for their happiness in a way that fits with the happiness of everyone and helps to increase it.
After all, because of the way things really are, this is the only way they can ever be happy.
So he sets his whole heart on defeating every attempt they make to find happiness their own way.
He will always be the enemy of all their selfish plans.
He makes every cup of selfish joy taste bitter. He “throws their” selfish “plans into confusion, and brings their violence back down on their own heads.”
So you see that sinners hate God because he is so holy.

As long as they stay selfish, and he is infinitely loving and kind, their characters, their plans, their desires, and all their ways are the exact opposite of his, and his are the exact opposite of theirs.
They are direct opposites. Until sinners change, what God said will always be true: “I cannot stand them, and they hate me.”
Holiness means caring about what is right.
God requires every moral being in the universe to do, feel, and say what is perfectly right, and the penalty for failing is infinite. He cannot require anything less than this without being unjust.
But sinners do not want to do what is right.

They want to be free to look out for their own private interests in everything. So of course they think of God as their enemy. He insists that they obey the law of what is right completely, no matter how totally it blocks their selfish plans.
Also, sinners hate God because he is so good.

He is good and he does good. He keeps on working for the good of everyone, and he often does it in a way that overturns all their selfish projects and scatters them to the winds. He knocks down the towers of Babel they are trying to climb up to heaven.

His heart is so set on doing good that, in carrying out his great plan, he has often brought down families and nations that stood in his way. Once he even drowned a whole world of sinners in a flood. He did it to stop the harm they were doing. He did it to bring the world back to a state where he could bring in the law and the Gospel, win mankind back, and save a huge number of people from hell.
Also, sinners hate God because he does not play favorites.
They see their own interests as the most important thing of all. They are working with all their might to make everything in the universe bend to serve those interests.
They want the weather, the winds, and the whole universe, both physical and moral, to fit in with their great goal. That goal is to make their own happiness complete and keep it going forever.

But God has a completely different goal from theirs. His aim is to increase the happiness of everyone. He increases the happiness of each person only as far as it fits with the happiness and rights of others. So he keeps blocking their favorite projects.
Even the elements of the physical universe are arranged and controlled in a way that often wrecks their dearest hopes. They destroy forever the dreams they cherish most.
But that is not all.
Sinners hate God because he warns that he will punish them for their sins.
He will not make a deal with them. He insists that they either obey or be damned.
He requires them to repent and change their lives, or else their souls will be destroyed forever.
A sinner who will not repent hates both of these choices more than anything.

To repent means admitting with all his heart that God is right and he is wrong. It means taking God’s side against himself. It means giving up the chase after his own happiness as the thing he wants most. It means giving himself, and all he is and has, to serving God and working for the good of everyone. He is completely unwilling to do this. But God insists on it. God will not make a deal. He demands complete surrender to his will, with no conditions, or else the eternal damnation of the sinner’s soul. So the sinner will not accept either one.
He thinks of God as his infinite and all-powerful enemy, and he fights against him with all his heart.
III. Now I will show that sinners hate God for the very reasons they should love him.
These are the very reasons why all holy beings do love him.

He is against all sin and every kind of harmful behavior. He cares deeply about the happiness of each person and of everyone together. In short, all the reasons selfish beings are so against him are the very reasons we have a duty to love him. They are why thinking beings who care at all about what is morally right feel that loving their Maker is right. They feel it is a duty that binds them without limit.
These are the reasons he deserves to be loved, and there are no others.
And these are exactly the reasons, and the only reasons, that sinners hate him.
They do not hate him because he deserves their hatred. They hate him because he deserves their love.
It is not because he is evil, but because he is good.
It is not because they have any good reason to hate him. It is because they have every possible reason to love him.
I mean exactly what I say.
Sinners hate God, and not only in spite of the infinitely strong reasons they have to love him. They hate him because of those very reasons.
It is not just that these reasons to love him fail to stop them from hating him. These reasons are the very things that make them hate him.
I will end this sermon with a few remarks.
First, this subject shows you how ridiculous and hypocritical unbelievers are.
They very often claim that when they study and search for the truth, they are fair and unbiased.
They insist that Christians have already taken sides. So, they say, Christians cannot look at Christianity honestly and without bias.
They say Christians cannot reach a conclusion anyone can trust, because they are already on Christianity’s side.
But unbelievers seem to think that they themselves are in a position to reach a fair and well-informed conclusion. They think they can examine the question and decide it without any prejudice.
But this is completely absurd.
They are not standing on neutral ground, as they think they are.
They have already taken sides against the Bible.
Their behavior proves that they are God’s enemies, even without the Bible.
It is a plain fact that no good being could approve of the way they live. If God is holy, he must hate their way of life.
You do not need a Bible to prove this.
Now here is a book that claims to be a message from God. It demands that they be holy in heart and life. It warns them that their sins will bring eternal death.
So is it not absurd?

These people are God’s enemies. They have already taken sides against God and against this message from him. Is it not ridiculous and hypocritical for them to set themselves up as the only fair judges?
Supposedly, they can sit down and study the subject without any bias.
They are on neutral ground, they say.
They have no opinions already formed that could lead their judgment astray.

The truth is this. Suppose Christians really are as biased in favor of Christianity as unbelievers say. Even so, unless unbelievers are willing to say that Christians are perfect—completely without sin and totally devoted to God—it will still turn out that Christians are less likely to be biased for Christianity than unbelievers are to be biased against it.

Unbelievers are completely against God. As I showed in my last two sermons, all sinners who have not repented are totally corrupt. Until Christians are completely perfect, they will not be as completely biased in favor of God as sinners are in favor of the devil.
So of course, until then, Christians will not be as likely to judge wrongly in favor of the Bible as sinners are to judge wrongly against it.

Christians are, on the whole, on God’s side, so they feel strongly attached to the Bible. Yet they still have a lot of sin left in them, so they can easily feel many objections to how strict its demands are. This puts them in the best position, and the best frame of mind, of anyone in this world to judge fairly.

They are not so wicked that they reject what they can see is true. And they are not such eager people-pleasers that they blindly give in, without checking, to everything that claims the right to be obeyed.

I do not mean that Christians can judge the truth of the Christian religion better this way than if they were perfect. But I do mean to push back against the absurd claim of unbelievers that a Christian’s faith is nothing more than blindly believing whatever he is told.
There has never been a time when the church was godly enough to put up with the limits that pure Christianity puts on people, unless the evidence for it struck them with the force of proof.
Second, this subject shows you that the wicked BEHAVIOR of sinners does not prove that their NATURE IS SINFUL.
People have thought that because everyone sins, we are forced to conclude that human nature must be sinful in itself.
People have said there is no other way to explain why everyone behaves sinfully.

They have argued that an effect must be the same kind of thing as its cause. Since the effects, or actions, of our nature are sinful in every case, they say, our nature, which is the cause, must be sinful too.

But if an effect must be the same kind of thing as its cause, and a cause must be the same kind of thing as its effect, then God must be made of matter. After all, he is the cause of all matter, so he would have to be matter himself.
The human soul would also have to be made of matter.
The soul acts on a person’s physical body. It makes the body act on other physical things around it. Since the soul is always causing physical changes all around, the soul would have to be physical.
That would be a quick way to get rid of the existence of all spirits!
But who would really accept this way of arguing? Who would seriously take as truth the absurd idea that an effect always decides what its cause is like?
The principles in this sermon explain easily and naturally why all people behave sinfully.

At the very start, every person takes selfishness as the main rule for how to act. Because of the very laws of how the mind works, this spoils all their moral behavior. It makes every moral action sinful.

Someone may ask, “How can it be that all children choose selfishness, unless their nature is sinful?” My answer is this. They choose to live for pleasing themselves, which is selfishness, because they have human nature. They also come into the world in the special circumstances in which all of Adam’s children have been born since the fall. But it is not because human nature is sinful in itself.
The reason they become sinners is found in two things. Their nature is what it is, and it is surrounded by the special temptations they face in a world full of sinners.
All the natural appetites and desires of the body and mind are innocent in themselves. But when they are strongly stirred up, they become a powerful temptation to give in to what is forbidden.
Temptation appeals to these natural appetites and desires so often that it leads every human being into sin.
Adam was created as a perfect, full-grown man. He certainly did not have a sinful nature. And yet temptation appealed to his innocent natural appetites, and that led him into sin.

Adam was a grown man without a sinful nature. He had lived for a time in obedience and perfect holiness. Yet temptation appealed to his innocent natural desires, and he changed his mind. Now think about babies. They have the same nature Adam had, and they are surrounded by even greater temptations. So how can the fact that all of them fall into sin prove that their nature itself is sinful?
Do we have to draw that conclusion?

Is it even a fair conclusion? Think about it! Adam was holy and grown up. Temptation appealed to his innocent nature and led him to choose selfishness. Yet no one suspects, or could suspect, that he had a sinful nature. But when little children are led into sin, in circumstances of temptation made even worse by the fall, we are supposed to believe their nature is sinful!

What wonderful reasoning! And what makes it even more absurd is this: to accept that our nature is sinful, we have to believe that sin is found in the material we are made of, and not in the choices we make. And that is impossible.

And what makes it especially guilty to conclude that our nature is sinful is this: to do it, we have to reject God’s own statement that “sin is breaking the law,” and accept a definition that is completely absurd.

Third, from the view of depravity I have given in these sermons, it is easy to see in what way sin is natural to sinners. It is also easy to see why people have blamed their nature when sin breaks out, as if their nature itself were sinful.
Everything we experience shows that, because of the way we are made, what our minds prefer most influences how we act, directly or indirectly.
In other words, when we want something more than anything else, it is natural for us to go after it. We may want some things that we do not go after.
But it makes no sense to say that we do not go after the thing we want most.

Wanting something most is the same thing as choosing it above all else, and that choice is in control. The will controls our actions. Just as surely, and just as naturally, we will go after the thing we want most.

So sinners have chosen selfishness as the ruling principle of their lives. As long as that selfishness stays in control, it is certain and natural that they will sin, and do nothing but sin. This fits exactly with the laws of how their minds work. In fact, it is the result of those laws.
As long as they hold on to selfishness as the most important thing, they cannot obey.
That is why “the sinful mind, the mind set on the flesh, does not obey God’s law, and in fact it cannot.”
So it is no surprise that sinners whose deepest choice is selfish find it very natural to sin, and extremely hard to do anything but sin.
Everyone has noticed this. So people have blamed human sin on human nature, and many have found fault with nature itself. But the truth is that sin is only the misuse of the powers our nature has.
Very many people have missed this fact: a deep but freely chosen preference for sin is the foundation, the source, and the cause of all other sins.
Sin is natural to people in only one way. It is natural for the mind to be guided in each thing it does by whatever it has chosen or prefers above all else.

So it will always be natural for a sinner to sin until he changes what his mind prefers most. He must come to prefer the glory of God and the good of God’s kingdom over his own separate interests that fight against them.
Fourth, here you can see what a change of heart is.
You can see what it is, why it is needed, and why the sinner has a duty to change his heart right away.
You can also see that the first thing a sinner will do, or can do, that God can accept must be to change his heart. That means changing the preference that rules his mind above everything else.
Fifth, someone may object, “If babies are not born with a sinful nature, then how are they saved by grace?”
But I ask in return, “If they are born with a sinful nature, how are they saved by grace?”
Does God create a baby as a sinner, and then call it grace when he saves the baby from the sinfulness of a nature that he himself created?

That is absurd, and it insults God! Think of it! People describe the ever-blessed God as either creating a sinful nature directly, or setting things up so that a nature sinful in itself had to be passed down from Adam, with no way around it. And then they call it grace when the baby is saved! (Saved not from what it has done, but from its nature!)
But let us take a look at this.
Here are two views. The first view says that babies have no moral character at all until they have actually broken God’s law.
It says that their first moral actions are always sinful, but that before they make moral choices they are neither sinful nor holy.
It says that since they have no moral character, they deserve neither praise nor blame. They deserve neither life nor death from God.
God could wipe them out of existence without being unfair, or he may give them eternal life as a free gift they have not earned.
The other view says that babies have a sinful nature that they inherited from Adam.

The Bible teaches that everyone in the human family who is ever saved must be saved by grace. Those who hold the view that babies’ nature is sinful think theirs is the only view that can give grace the credit for saving babies who die before they actually sin.
But let us look at these two views for a few moments.
The Bible clearly uses the word grace in different ways.
Sometimes it means the same thing as holiness.
To grow in grace means to grow in holiness.
Its most common meaning seems to be kindness that we do not deserve.
Sometimes it is used in a wider way that includes the idea of mercy or forgiveness.
Now, when babies die before they actually sin, the only way their salvation can come from grace is in the sense of kindness they did not deserve or earn.
If they have never sinned, they cannot be saved by grace if by grace we mean mercy or forgiveness.

To say a child can be forgiven for having a sinful nature is ridiculous nonsense. A baby who dies before actually sinning can be called saved by grace only in the sense of kindness it did not deserve, and not in the sense of mercy or forgiveness.
In this sense, the baby’s salvation is by grace.
The baby has never earned eternal life. He has never done anything that makes God owe it to him to save him. God could wipe him out of existence without being unfair at all.

But suppose it pleases God, for Christ’s sake, to give eternal life to someone he could fairly wipe out of existence. I fully believe it does please him. Then he is showing that child infinite kindness.
But let us look at the other view for a moment.

This view denies that babies have a sinful nature. It rejects the monstrous idea that God created their nature sinful and then pretends to save the baby by grace from a nature he himself created, as if the baby deserved to be damned for being what God made it.
People who hold this view insist that their view shows just as much grace in saving babies as the impossible teaching of a sinful nature does.
The truth is that the very existence of the whole human race is purely a matter of grace, and it is connected to the atonement of Jesus Christ.
If the atonement had not already been planned, Adam and Eve would have been sent to hell right away and would never have had any children or descendants.
The human race could never have existed.
There could never have been any babies or adults (except Adam and Eve) if Christ had not graciously stepped in for mankind by his atonement.
No doubt it was because God looked ahead to this, and because of it, that Adam and Eve were spared. That is why the law’s sentence was not carried out on them right away.

So every baby owes its very existence to God’s grace in Jesus Christ. And if it dies before it actually sins, it owes its eternal life to Christ just as completely as if it had been the worst sinner on earth.

In neither of these views does the grace that saves babies include forgiveness. But in both views they are saved by grace, because they owe their very existence to Christ’s atonement. And in both cases they are rescued from circumstances in which, if they had lived long enough to form a moral character, they certainly would have sinned and deserved eternal death.

So suppose someone objects to the view of depravity I have given in these sermons by saying it denies God’s grace in saving babies. That person either misunderstands what I have taught or is twisting it on purpose.
I want to ask a question, and I wish someone would answer it, if it can be answered. How does one view show any more grace in saving babies than the other?

Will someone say that if babies’ nature is sinful, grace must change it? Will they say this is the difference: in neither case does the baby need forgiveness, but in one case its nature needs to be changed, and in the other it does not?
But suppose his nature does need to be changed.
I deny that changing it is an act of grace. If God made his nature wrong, so that it can do nothing but sinful actions, then God is obligated to change it.

Calling this grace is the worst kind of trifling. Think of making a being come into existence with a sinful or faulty nature, and then calling it grace to change that nature and make it what it should have been in the first place. That is playing games with serious things, and it is telling lies on God’s behalf.
Sixth, sinners’ hatred is also cruel.
It is just as God says: they are “giving back hatred for his love.”
God is love. That is why they hate him, and it is the only reason.
Notice this: it is not because they overlook the fact that he is infinitely kind and good.
They do not just hate him for other reasons, in spite of this fact. They hate him because of this fact.
In the most literal and complete sense, they are paying back his love with hatred.
He is against their hurting each other.
He wants them to be happy. He is infinitely against their making themselves miserable.

Think of a parent on earth who could see ahead that his beloved child’s way of life would ruin the child. God is infinitely more against sinners doing anything that will harm themselves than that parent ever was against his child’s behavior.
His heart longs for them with a tenderness infinitely greater than any parent’s.
He pleads and reasons with sinners. He says, “Oh, do not do that disgusting thing that I hate.”
“How can I give you up, Ephraim?
How can I hand you over, Israel?
How can I make you like Admah?
How can I treat you like Zeboim?
My heart is turned over within me, and all my pity is burning.”

He feels all the tender love that pours out of a father’s heart. He also feels all of a father’s opposition to anything that will harm his children. Children sometimes hate and insult their parents for standing against the wayward paths that lead them to destruction. In the same way, sinners hate God more than they hate any other being, because he is infinitely more opposed to their destroying their own souls.
Seventh, the better God is, the more sinners hate him.
The better he is, the more he opposes their selfishness. And as long as they stay selfish, the more he opposes their selfishness, the angrier they get with him.
In my second sermon on depravity, I showed that people hate God more than anything else.
The only reason is that his excellence is the highest excellence there is.
His goodness is pure goodness, with nothing else mixed in. So their hatred is pure hostility, with nothing else mixed in.
If there were any flaw in his character, people would not hate him so much.

Suppose God were not perfectly good—in fact, infinitely good. Then people might not be totally depraved. I mean they might not be totally against his character. But his character has no flaw at all. That is why they hate him sincerely, wholeheartedly, and perfectly.
Eighth, as long as sinners refuse to repent, the more God tries to do them good, the more they will hate him.

Think of all God does while they hold on to their selfishness. He works to hold it back, to fence them in, and to keep them from getting what their selfish desires want. He steps in to tear away their idols and to wean them from the world. He makes bitter every cup of joy they try to satisfy themselves with. He uses more and more ways to win them back, to make them holy, and to save them. But if their selfishness stays unbroken, then the more he does all this, the more deeply and eternally they will hate him.
Ninth, sinners are infinitely to blame for acting this way, and it deserves eternal death.
It is impossible to imagine guilt deeper or more deserving of damnation than the guilt of sinners who live under the Gospel.
They sin in such special circumstances that their guilt is even worse than the guilt of devils.
Devils have broken the law, and so have you, sinners.
But devils never rejected the Gospel.
They are guilty of rebellion, and so are you.
But they have never rejected the offer of forgiveness. They have never, as it were, kicked away the offer of eternal life through the blood the Son of God shed to atone for sin.
Sinners, if you do not deserve eternal death, then I cannot imagine that any devil in hell deserves it.
And yet, strange as it sounds, sinners often talk as if it were doubtful whether they deserve to be damned.
Tenth, this subject makes it easy to see that saints and angels will be completely satisfied with God’s justice when he damns sinners.

They will never enjoy the misery of those who are damned. But they will take pleasure in seeing justice shown. They will be glad to see God’s insulted majesty and wounded honor defended. They will be glad for the respect that punishment will create for God’s law and character. They will see that the way God shows his justice is glorious. And they will shout “Hallelujah!” while “the smoke of their torment will rise forever and ever.”
Amos 3:3 — “Can two people walk together unless they agree?”
In the Bible, we often find a “no” statement written in the form of a question.
Our text is an example of this. So we should understand the prophet to be saying that two people cannot walk together unless they agree.
For two people to agree means more than agreeing in their ideas or their understanding. We often see people who agree in their beliefs but are very different in how they feel and how they live.
Their minds may accept the same truths, while those truths affect their hearts and actions in very different ways.
Saints and sinners often hold the same religious beliefs on paper. Yet it is clear that they are very different in how they feel and live.
We have reason to believe that holy angels and demons understand and accept the same truths in their minds. And yet how differently those truths affect them!
The same truths have different effects on different minds. This happens because each person’s heart, or feelings, are in a different state.
To put it another way, the difference lies in how each person receives these truths—how they feel and act because of them.
We should also notice that the same things and truths will affect the same person very differently at different times.
This, too, comes from the different state of that person’s feelings at those times.
Or, to say it better, this difference lies in the different way the mind is acting at those times.
All pleasure and pain, all happiness and misery, all sin and holiness, live in the heart and its feelings. That is where they belong.

Whenever a truth or a thing is put before our minds, we feel either satisfied or dissatisfied, pleased or pained. That reaction depends completely on the state of our feelings at that moment. In fact, the reaction is made up of those feelings.
If the thing matches our feelings, and stirs them up and feeds them in a pleasant way, of course we are pleased. That is because our pleasure and happiness are made of those pleasant feelings.
So the higher something lifts these feelings when it is put before our minds, the greater our pleasure is.

But if the thing or truth does not match our feelings, it cannot please us. Suppose it is off to the side of what we are feeling right now, and we refuse to change the direction of our feelings. Then one of two things will happen. Either we will not care about it, because our feelings are busy with something else. Or, if it keeps pushing on us, we will turn away from it and resist it.
Now suppose it is not only off to the side of what we care about right now, but actually against it. Then, as long as our feelings stay the same, we will—and must—resist it and fight it.

Sometimes a subject is brought up and pushed on us that is different from the one our feelings are caught up in. Then we feel bored, or even annoyed and disgusted. But that is not all. Even on the same subject, something may be presented that is far above or far below the level of our feelings. If our feelings stay the same, and we refuse to be drawn in and lifted to that level, we will feel bored—and perhaps hurt and offended.

Suppose the subject is shown in a way that is below the level of our present feelings. Then we cannot be interested until it comes up to our level. And suppose the subject keeps being held before us in this cooling way, which seems cheap to us, while we are struggling to keep our high feelings. Then we become unhappy, because our feelings are not being fed. They are being fought.

Now suppose the subject is presented in a way that is far above the level of our feelings, and our feelings stay low and refuse to rise. Then it does not match or feed our feelings, so we cannot be interested. It seems like wild fanaticism to us. We are annoyed by the warmth we do not choose to share. And the higher it is above our own temperature, the more disgusted we are.
Everyone’s experience will prove these things true. They hold true on every subject and in every situation, because they are based on principles built into human nature itself.

Take a passionate politician. Talk to him about his favorite subject, in the way he likes best. Once his feelings are caught up in it, add the fire of powerful speaking. Make it burn and blaze in his mind, and you will delight him greatly.
But change your style and tone. Turn down your fire and feeling. Turn the subject over. Present it in a drier way. At once he loses almost all his interest and becomes uneasy as things go downhill.
Now change the subject. Bring up death and the solemn judgment. He is shocked and stunned. Keep pressing him with them, and he is disgusted and offended.

Why does he lose interest in his favorite subject? It is the natural result of taking away the burning picture of it that was pouring fire through his feelings. Why is he disgusted when you change the subject? It is the natural result of putting in front of him something that went directly against the way he felt at that moment.
Unless he chooses to turn his mind along with you as you change the subject, he cannot help being displeased.
Picture a trained musician listening, almost carried away with joy, as a beautiful piece of music is played with great skill.
Now throw some clashing, off-key notes at him. In a moment he is in pain.
Make the harsh sounds louder and longer, and he walks out of the room in disgust.

Or imagine this. You love music, but right now you are sad. You are going through great trouble, and you feel like crying. The gentle, mournful sound of a wind harp drifts softly to your ears and seems to melt around your heart. Your tears flow fast. But then the racket of trumpets, drums, and cymbals bursts in, along with a shrill fife playing a cheerful, quick march. It drowns out the soft whispers of the harp. You feel upset. You turn away and cover your ears.
The mournful harp touched you in a tender spot. It matched your feelings, so you enjoyed it.
The military music went against the way you felt. You were too sad for it to lift and cheer your feelings. So it could not help but upset you.

Now suppose your heart is glowing with religious feeling. At that moment you do not want anyone to bring up a different subject. You are also not interested in anything on the same subject that is far below the level of your feelings.

Suppose you hear a cold man preach or pray. As long as he stays cold and you are warm with feeling, you are not interested. Your feelings are not fed and warmed unless he comes up to your level. If that does not happen, you are upset, and perhaps disgusted by his coldness.
This is only natural.

Suppose that, like Paul, “you have great heaviness and constant sorrow in your heart” for sinners who are dying. Suppose “the Spirit helps you in your weakness, pleading for you just as God wills, with groanings that cannot be spoken.” While you feel this way, you hear someone pray who never mentions sinners. You hear a minister preach who says very little to them, and says it in a heartless, empty way. You are not interested. Feeling as you do, you cannot be. Instead, you are hurt and upset.

Now suppose you are lukewarm, and your feelings are worldly and earthly. You hear someone encourage, pray, or preach who is very spiritual, passionate, and loving. Maybe you cling to your sins and your feelings will not rise. Maybe prejudice, or pride, or the earthly, fleshly state of your feelings makes you refuse to catch fire and take hold of the subject. Then even though you agree with every word he says, you are not pleased.
He is warmer than you are. You are annoyed by the man’s manner, his fire, and his spirit.
If your feelings stay low, then the higher he rises, the farther apart you are, and the more annoyed you become.
While your heart is wrong, the more right he is, the more he burns you. If your heart will not catch fire, the more disgusted you become.
In both of these cases, the people whose feelings are at or near the same level as the one speaking or praying will not feel bothered. They will be pleased.
Lukewarm people will listen to the dull man and say, “That was pretty good.”
Their pleasure will be small, because their feelings are low. But overall, they are pleased.
People who have no feelings at that moment will, of course, feel nothing at all.
Everyone who feels deeply will listen with sadness and pain.
These same people would listen to the passionate man with great interest.
Let him glow and blaze, and they are thrilled.
But as long as worldly, cold-hearted people refuse to rise, they cannot help being bothered and offended by his fire.
From what we have said, we can learn several things.
First, we learn why people who disagree about points of doctrine, and who belong to different church groups, will often walk together for a while in great harmony and love.
It is because they feel deeply, and they feel the same way.
While their feelings match, their differences are mostly lost or forgotten. They will walk together as long as their hearts agree.
Next, we see why new believers love to spend time with each other, and with older Christians who have the most religious feeling. These walk together because they feel the same way.
Next, we see why lukewarm people who say they are Christians, and sinners who have not repented, have the same problems with the methods used in revivals.
We often hear them complain about the way people preach and pray.
Their complaints are the same. They find fault with the same things, and they use the same arguments to back up their complaints.
The reason is that, at that time, their feelings are almost the same. It is the fire and the spirit that bother their frozen hearts.
For now they walk together, because in their feelings they agree.
Next, we see why ministers and Christians who visit revivals often raise objections at first to the methods being used. They nitpick, and sometimes they even take the side of the wicked.
The truth is, they often come from places where no revivals are happening at the time. So they often feel scolded and annoyed by the warmth and spirit they see.
The praying, preaching, and talking are warmer than they are right now.

Sometimes something holds their feelings down so that they do not enter into the spirit of the work. It may be prejudice because the revival is happening in a church group different from theirs. It may be prejudice against the preacher or the people. Or perhaps it is pride, or envy, or love of the world, or something like that.
While their hearts stay wrong, of course they will nitpick. And while their feelings stay low, the more right something is—the more spiritual and holy—the more it is bound to displease them.
Next, we see why ministers and ordinary Christians disagree about which methods are wise.

Think of a man who sees and feels the endlessly serious things of eternity. He will judge what is wise or unwise in the use of methods very differently from someone whose spiritual eyes are almost shut.

A man whose heart is breaking for sinners who are perishing will, of course, think it wise, right, and necessary to “speak very plainly.” He will think he must deal with them in a very earnest and loving way.
He would think the opposite approach was very unwise, dangerous, and even criminal.

But a man who feels very little for them, and sees little of their danger, will be happy to use very different methods, or to use them in a very different way. And of course he will have very different ideas about what is wise.
This is why we see the same person holding very different ideas about wisdom at different times. As a result, he acts very differently at those times.
In fact, a man’s ideas about which methods are wise in revivals will depend on the state of his own feelings, and on the feelings of the people around him. And to a large degree, they ought to.
After all, what would be wise in some situations would be very unwise in others.
What would be wise for one man might be very unwise for another.

What would be wise for a man when his feelings are in a certain state, and in certain circumstances, would be extremely unwise for the same man when his feelings are different and his circumstances have changed.

Suppose God’s word does not condemn a method. In most cases, it is then extremely hard to form the opinion that the method is unwise. And it is often very wrong to say so in public. That is, unless you are in a position to enter into the feelings and circumstances of the person and the people at the time the method was used.
If Christians and ministers would remember these things, a great many unkind and judgmental speeches would be avoided. And much harm to the cause of truth and goodness would be prevented.
Next, we see why lukewarm Christians and sinners are not bothered by dull preaching or praying.
It does not touch their feelings at all. So it does not upset or offend them.

So we see what happens during a revival, when cold and wicked hearts are being stirred up by plain, sharp preaching. If a dull minister is invited to preach to the people, the wicked and cold-hearted will praise his preaching.
This explains why, during times of revival, we often hear sinners and lukewarm Christians wishing their minister would preach the way he used to. They wish he would be himself again.
The reason is plain. He never used to move them. But now his fire, his spirit, and his sharpness annoy them and disturb their worldly sleep.
Next, we can learn here how much weight to give to the opinions of ministers and Christians—and to our own opinions—when our feelings are in a bad state.
How much does this man approve of what was said or done?

What does he think about the methods being used? People often ask and answer questions like these. Then they trust the answer as a great authority, without paying any attention to the state of that man’s feelings at the time.

In most cases, we are completely wrong to put much trust in our own opinions, or in other people’s opinions, about which methods are wise—unless we have evidence that our feelings, or theirs, are in the right state. If our feelings changed, we would almost certainly see things differently and change our opinion.

Christians would do well to remember and follow the resolution of President Edwards: “that he would always do what seemed most fitting to him at the times when he saw the things of religion most clearly.”
Next, we learn why churches are sometimes shaken up by revivals.

Most churches probably have at least a few hypocrites in them. Sometimes a revival has much of its mere human emotion stripped away and becomes very spiritual. Then its fire and spirit bother these people. They oppose it inside, and sometimes openly.

But sometimes only part of the true Christians in a church wake up from their sleep and become very spiritual and heavenly-minded, while the rest stay worldly and earthly in their feelings. Then the church is in danger of being torn in two.

As those who are awake become more committed, more spiritual, and more active, the others will become jealous and offended, if they will not wake up. The commitment of the others makes them feel scolded. So they will nitpick. And the higher the more spiritual people rise above them, the more annoyed they become.

The closer the committed ones come to the right state of feeling, the farther apart the two groups are. As the committed ones climb higher in holy feeling, if the others will not climb with them, those others will almost certainly sink lower. In the end they really share no feelings at all. They can no longer walk together, because they do not agree.

When a church is in this state, all its members need to search their hearts deeply. This situation is greatly to be feared and deeply to be mourned when it happens. But it is easy to explain by these simple principles of our nature. And sometimes it will happen, no matter how wisely men or angels try to prevent it.
Next, we see why ministers sometimes lose their churches because of revivals.
Sometimes, even when the minister has not acted unwisely, many people in his church and congregation will not enter into the spirit of a revival.

If his own feelings catch fire, and he cares deeply for his flock and for the honor of his Master, he will certainly press the truth on them. He will annoy them with his spirit, his sharpness, and his fire, until he offends them.

If their feelings are wrong, then the more powerfully and forcefully he pushes the truth on them, the more he will offend them—unless their feelings change. In the end, he may find it best to leave them.

All this may happen, and it may be just as right and necessary for a minister as it was for Paul. Paul left places and people when some became hardened, argued against him, spoke against God, and said evil things about the Way in front of the crowds.
Another situation may happen too. The church and people may wake up while the shepherd sleeps and refuses to wake.
This will surely turn their hearts away from him and destroy their trust in him.
In either case, they may find they cannot walk together, because they do not agree.
In the first case, the minister should obey Christ’s command and “shake the dust off his feet as a witness against them.”
In the second case, the church should shake off their sleepy minister. They are better off without him than with him.
“How terrible it will be for the shepherds who feed only themselves!
Aren’t shepherds supposed to feed the sheep?
But you do not feed the flock.
So listen, you shepherds, to the word of the Lord.

This is what the Lord God says: Look, I am against the shepherds. I will demand my flock back from them. I will stop them from feeding the flock, and the shepherds will not feed themselves anymore. I will save my flock from their mouths, so that the sheep will not be their food anymore.”
Ezekiel 34:2, 3, 9, 10. President Edwards says:

“Ministers may preach very good teaching, and work very hard and carefully. But if they show their people that they do not like this work, and are doubtful and suspicious of it, they will very likely do their people much more harm than good.

Think about what could happen if their people were allowed to believe that this great and unusual work is God’s work. The very nature of the work itself, together with the example of other towns and whatever preaching they might hear now and then, would likely do much more to wake up their people and stir them up in their faith than all the minister’s other efforts with them.

What is more, the minister’s opinion will make them suspicious of the work they hear about in other places. Because of this, the mighty hand of God that shows in it will lose its effect on their minds. But that is not all. It will also make them suspicious of anything like it that appears among themselves. They will think it is part of the same sickness that has spread so widely through the land.

And what does this really do? It makes people suspicious of all living faith. It gets people talking against it and discouraging it wherever it shows up, and knocking it on the head as fast as it rises.

We ministers, by frowning at this work year after year, will keep the sheep away from their pasture instead of doing a shepherd’s job and feeding them. In a time like this, our people would be much better off with no regular minister at all.
“Those of us who hold this sacred office need to be careful about what we do and how we behave at this time. A smaller thing in a minister will hinder God’s work than in other people.

We might be very silent, or say little about the work in our public prayers and preaching, or seem to carefully avoid speaking about it in conversation. If so, our people will take it to mean that we are suspicious of it—we who are their guides, the ones they look to for spiritual teaching. This will tend to make them suspicious too. And then the results I described earlier will follow.
It is our job more than anyone else’s to promote the work of God. So if we actually hinder it and stand in its way, how can we expect to share in its wonderful blessings?
And by keeping others from those blessings, we will keep them out of heaven. So we should think about those terrible words Christ spoke to the Jewish teachers in Matthew 23:13:
‘How terrible for you! You lock up the kingdom of heaven. You do not go in yourselves, and you do not let those who are trying to enter go in.’
If we keep the sheep away from their pasture, how will we answer to the great Shepherd? He bought the flock with his precious blood, and he has put them in our care.

I humbly ask every minister who has for so long been against this work, and has looked down on it, to think about this: has he been like Michal, who had no child? Or at least, has he been mostly barren and unsuccessful in his work? I pray to God it may not be a barrenness that lasts forever, as hers did.”
Next, we can see that worldly church members and sinners have no problem with mere human emotion.
During revivals, it is common to hear a lot of complaints against what people call “mere emotion.”

No one denies that a lot of this kind of emotion is sometimes stirred up in revivals. That is not strange. In fact, it is impossible for real religious feelings to be stirred up very much without also stirring up our natural human emotions and sensitivities. To be surprised at this, or to object to a revival because of it, is clearly foolish.
But in most cases, it is not the human emotion that offends people. As far as those emotions go, saints and sinners, and worldly and spiritual Christians, all feel exactly the same.
Sinners have as much natural emotion as saints. Cold church members have as much of it as warm, spiritual Christians.
So as far as natural emotion goes, they can all share it. And in fact, we often see that they do.

Try a style of encouraging or preaching that is designed to stir up only sympathy and natural emotion. You will soon see that cold Christians, warm Christians, and sinners all feel exactly alike. They will all cry and seem to melt, and no one will be offended. And, I might add, no one will be convinced of their sin or converted.

But change your style. Make your message more spiritual and holy. Throw yourself into it with passion and power, and appeal directly to the conscience and the heart. Their tears will soon dry up. The worldly and cold-hearted will become uneasy, and soon they will find themselves offended.

As far as natural emotion goes, they walk together, because in this they agree. But as soon as the feeling becomes spiritual and holy, they cannot go any farther together. Here they do not agree. And as long as sinners refuse to repent and cold hearts stay cold, they cannot agree.
Next, we can see why sinners who have not repented cannot like pure revivals.
It is because God is in them.
Sinners hate God. That is why God commands them to make themselves a new heart.
This is the reason—the only reason—why sinners need a new heart.

While they are ruled by “a worldly mind, which is at war with God,” it is obvious that they do hate, and must hate, everything that is like God. They hate it exactly as much as they see that it looks like him.
So we see that the more a revival has mere emotion and everything wrong stripped away, the more it is bound to offend wrong hearts.
The more of God and the less human weakness people can see in revivals, the more they will—and must—stir up the hatred of worldly hearts.
Next, we learn how to judge what look like revivals when the wicked do not oppose them.
If people ruled by a worldly mind do not oppose a revival, it must be for one of three reasons.

First, they may be so convinced of their sin that they do not dare to oppose it openly (and even then, they oppose it in their hearts). Second, there may be nothing of the Holy Spirit in these revivals. Or third—and this often happens—the methods may have been used unwisely to stir up the crowd’s emotions. Then the work of the Holy Spirit is kept out of the sinner’s sight, buried under a pile of mere emotion.
Anything that keeps the Holy Spirit’s work out of the sinner’s sight tends to prevent opposition.
And anything that lets the sinner see the hand of God will surely stir up the opposition of his unchanged heart.

So if a stirring does not bring out the opposition of the wicked and those whose hearts are wrong, then either it is not a revival at all, or it is being run in such a way that sinners do not see God’s finger in it.

So we see this: the purer and holier the methods used to promote a revival, the more they are stripped of human weakness and mere sympathy, and the more like God they are, the more they are bound to stir up the opposition of every wrong heart.
When a man’s heart is wrong about any subject, it is obvious that he cannot truly approve of what is right about that subject. That would be a contradiction.
It would be like saying he could feel both right and wrong about the same thing at the same time.

So it seems that, if all other things are equal, some methods and ways of preaching are nearest to right. They are the ones that bring out the most of the heart’s natural hatred, and that stand most directly against wrong hearts—both in what is said and in how it is said.
This shows how foolish it is to work hard at pleasing people whose feelings about religion are in a wrong state.
They cannot be pleased with anything right and holy while their hearts are in this wrong state. As we have just seen, that would be a contradiction.
This shows why so many wrong feelings are often stirred up during revivals.
Pure revivals naturally stir up wrong feelings in wrong hearts.

Revivals on earth stir up wrong feelings in hell. Whenever they come in contact with rebellious hearts, whether in the church or outside it, they will disturb that same spirit and stir up those same feelings.
Wherever the Holy Spirit comes, or is seen at work, the opposite spirit is naturally disturbed.
When saints have a great deal of right and holy feeling, it will naturally stir up a great deal of unholy and wicked feeling in all the hearts that are set on being wrong.
The more right and holy feeling there is, the more wrong and unholy feeling there will be—unless sinners and worldly church members bow down and give in.

They cannot walk together, because they do not agree. And the more holy and heavenly the saints become in their feelings and actions, the farther apart they will be. In the end, the light of eternity will set them as far apart in their feelings as heaven is from hell.

This shows what the difference between heaven and hell really is, when it comes to moral character, happiness, and misery. It is the different state of the hearts and feelings of the people who live there.
This proves beyond any argument that sinners cannot be saved unless they are born again.
In other words, by the very nature of things, it is clearly impossible for sinners to walk with saints and holy angels and be happy with them—unless their feelings are completely changed.
Sinners cannot walk with the saints here on earth.
As soon as the saints stop living “the way this world lives,” sinners think it strange that they no longer rush with them into the same wild living. So they start “speaking evil of them.”
As soon as Christians wake up and become spiritual, active, holy, and heavenly-minded, and break away from their empty and wicked friendships with the world, sinners are always upset and offended.
They try to imagine that it is something wrong in the saints, and in revivals, that offends them.
But the truth is, it is the little bit that is right in the saints—and the part of revivals that has the most of God in it—that offends them most.

If the saints were as holy as the angels, or as holy as they will be in heaven, sinners would be that much farther from sharing any feelings with them. And as saints rise in holiness and sinners sink in sin, they will move farther and farther apart forever and ever.

Lastly, I note that this shows why the lives and preaching of the prophets, of Christ and his apostles, and the revivals of the early church met with so much more violent opposition than preachers and revivals meet today. That opposition came from worldly people who claimed to be religious and from ungodly sinners.

No one can deny that the saints in those days “were cruelly mocked and whipped, and even chained and put in prison. They were stoned, sawn apart, tempted, and cut down with the sword. They wandered around in sheepskins and goatskins. They were poor, suffering, and tortured (the world was not worthy of them). They wandered in deserts and on mountains, and in caves and hideouts in the earth.”

No one does or can deny this: many people who claimed to be saints, and huge numbers of ungodly sinners, bitterly opposed the preaching of the prophets, of Christ and his apostles, and of the first ministers. They opposed it more than they oppose any preacher today.

We should not hide the fact that religious people were often the leaders of this opposition. They stirred up the Romans to crucify Jesus, and later to persecute and destroy his followers and crucify his apostles.

Even the religious teachers and scholars of the law tried to turn the crowds against the Savior and keep them from listening to his teaching. “He has a devil in him, and he is mad,” they said. “Why do you listen to him?”
They led the way in opposing the apostles in the revivals the apostles were part of.

We must also admit that those revivals made a great deal of noise in the world. The apostles were even accused of “turning the world upside down.” Sinners were often badly hardened by the preaching of Christ and his apostles. They “were filled with great anger” and opposed them so bitterly that Christ told his apostles to “leave them alone.”

In some places where the apostles preached, “some” became so “hardened” that they “argued, spoke against God, and said evil things about the Way.” So the apostles were forced to leave and go to other places. Sometimes they had to leave in very humiliating ways, barely escaping with their lives.
We do not need to be embarrassed to face these facts. They are easy to explain by the principle in our text, which this sermon has illustrated.

None of these things proves that the prophets, and Christ and his apostles, were unwise and unholy men. It does not prove that their preaching was too harsh and severe, or that revivals were being handled wrongly in those days.

The truth is this. The prophets lived much holier lives, and they were much bolder and more faithful in giving their messages. Christ was much more searching, plain, sharp, and personal in his preaching, and in his life he was completely “separate from sinners.” The apostles were very sharp and plain in dealing with sinners and with people who claimed to be saints, and they lived very holy lives of self-denial. That is why worldly church people and ungodly sinners could not walk with them.
The methods used back then to promote revivals were holier and purer than they are now.
There was less mere sympathy. There was less of that fake, smooth manner, and less of that fancy language designed to win the applause of the ungodly.

They “refused to use hidden, dishonest methods. They did not act with trickery or twist the word of God.” They preached “not with the smooth, tempting words of human wisdom,” but “very plainly.” As a result, the ungodly, both inside and outside the church, were filled with anger.
Stephen spoke in such a holy and searching way that the leaders of Israel “ground their teeth at him.”
But this does not prove that he was unwise.

Today’s revivals move much more quietly and slowly than they did on the day of Pentecost and at many other times and places. They also cause much less noise and opposition among cold church members and ungodly sinners. But that does not prove that people understand revivals better now than they did then. Nor does it prove that the ministers and Christians involved in today’s revivals are wiser than the apostles and the first Christians. To think so would show great spiritual pride in us.
And we must not say that the human heart has changed, or that God’s character has become less offensive “to the worldly mind.”

No! The truth is that the prophets, Christ, his apostles, and the early saints were holier, bolder, and more active. They were plainer and sharper in their preaching. They were less like this crazy world. In a word, they were wiser and more like heaven than we are. That is why they were hated more than we are, and why their preaching and praying offended people so much more than ours does.

In their days, revivals were freer from worldly scheming, and from the kind of management that tends to hide the bare hand of God from the sinner’s sight. That is why those revivals made so much more noise than the ones we see today. That is why they stirred up so much of earth and hell to oppose them, and why they shook the world and turned it upside down.
Back then, people knew that “people could not serve God and riches.”
They could see that it was true: “if anyone is determined to live for God in Christ Jesus, he will suffer persecution.”
People understood then that if “ministers pleased people, they were not the servants of Christ.”
The church and the world could not walk together, because back then they did not agree.

We must not become proud and imagine that we are wise and clever. We must not think we have learned how to handle worldly church members and sinners, whose “worldly mind is at war with God,” in a way that does not stir up their opposition to truth and holiness. Christ and his apostles did stir it up.

Instead, we should understand this: if they have less trouble with us—with our lives and our preaching—than they had with Christ and the apostles, it is because we are less holy, less heavenly, and less like God than they were.
If we walk with the lukewarm and the ungodly, or they walk with us, it is because we agree.
For two cannot walk together unless they agree.
Our text: “…does not seek its own interests.” — 1
Corinthians 13:5.
This means that charity, or Christian love, does not seek its own interests.
Tonight I want to prove this statement:
CARING ABOUT OUR OWN HAPPINESS MORE THAN ANYTHING ELSE CANNOT GO TOGETHER WITH TRUE RELIGION.

This statement really belongs first in the series of ideas I have been working to explain in these lectures. I would have talked about it first if I had known that many people who call themselves Christians seriously doubted it.
But I can honestly say that when I started these lectures, I did not expect anyone to have a real problem with this point. So I mostly took it for granted that selfishness is not religion.
That is why I passed over this point and only tried a little to prove it.

But since then I have learned that many people who call themselves Christians believe that caring most about our own happiness is true religion. So I think I need to look at this subject more carefully. I will give you the arguments for what I believe is the truth.
To prove my point, I want to keep apart things that are different. So I will do three things:
I. Show what this statement does not mean when I say that caring most about our own happiness is not religion.
II. Show what it does mean. And
III. Try to prove it.

blocks.x: I. First, I will explain what this statement does not mean.

s: 1. The question is not whether it is right to care about our own happiness at all.
In fact, I agree, and even insist, that caring properly about our own happiness is part of our duty. We should value it as much as it is really worth when we weigh it against other interests.
God has commanded us to love our neighbor as ourselves.
This clearly makes it a duty to love ourselves, or to care about our own happiness. We are to use the same rule for ourselves that we use for others.
2. The statement does not mean that we should ignore God’s promises and warnings as they apply to us.

It is clearly right to pay attention to God’s promises and his warnings of punishment as they apply to us. But we should weigh them by how much our own interests are really worth compared with other interests.
But anyone can see that a warning against us is not as important as a warning against a great many people.
Imagine a warning of trouble aimed at you alone.
Clearly, that is not as important as a warning that included your whole family.
Now imagine it reached the whole church, or the state, or the whole nation, or the whole world.
Here it is easy to see that one person’s happiness, even though it matters a great deal, should not be put above everything else.
I am a minister.
Imagine God says to me, “If you do not do your duty, you will be sent to hell.”
That would be a terrible thing, and I should try to avoid it.
But imagine he says, “If your people do not do their duty, they will all be sent to hell. But if you do your duty faithfully, you will probably save the whole church.”
Should the fear of something bad happening to me move me as much as the fear of a whole church being sent to hell? Clearly not.
3. The question is not whether we should put our eternal good ahead of our good in this life.
I clearly teach, and so does the Bible, that we must treat our eternal good as far more important than our good in this life.
For example, the Bible tells us, “Do not work for food that spoils. Work for what lasts on into eternal life.”
This teaches that, compared with eternal life, we should not value the things of this life at all.

Our Savior teaches the same thing when he says, “Do not pile up riches for yourselves on earth, where moths and rust eat them away and thieves dig through the walls and steal them. Instead, pile up riches for yourselves in heaven, where no moth or rust eats them away and no thieves dig through or steal.”
Here we are given the same duty: to choose what lasts forever over what lasts only for this life.

Here is another example. Christ once sent out his disciples in pairs to preach and to do miracles. They came back full of joy and excitement, because they found that even the demons had to give in to their power.
“Lord, even the demons obey us.”
Jesus answers, “Do not be glad that the demons obey you. Be glad instead that your names are written in heaven.”
Here he teaches that having our names written in heaven is a greater good than having the greatest power in this world—even power over the demons themselves.
Everywhere the Bible teaches that in everything we do, we should choose eternal good over the good of this life.
But that is very different from saying that our own personal eternal good should be the highest thing we aim for.
4. The statement does not mean that hope and fear should not affect what we do.
It only means this: when hope and fear move us, we should weigh the things we hope for or fear by what they are really worth, compared with other interests.

5. The question is not whether certain people in the Bible did right. The Bible says they were moved, at least somewhat, by hope and fear. They kept their eyes on the reward to come, or on the joy that was set before them.
