We agree they did right. Noah was moved by fear and built the ark.
But what mainly moved him? Was it the fear of drowning himself, or fear for his own safety?
The Bible does not say so.
He was afraid for the safety of his family. Even more, he dreaded the destruction of the whole human race and of everything that depended on it.
Whenever the Bible says that good people were moved by hope and fear, we agree.
But to use that in this argument, you would have to show that hope or fear about their own personal good was their main motive.
And the Bible never says that anywhere.
It was right for them to be moved by God’s promises and warnings.
Otherwise, they could not obey the second part of the law: “Love your neighbor as yourself.”

blocks.x: II. Next, I will show what this statement does mean: that caring about our own interests more than anything else cannot go together with true religion.

s: The question is whether caring about our own happiness more than anything else is religion.
It is whether we should fear our own damnation more than the damnation of everyone else, and more than the dishonor this would bring to God.
And it is whether we should work to secure our own happiness more than the happiness of everyone else and the glory of God.
And it is whether, if we do this, we are doing what true religion requires, or acting against true religion.
This is the real question. I want you to keep it in mind the whole time. Do not mix it up with any of the other points I have mentioned.

blocks.x: III. Now for the proof of this statement.

s: Before I prove that caring most about our own happiness cannot go together with true religion, I want to point something out. All true religion is being like God. It means acting on the same principles and reasons that he does, and feeling about different things the way he feels about them.
I do not think anyone will deny this.
In fact, no one in his right mind can deny it.
So here is my first proof of the statement:
1. Caring most about our own happiness does not follow God’s example. It makes us completely unlike him.
The Bible tells us that “God is love.”
This means that goodwill toward others is the whole of his character.
All his other moral qualities, like justice and mercy, are just different forms of this goodwill.
His love shows itself in two ways.
One is goodwill—wanting good things for others and wanting them to be happy.
The other is delight—approving of the character of others who are holy.
God’s goodwill reaches out to every being that can be happy.
It is for everyone. And toward all holy beings he shows the love of delight. In other words, God loves his neighbor as himself.
He cares about the interests of every being as much as his own, according to what each is really worth.
He seeks his own happiness, or glory, as the highest good.
But he does this not because it is his own. He does it because it is the highest good.
He is an infinite being. So the total of his happiness is infinitely greater than the total happiness of all other beings put together—or of any number of limited creatures you could imagine.
Let me give you a very simple example.
Here is a man who is kind to animals.
This man and his horse fall into a river.
Now, does true goodwill require the man to drown himself in order to get his horse out?
No. It would be true, unselfish goodwill for him to save himself and, if he has to, let his horse die. That is because his happiness is worth so much more than the horse’s happiness.
You can see this right away.
But the difference between God and all created beings is infinitely greater than the difference between a man and a horse, or between the highest angel and the smallest insect.
So God cares about the happiness of every creature exactly according to what it is really worth.
And unless we do the same, we are not like God.
If we are like God, we must see God’s happiness and glory the way he does. That is, we must see them as the highest good, above everything else in the universe.
And if we want our own happiness more than God’s happiness, we are infinitely unlike God.
2. Aiming at our own happiness above everything cannot go together with true religion, because it goes against the spirit of Christ.
We are told that “if anyone does not have the spirit of Christ, he does not belong to Christ.”
And the Bible says again and again that Jesus, as a man, did not seek his own interests. It says that he did not seek his own glory, and other things like that.
What was he seeking?
Was it his own personal salvation?
No. Was it his own personal happiness?
No. It was the glory of his Father and the good of the whole universe, through saving people.
He came on a mission of pure goodwill. He came to do good for the kingdom of God, not to do good for himself.
This was “the joy that was set before him.” Because of it “he endured the cross and thought nothing of the shame.”
It was the great good he could do by giving himself completely to work and suffer so that people could be saved.
3. Making our own happiness the main thing we chase goes against the law of God.
I have mentioned this before. But I am coming back to it so that my proof here will be complete.
The whole law comes down to this: “Love the Lord your God with all your heart, with all your soul, with all your mind, and with all your strength. And love your neighbor as yourself.”
This is the great thing God requires: goodwill toward God and toward people.
The first thing is to truly love God’s happiness and glory more than anything else. That is because it is so infinitely lovely and worth wanting, and it really is the highest good.
Some people have argued that it is not our duty to seek God’s happiness, because his happiness is already safe.

Now imagine that the king of England does not need me at all, and his happiness is safe without me. Does that make it any less my duty to wish him well, to want him to be happy, and to be glad about his happiness?
God is happy in himself and does not need his creatures. But is that a reason for us not to love his happiness and be glad about it? How strange!
Again, the terms of God’s law require us to delight in God, because he is holy—infinitely holy.
Again, this law requires us to show the same goodwill to others that we show to ourselves. That is, we must seek both their interests and our own, according to what each is really worth.
Which of you is doing this?
And we are required to show the love of delight toward those who are good and holy.
So we see what God’s law comes down to. We must show goodwill toward God and all beings, according to what each is really worth. And we must delight in all who are holy.
Now here is what I say: to care about our own happiness above all, or to make it our highest goal, goes against that law. It goes against both its words and its spirit. And
4. It goes against the gospel just as much as it goes against the law.

In the chapter our text comes from, the apostle begins like this: “I may speak in the languages of men and of angels. But if I do not have charity, I have become like a clanging piece of brass or a jingling cymbal.
I may have the gift of prophecy and understand all mysteries and all knowledge. I may have so much faith that I could move mountains. But if I do not have charity, I am nothing.”
Here the word charity means love.
In the original language, it is the same word that is translated love.
“I may give away everything I own to feed the poor. I may even give my body to be burned. But if I do not have charity, it does me no good at all.”
Now, notice this! He could not have used stronger words to say that charity, or goodwill, is necessary for true religion.
See how he puts up guards on every side, so that no one can possibly mistake what he means.
If a person does not have true charity, he is nothing.
Then he goes on to describe what this true charity is like.

“Charity puts up with a lot for a long time and is kind. Charity does not envy. Charity does not brag about itself and is not full of pride. It does not behave improperly. It does not seek its own interests. It is not easily made angry. It thinks no evil. It is not glad about wickedness, but is glad about the truth. It bears all things, believes all things, hopes all things, and endures all things.”
Here you see that one main mark of this love is that charity “does not seek its own interests.”
Notice that! If this is true religion, and there is no religion without it, then one mark of true religion is that it “does not seek its own interests.”
Some of you have Bibles with cross-references in the margins. You can follow those references and find a great many passages that clearly teach the same thing.
Remember the passages I quoted in my last lecture.
I will mention just one of them: “Whoever wants to save his life will lose it.”
Here you see it stated as a fixed rule of how God governs: if a person aims above all at his own interests, he will lose them.
The same thing is taught in the tenth chapter of this letter, verse 24: “No one should seek his own interests. Instead, everyone should seek another person’s wealth.”
If you look at this passage, you will see that the word wealth is printed in italics. That shows it is a word the translators added. It is not in the Greek.
They could just as well have used the word happiness, or welfare, instead of wealth.
It is the same in verse 33: “In the same way, I please everybody in every way. I am not looking for what benefits me, but for what benefits many people, so that they can be saved.”
So I say that making our own interests the main thing we chase goes against the gospel just as much as it goes against the law.
5. It goes against conscience.
The conscience of all people everywhere has decided that caring about our own happiness above everything is not goodness.
People have always known that serving God and doing good to others is right. And they have always known that seeking their own personal interests above everything is not right.

They have always thought it low and shameful for people to make their own happiness their highest goal. That is why we see people work so hard to hide their selfishness and to look as if they care about others.
Anyone can see that it is sinful to put his own happiness above other, more important interests—unless his conscience has been strangely dulled by sin or twisted by false teaching.
6. It goes against clear thinking.
Clear thinking teaches us to value everything according to what it is really worth.
God does this, and we should do the same.
God gave us the ability to reason for this very purpose: so that we could weigh and compare how much different things are worth.
It makes a joke of reason to deny that it teaches us to value things according to what they are really worth.
And if that is true, then aiming at our own interests and putting them first, as our highest goal, goes against reason.
7. It goes against common sense.
What has the common sense of humanity decided about this?
Look at what people’s common sense says about what we call patriotism.
No one was ever thought of as a true patriot for fighting for his country if his goal was to serve his own interests.
Imagine it turned out that his goal in fighting was to get himself crowned king. Would anyone give him credit for being a patriot?
No. Everyone agrees that it is patriotism when a man is unselfish, like Washington, and fights for his country for his country’s sake.
The common sense of humanity has stamped its disapproval on the attitude that seeks its own things. It condemns putting our own interests ahead of the greater interests of others.
It is clear that everyone sees it this way.
If not, why does everyone want so much to look unselfish?
8. It goes against the way our minds are made.
I do not mean that the way we are made makes it impossible for us to seek our own happiness as our highest goal.
But we are made in such a way that if we do this, we can never reach it.
As I said in an earlier lecture, happiness is the satisfaction of desire.
We must want something, and then get the thing we want.
Now imagine a man who wants his own happiness. What he wants will always stay just out of reach, like his shadow. The faster he chases it, the faster it runs away.
Happiness is always tied to getting the thing we want.
Suppose I want a thousand dollars.
That is the thing my desire is fixed on. When I get it, that desire is satisfied, and I am happy—at least as far as satisfying this desire can make me happy.
But suppose I want the thousand dollars so I can buy a watch, some clothes, and things like that. Then my desire is not satisfied until I get those things.
But now imagine that the thing I wanted was my own happiness.
Then getting the thousand dollars does not make me happy, because that is not what my desire was fixed on.
And getting the watch and the clothes and the other things will not make me happy either, because they do not satisfy my desire.
God has set things up, and given our minds such laws, that people can never gain happiness by chasing it.
The very way we are made clearly shows that it is our duty to have unselfish goodwill.
In fact, God has made it impossible for people to be happy except to the degree that they are unselfish.
Picture two men walking down the street together.
They come upon a man who has just been run over by a cart. He is lying there covered in his own blood.
They pick him up, carry him to the doctor, and get him help.
Now it is clear that their satisfaction is as great as their desire to see him helped.
If one of them felt very little and cared very little about the poor man’s suffering, he will feel very little satisfaction.
But if his desire to see the man helped was so strong that it was agony, his satisfaction would be just as great.
Now imagine a third person who had no desire to help the injured man. Helping him certainly could not give that person any satisfaction.
He could walk right past him and watch him die.
So he feels no satisfaction at all.
So you see, our happiness is exactly as great as our desires are satisfied by getting the things we want.
Notice this too: for the happiness of a satisfied desire to be complete, the desire itself must be good.
If the desire is selfish, the satisfaction will be mixed with pain, because the mind is at war with itself.
We know all this is true because we are aware of it inside ourselves. That is the very strongest kind of evidence we can have.
And anyone who denies it is accusing God of acting foolishly—as if he had made us in a way that would not let us be happy when we obey him.
9. Making our own interests our highest goal also works against our own happiness.
This follows from what I just said.
People may enjoy a certain kind of pleasure, but not true happiness.
Any pleasure that does not come from satisfying a good desire is a false thing that fools us.
Everyone wants happiness so badly. So why doesn’t everyone find it? The reason is that they are chasing IT.
If they would seek the glory of God and the good of the universe as their highest goal, IT would chase them.
10. It works against the happiness of everyone together.
Imagine that each person aims at his own happiness as his main goal. Then all these interests will clash and crash into each other. When everyone is selfish, war and chaos everywhere will follow.
11. To say that caring most about our own interests is true religion goes against the experience of every real saint.
I say it plainly: every real saint knows that his greatest happiness comes from getting outside himself and caring about the glory of God and the good of others.
If he does not know this, he is not a saint.
12. It also goes against the experience of everyone who once had a selfish religion, then found out their mistake and got true religion.
This happens often.
I think I have known hundreds of cases.
Some members of this church have recently made this discovery.
And they can all tell you that they now know from experience that goodwill is true religion.
13. It goes against the experience of everyone who has not repented.
Every sinner who has not repented knows that he is aiming above all at getting ahead for himself. And he knows that he does not have true religion.
The very thing his conscience condemns him for is this: he is looking after his own interests instead of the glory of God.
Now let’s turn the page for a moment. Let’s suppose that caring most about our own happiness really is true religion. Then see what would follow.
1. Then it would follow that God is not holy.
That is, if caring most about our own interests, just because they are our own, is true religion, then it would follow that God is not holy.
God cares about his own happiness. But that is because it is the greatest good, not because it is his own.
But he is love, or goodwill. So if goodwill is not true religion, God’s nature would have to change.
2. The law of God would have to be changed.

If caring most about our own happiness is religion, then the law should say, “Love yourself with all your heart, with all your soul, with all your mind, and with all your strength. And love God and your neighbor infinitely less than yourself.”
3. The gospel would have to be turned upside down.
Instead of saying, “Whether you are eating or drinking, or doing anything at all, do everything to bring glory to God,” it would say, “Do everything for your own happiness.”

Instead of “Whoever wants to save his life will lose it,” we would find it saying, “Whoever is extremely anxious to save his own life will save it. But whoever is full of goodwill, and willing to lose his life for the good of others, will lose it.”
4. People’s consciences would have to be changed. They would have to speak up for selfishness, and condemn and reject anything that looks like unselfish goodwill.

5. Clear thinking would have to be made to stop weighing things by what they are really worth. Instead, it would have to decide that our own small interests are worth more than the greatest interests of God and the universe.
6. Common sense would have to decide that true patriotism means every man seeking his own interests instead of the good of everyone, and each one trying to build himself up as high as he can.
7. The way human beings are made would have to be turned upside down.
If extreme selfishness is goodness, then human beings were made wrong.
We are made in such a way that we can be happy only by having goodwill toward others.
And if this teaching is true—that religion means seeking our own happiness as the highest good—then the more religion a person has, the more miserable he is.
8. And the whole structure of society would have to be changed.
Right now, the good of the community depends on how much each person cares about the good of everyone.
If this teaching holds, that would have to change. Then the good of everyone would be served best when every person is scrambling for his own interests without caring about the interests of others.
9. The experience of the saints would have to be turned upside down.

Right now they find that the more goodwill they have, the more religion and the more happiness they have. Instead, they would have to say that the more they aim at their own good, the more they enjoy religion and God’s favor.
10. And people who have not repented would have to say that they are extremely happy in their extreme selfishness, and that they find true happiness in it.
I will not take this proof any further. It would start to look as if I were not being serious.
If anything can be proved at all, then this has been fully proved: aiming at our own happiness above everything cannot go together with true religion.

blocks.x: REMARKS.

s: I. We see why so few people find happiness, even though everyone is chasing it.
The fact is plain to see.
Here is the reason. Most people do not know what true happiness is. They are looking for it in things that can never give it.
They do not find it because they are chasing it.
If they would turn around and chase holiness, happiness would chase them.
If they would become unselfish and put all their effort into doing good, they could not help being happy.
If they choose happiness as their goal, it runs away from them.
True happiness is the satisfaction of good desires. If people would set out to glorify God and do good, they would find it.
The only people who never find it, in this world or the world to come, are the ones who make it their goal.
II. The way God made the human mind and the universe gives us a beautiful picture of how God arranges things.
Imagine that people could find happiness only by chasing their own happiness.

Then each person would have only the happiness he had gotten for himself. All the happiness in the universe would just be the total of what each person had gotten—minus all the pain and misery caused when people’s interests clash.
Now notice this! God has set things up so that while each person works hard for the happiness of others, his own happiness is made safe and complete.
So the total happiness in the universe is far, far greater than it would have been if selfishness had been the law of Jehovah’s kingdom!
That is because everyone who obeys God’s law fully secures his own happiness through his goodwill. And the happiness of everyone together grows by as much as each person receives from all the others.
Many people say, “Who will take care of my happiness if I don’t?
If I am supposed to care only about my neighbor’s interests and neglect my own, none of us will be happy.”
That would be true if caring about your neighbor’s happiness took away from your own.
But if your happiness comes from doing good and making others happy, then the more you do for others, the more you add to your own happiness.
III. When I announced the topic of this lecture, I avoided using the word selfishness. I was afraid it would sound insulting.
But now I say it clearly: caring most about our own interests is selfishness, and nothing else.
If God cared most about his own interests just because they are his own, that would be selfishness in God.
And it is selfishness in people.
So anyone who says that caring most about our own interests is true religion is saying that selfishness is true religion.
IV. If selfishness is goodness, then goodwill is sin.
They are exact opposites. They cannot both be goodness.
When a man sets his own interests above God’s interests—when he prefers them and sets them against God’s interests—that is selfishness.
And if that is goodness, then Jesus Christ, by seeking the good of humanity the way he did, turned away from what is good.
Who would dare to claim that?
V. People who put their own interests first and still think they have true religion are deceived.
I say this very seriously, because I believe it is true. I would say it even if it were the last thing I said before going to face God’s judgment.
Dear listener, whoever you are, if you are doing this, you are not a Christian.
Do not call this being judgmental.
I am not being judgmental.
I would not condemn anyone.
But as surely as God is true, and as surely as your soul is going to face judgment, you do not have the religion of the Bible.
VI. Some will ask here, “What? Are we not supposed to care about our happiness at all? And if so, how are we supposed to tell whether we care about it most or not?”
I do not say that.
I say you may care about it according to what it is really worth.
Now I ask you, is this really hard to figure out in practice?
I appeal to what you know inside yourself.
If you are honest, you cannot help knowing what you care about most.
On one side are your own interests. On the other side are God’s glory and the good of the universe. Are these so evenly balanced in your mind that you cannot tell which one you prefer?
That is impossible! You should be as sure that you prefer God’s glory to your own interests as you are sure that you exist. If you are not, you can take it for granted that you are completely wrong.
VII. You see why the joy of so many people who claim to be religious depends on their proofs that they are saved.
These people are always hunting for proof. And their joy goes up and down as that proof changes.
Now notice this! If they really cared about the glory of God and the good of humanity, their joy would not depend on their proofs.
People who are completely selfish may enjoy religion a lot. But it is the joy of looking forward to something.
They like the idea of going to heaven.
But those who get outside themselves and are full of pure goodwill have heaven in their hearts right now.
VIII. You see from this that all of you who had no peace and joy in religion until you had a hope of being saved are deceived.
Maybe I can describe what happened to you.
You were woken up spiritually. And you were upset, as you had reason to be, because you were afraid of going to hell.
After a while, maybe while you were praying, or while someone was talking with you, your distress went away.
You thought your sins were forgiven.
A flash of joy went through your mind and warmed your heart until it glowed. You took that as proof, and that made you even happier.
How very different the experience of a true Christian is!
His peace does not depend on his hope. Real surrender to God and real goodwill bring peace and joy all by themselves, apart from his hope.
Imagine a man in prison who has been sentenced to be hanged the next day.
He is very upset. He paces back and forth in his cell, waiting for the day to come.
After a while a messenger comes with a pardon.
He grabs the paper and holds it up to the dim light coming through the bars of his window. He reads the word PARDON. He almost faints with emotion, and he jumps for joy.
He believes the paper is real.
Now suppose it turns out that the paper is a fake.
Suddenly all his joy is gone.
It is the same with a person who is deceived.
He was afraid of going to hell. So of course he is happy if he believes he is forgiven.
If the devil told him so, and he believed it, his joy would be just as great—as long as he kept believing it—as if it were real.
True Christian joy does not depend on proofs.
The true Christian puts himself into God’s hands with such trust, and that very act gives him peace.
He had a terrible fight with God. But all at once he stops arguing and gives in. He says, “God will do what is right. Let God’s will be done.”
Then he begins to pray. He is humbled. His heart melts before God. And that very act brings sweet, calm, heavenly joy.
Maybe he has not even thought about having a hope.
He may go for hours, or even a day or two, full of joy in God, without thinking about his own salvation.
If you ask him whether he has a hope, he never even thought about it.
His joy does not depend on believing that he is forgiven. It comes from a state of mind that accepts God’s rule.
With a mind like that, he cannot help being happy.
Now let me ask you: which religion do you have?

If you practice true religion, imagine that God put you into hell and let you keep loving God above all, and loving your neighbor as yourself. That state of mind itself could not go together with being miserable.
I want you to understand this completely.
These people who chase after a hope will always be disappointed.
If you run after hope, you will never have a hope worth anything.
But if you pursue holiness, then hope and peace and joy will come naturally.
Is your religion a love of holiness—a love of God and of people’s souls?
Or is it only a hope?
IX. You see why sinners who are worried about their souls do not find peace.
They are looking at their own guilt and danger.
They see God as someone who punishes, and they shrink back from his terrors.
This will make it impossible for them ever to find peace.
While they look at God’s anger, which makes them wither and shake, they cannot love him. They hide from him.
Worried sinners, let me tell you a secret.
If you keep looking at only that side of God’s character, it will drive you to despair. And despair does not go together with true surrender to God.

You should look at his whole character. See the reasons why you should love him. Throw yourself on him without holding anything back and without any distrust. Instead of shrinking back from him, come straight to him and say, “O Father in heaven, you are not stern and unbending. You are the ruler of all, but you are good. I accept your rule, and I give myself to you—everything I have and everything I am, body and soul, for now and for eternity.”
My next lecture will be about the difference between submitting to God under the law and submitting to God through the gospel—or between the religion of the law and the religion of faith.
And let me point out that when I started preaching about selfishness in religion, I never dreamed anyone would think it was a controversial subject at all.
I do not like arguing. To me, calling this a controversial subject makes as little sense as calling the teaching that God exists controversial.
This question is extremely important. We should weigh the arguments and decide according to the word of God.

Soon we will all stand together before God’s judgment seat. You must decide whether you will go there with selfishness in your hearts, or with that unselfish goodwill that does not seek its own interests. Will you be honest now?
Because as surely as God is true, if you are seeking your own interests, you will soon be in hell—unless you repent.
Oh, be honest! Put aside your prejudice, and act with eternity in mind.
Text: “Love never harms its neighbor. That is why love fully keeps the law.” — Romans 13:10
As I speak on these words, I plan:
I. To say some things about what love is.
II. To show that love is all there is to true religion.
III. To name some things that perfect love does not require.
IV. To name some things that it does require.
V. To name some of the things that perfect love produces.

blocks.x: I. First, some things about what love is.

s: 1. My first point is that love can take different forms.
When it comes to religion, the two main forms are goodwill and delight.
Goodwill is a settled attitude of the mind. In other words, it is a choice made by the will.
It means wanting good for someone. It is a desire to make that person happy.
Delight means respecting someone and approving of their character.
We should show goodwill to every being, whether they are good or bad.
But delight belongs only to those who are good and holy.
2. Love can exist in two ways: as an affection or as an emotion.
When love is an affection, it is something we choose. It is an act of the will.
When love is an emotion, we do not choose it directly.
What we call feelings, or emotions, are not directly chosen.
They do not depend directly on the will. We cannot control them just by deciding to.
The goodness, or virtue, of love is found mostly in love as a choice.
The happiness of love is found mostly in love as a feeling.
If the choice to love is very strong, it brings a lot of happiness. But the feeling of holy love is happiness itself.
I said that the feeling of love is not directly chosen.
I do not mean that the will has nothing to do with it. I mean that it does not come just from a direct decision of the will.
Nobody can feel love just by deciding to feel it.
And sometimes the feeling is there even when the will is against it.

People often feel emotions rising in their minds that they know are wrong. They try hard, by pure willpower, to push them out. When they find they cannot do it, they decide that they have no control over these emotions.
But the will can always control them in an indirect way.
The mind can bring up any kind of emotion it wants by paying enough attention to the right thing.
The more closely you fix your attention, the more surely those feelings will come—as long as your will is right toward the thing you are paying attention to.

It works the same way with emotions that are wrong or unpleasant. The mind can get rid of them by turning its attention completely away from the thing that causes them, and not letting the thoughts stay on it.
3. Usually, we feel love for God when we are choosing to love him.
But this is not always true.
We can have goodwill toward someone and still, at times, feel no love at all in our emotions.
We cannot be sure that even the Lord Jesus Christ felt love for God as an emotion at every moment.

From what we know about how the mind works, a person can have a steady affection and be guided and ruled by it all the time, in everything he does. And yet at that moment he may not feel any emotion of love for the one he loves.

For example, a husband and father may be working hard for the good of his family. His whole life is ruled by his love for them. Yet his thoughts may not be on them at that moment, so he does not feel any strong feelings of love for them right then.
The work he is doing may fill his mind so much that he hardly thinks about them. So he may feel no emotion toward them. And yet the whole time, his love for them is guiding and ruling him.
Notice that I am using the word “affection” the way President Edwards used it. He explained it in his famous Treatise on the Will.
In his book, an affection is an act of the will—a choice.
4. Loving our neighbor naturally means that we also love God. And loving God naturally means that we love our neighbor.
The same thing is said in verse 8: “Do not owe anyone anything, except to love one another. Whoever loves another person has done all the law asks.

Commands like ‘Do not commit adultery,’ ‘Do not kill,’ ‘Do not steal,’ ‘Do not tell lies about others,’ and ‘Do not crave what belongs to others’—and any other command there is—are all wrapped up in this one saying: ‘Love your neighbor as yourself.’”
This verse takes it for granted that loving our neighbor means we also love God. Otherwise it could not say that “whoever loves another person has done all the law asks.”
The apostle James sees the same principle. He says, “If you keep the royal law found in the Scriptures, ‘Love your neighbor as yourself,’ you are doing well.”
Here, loving our neighbor is described as obeying the whole law.
Goodwill toward our neighbor naturally includes love for God.
It is a love for the happiness of all beings.
In the same way, delighting in holy beings naturally includes love for God, because he is infinitely holy.

blocks.x: II. Next, I will show that love is all there is to true religion.

s: In other words, everything God asks of people comes down to love, in its many different forms and results.
Love is the total of it all.
1. My first proof is that this idea is taught in our text and in many other Bible passages.
The Bible clearly teaches that love is the total of everything required, both in the law and in the gospel.

Our Savior says that the great command is this: love the Lord your God with all your heart, soul, mind and strength, and love your neighbor as yourself. He says this is the total of all the law and the prophets. In other words, it contains everything the whole Bible—both the law and the gospel—asks of us.
2. God is love. So to love is to be like God. And to be perfect in love is to be perfect as God is perfect.
All of God’s moral qualities are really love, acting in certain situations and for certain purposes.
When God punishes the wicked in his justice, or is angry at sin, and so on, these are simply his love at work for the happiness of his whole kingdom.
It is the same with people.
Everything good in a person is some form of love.
Hating sin is simply love for goodness in action, fighting against whatever fights against goodness.
In the same way, true faith includes love. Faith that has no love in it, or that does not work through love, is no part of religion.
The faith that is part of religion is a loving trust in God.
There is a kind of faith in God that has no love in it.
The devil has this kind of faith.
So does the sinner who has been made to feel his guilt.
But there is nothing of religion in it.
Faith could even become strong enough to do miracles. But if it has no love in it, it is worth nothing.

The apostle Paul says in 1 Corinthians chapter 13, “I might be able to prophesy. I might understand every secret and know everything. I might have faith so great that I could move mountains. But if I do not have love, I am nothing.”
Repentance is the same.
If repentance does not include love, it is not true “repentance toward God.”
True repentance means obeying the law of love, and as a result, standing against sin.

blocks.x: III. Now I will mention some things that perfect love does not require.

s: 1. Perfect love does not require the strongest possible feelings.
It is clear that the Lord Jesus Christ very rarely had the strongest feelings of love. Yet he always had perfect love.
He usually showed very little emotion or excitement.
Excitement always matches how strong the emotions are, because excitement is made up of emotions.
The Savior usually seemed very calm.
Sometimes he was strongly angry at wrong, or deeply grieved at how hard people’s hearts were. And sometimes we read that he was full of joy in his spirit.
But most of the time he was calm and did not show strong emotion.
So it is clear that perfect love does not require the feeling of love to be very strong.
2. Perfect love does not mean that love cannot grow. It does not rule out growing in grace.
I believe that because the mind will keep growing in knowledge forever, it will naturally keep growing in love forever too.
The Lord Jesus Christ, as a human being, grew taller and grew in favor with God and people.
No doubt, as a child he grew in knowledge. And as he grew in knowledge, he grew in love for God, as well as in God’s favor.
His love was perfect when he was a child, but it was greater when he grew up.
As a human being, he probably kept growing in his love for God for as long as he lived.
From the way the mind works, we can see that it may be the same for all the saints in heaven. Their love will keep growing forever, and yet it will always be perfect love.
3. Perfect love does not require us to love every person in exactly the same way at all times.
We cannot think of everyone at the same time.
You cannot even think of every person you know all at once.
How much love we feel toward someone depends on whether that person is in our thoughts.
4. Perfect love does not require us to have the same spirit of prayer—the same deep urge to pray—for every person, or for the same person at all times.
Pure and perfect love does not always come with the spirit of prayer.
The saints in heaven have pure and perfect love for all beings. Yet we do not know that they feel led to pray for anyone.
You may love someone very strongly and still not have the spirit of prayer for that person.
That is, God’s Spirit may not lead you to pray for that person to be saved.
You do not pray for the wicked who are in hell.
The spirit of prayer depends on the Holy Spirit working in us. He leads our minds to pray for things that match God’s will.
You cannot pray in the Spirit with the same passion and faith for every person in the world.
Jesus Christ said plainly that he did not pray for everyone: “It is not the world I am praying for.”
People have made a big mistake here about the spirit of prayer.
Some people think that Christians have not done all their duty unless they have prayed in faith for every single person, as long as there is still one sinner on earth.
If that were true, Jesus Christ never did all his duty, because he never did this.
God has never told us that he will save every person. He has never given us any reason to believe he will.
So how can we pray in faith for everyone to be saved?
What would that faith be based on?
5. You can have perfect love even when you feel weak and worn out because you are exhausted or sick.
We are made in such a way that strong excitement naturally wears out our strength.
But love can still be perfect.
A person may feel more like lying down to sleep than like praying, and still his love may be perfect.
The Lord Jesus Christ often felt this tiredness and exhaustion. His spirit was still willing, but his body was weak.

blocks.x: IV. What perfect love does require.

s: 1. It means there is nothing in the mind that goes against love.
There is no hatred, spite, rage, jealousy, or any other evil feeling that goes against pure and perfect love.
2. It means there is nothing in the way we live that goes against love.
All our actions, words, and thoughts are always fully and perfectly controlled by love.
3. It means that our love for God comes first, above everything.
Love for God is completely in first place. It is so far above everything else that nothing else is loved compared to God.
4. It means that we love God without selfish motives.
We love God for who he is. We love him not because of his relationship to us, but because his character is so excellent.
5. It means that we love our neighbor equally with ourselves. His interests and happiness should matter to us as much as our own, and we should treat him and his interests that way.

blocks.x: V. Now I will mention some of the things perfect love produces.

s: 1. One sure result of perfect love for God and people is joy in giving things up to help God’s kingdom and to see sinners saved.
Look at loving parents. See how happy they are to give things up so that their children can be happy.
Look at that father. He wears himself out with hard work day after day and year after year, for his whole long life. He gets up early and lives with constant worry, all to take care of his family.
And he does not see all this sacrifice and hard work as sad or heavy. He sees it as a joy, because he loves his family.
Look at that mother. She wants to send her son to college.
Now, instead of finding it hard, she is glad to stay up late and work without stopping to help him.
It is because she really loves her son.
Parents like this are happier giving good things to their children than they would be enjoying those things themselves.
What parent does not enjoy a piece of fruit more by giving it to their little child than by eating it?
The Lord Jesus Christ found more deep satisfaction in winning salvation for people than any of his saints can ever find in receiving his gifts.
He said that giving brings more blessing than receiving.
This was the joy that lay ahead of him. For the sake of that joy he put up with the cross and thought nothing of the shame.
His love for people was so great that it drove him to take on this work. And it carried him in victory all the way through it.
The apostle Paul did not think it was sad or hard to be chased from place to place, put in prison, whipped, stoned, and treated like garbage, all to spread the gospel and save souls.
It was his joy.
The love of Christ drove him so strongly, and he wanted so much to do good, that his greatest joy was to offer himself on that altar as a sacrifice for the cause.
Other people have had the same attitude as the apostle.

Some people have been willing to live a thousand years, or until the end of time, if they could spend it doing good, building God’s kingdom, and saving people’s souls. They were even willing to go without sleep and food to help those they loved so much.
2. It frees the soul from the power of law-based motives.
Perfect love makes a person obey God, not because he is afraid of God’s anger or hopes to get a reward for doing this or that. He obeys because he loves God and loves to do what God wants.
People go to two extremes on this topic.
One group says goodness means doing right just because it is right. They leave out God’s will and any love for God.
Another group says goodness means doing things because you enjoy doing them. They leave out God’s authority as Ruler and Lawgiver.
Both groups are wrong.
Doing something only because you think it is right, and not because you love God, is not true goodness.
And doing something because you like doing it, without caring about God’s will, is not true goodness either.

A wife might do certain things because she knows it will please her husband. But if she did the same thing only because she liked doing it, and without any thought of her husband, it would not be a virtue toward her husband.
If a person loves God, as soon as he knows what God wants, he will do it because God wants it.
Perfect love will lead to obeying in everything—doing God’s will in all things, because it is what God wants.
3. A person who has perfect love will be dead to the world.
By this I mean that worldly concerns will no longer have a hold on him.
Perfect love will wipe out selfishness so completely that he will want nothing except what God wants, and care about nothing except God’s glory.
He will not be moved by what the public thinks, or by what this or that person will say or think.
Look at what a woman will do out of natural love for her husband.

She is willing to break away from all her friends, as if she were dead to them. She will not pay the slightest attention to what they say. She will leave behind all the wealth, honor, and pleasures they can offer, to join the man she loves and live with him in poverty, in shame, and far from home.
Her love is so great that she does it with joy. She is ready to move from a palace to any cottage or cave on earth and be perfectly happy.
Nothing her friends say against the man she loves has any effect on her, except to make her hold on to him even more tightly.
This one ALL-CONSUMING love has actually killed every influence that used to work on her.
Trying to change her mind with such things is useless.
There is only one way to reach her mind. Only one kind of motive moves her, and it comes through the one she loves.
As far as the science of the mind goes, perfect love for God works in the same way.
When a mind is filled with perfect love, it cannot be turned away from God as long as that love keeps working.

Take away his things, his friends, his good name, and his children. Send him to prison, whip him, tie him to a stake, stuff his flesh with pine knots and set them on fire. Then leave him his God, and he is happy.
His strong love can make him feel nothing of anything else.
It is as if he were dead to the whole world except his God.
There have been martyrs who, while their bodies were burning at the stake, were so completely happy in God that they stopped feeling the pain.
Put a person like that in hell, in the lake of fire and burning sulfur. As long as he enjoys God and God’s love fills his soul, he is happy.
Who has not seen or heard of love almost as strong as what I have described? In such cases a person really is dead to everything else and lives only for the one they love.
How often do you see loving parents who live for their only child, and when that child dies, they wish they were dead too!
Sometimes a husband and wife love each other so completely that they live for nothing else. If the husband dies, the wife wastes away with grief and dies too.
The one who filled her whole soul, the one she lived for, is gone. So why should she go on living?

In the same way, when a person is filled with perfect love for God, he wants to live only to love and serve God. He is dead to the world and dead to his own reputation. He has no wish to live for any other reason—here, in heaven, or anywhere else in the universe—except to bring glory to God.
He is willing to live here or anywhere else, and to suffer and work for a thousand years, or forever, if it will bring glory to God.
I remember a friend who often said, “I don’t think I have a single thought of living even one moment for any purpose except to glorify God—any more than I would think of jumping straight into hell.”
He said this seriously and thoughtfully, and his whole life matched what he said.
He was intelligent, serious, and honest. I have no doubt that he was saying what he had fully believed for years.
What was this, if not perfect love?
Does any angel in heaven do more than this?
An angel’s love may be greater in amount, because the angel is stronger.
But even the highest angel could not love more perfectly than to be able to say honestly, “I would sooner think of jumping into hell than of living one moment for any other goal but to glorify God.”
What more could Jesus Christ himself say?
4. I hardly need to say that perfect joy and peace come naturally from perfect love.
But here I want you to look at what the apostle says in 1 Corinthians chapter 13, where he speaks about charity, or love.
Notice that the word translated “charity” here is the same word that is translated “love” in other places.
It means love. “Even if I spoke the languages of humans and of angels, if I had no love, I would only be clanging brass or a tinkling cymbal.
I might be able to prophesy, and understand every secret and know everything. I might have faith so great that I could move mountains. But if I had no love, I would be nothing.”
A person might even have faith to work miracles, faith so strong that he could move mountains off their ancient foundations, and still have no love.
“If I gave away everything I own to feed the poor, and even gave up my body to be burned, but did not have love, it would do me no good.”
You see how far the apostle thinks a person can go and still not have love.
“Love puts up with things for a long time.” Being long-suffering means staying gentle when people oppose you or hurt you.
This is one of the things love does. It puts up with a lot of provoking and does not strike back or insult in return.
Love “is kind.” It is warm and caring in all its dealings with others. It is never harsh or rude, and never hurts anyone without need.
Love “never envies.” It never dislikes others because they are more respected or noticed, more honored or useful, or because they have gone further in knowledge, happiness, or godliness.
It “does not swell with pride,” but is always humble and modest.
It “does not act in an ugly or improper way.” Instead, it naturally makes a person pleasant and polite to everyone.
A person moved by perfect love may know very little about fine manners, but he always comes across well. Being kind, gentle, and polite comes naturally to him.
It “is not out for itself.” It has no selfishness.
It “does not get angry easily.”
Love always has this effect.
Look at that mother and how patient she is with her children for so long, because she loves them.
If you see someone who is touchy or grumpy, who quickly loses his temper when anything goes wrong, he is far from perfect in love—if he has any love at all.
Getting angry easily is always a sign of pride.
If a person is full of love, you cannot make him sinfully angry as long as that love lasts.
He feels the kind of anger at low and wrong things that God feels and that holy angels feel. But he will not lose his temper over it.

It “does not think the worst.” Show me a person who is always suspicious of why others do things, and who always takes other people’s words and actions in the worst way. I will show you someone who has the devil in him, not the Holy Spirit.
There is something in his own mind that makes him think badly of others.
If a person is honest and sincere himself, he will be the last to think badly of others.
He will not always be sniffing out false teaching or trouble in other people.
In fact, people like this are often taken advantage of by tricky people. This is not because they lack good sense, but because of how love affects them.
They do not suspect evil when things look fine on the outside, and they will not suspect it without very strong proof.
Love “is never glad about wrongdoing, but is glad about the truth.”
Look at a man who is glad when his neighbor falls, or shouts, “I told you so!” I tell you, that man is very far from being perfect in love.
It “puts up with everything”—every insult and injury—without taking revenge.
It “believes all things.” Instead of being slow to believe good things about others, it is always ready to believe the good wherever there is even a little evidence for it.
It “hopes all things.” Even when there is reason to suspect something bad, as long as there is room for hope, it takes things in the best way possible.
Whenever you see someone who does not have this spirit, you can be sure he is far from perfect in love.
In fact, he has no love at all.
I could keep going with this, but I do not have time.
“Love never harms its neighbor.”
Notice that: NO HARM!
Perfect love never takes advantage of a neighbor, never cheats him, never crushes him, and never does him any harm.
Would a man ruled by perfect love sell his neighbor rum?
Never! Would a man who loved God perfectly, with all his heart, keep his neighbor as a slave?

“Love never harms its neighbor.” But slavery refuses to pay him the wages he has earned. It may sell him and tear him away from his family. It keeps the Bible from him and tries as hard as it can to turn him into an animal.
There is no greater lie and hypocrisy than for a man who does that to pretend he loves God.
Now light has been shed on this subject, and people’s attention has been turned to it.
Would a man hate his own flesh and blood?
How can someone who hates or hurts his neighbor love God?
I planned to mention one more result of perfect love.
It always shows itself in great efforts to make the church holy and to save souls.
If a person is careless or falls short in either of these, he is far from perfect in love, no matter what he claims.

blocks.x: Closing lessons.

s: I. You can see why the apostle James is right when he says, “If anyone among you seems to be religious but does not keep his tongue in check, he is deceiving his own heart, and his religion is empty.”

A man may claim to be religious and still let his tongue run wild, speaking against his neighbor and hurting him. If he thinks he loves his neighbor as himself, he is fooling himself. What a strange kind of love!
II. A person’s mind can know a lot about religion and still have no love.
You often see people who understand a great deal about religion in their heads, and can explain it to others, while it is clear that the spirit of love is not what drives them.
Their words are not ruled by kindness.
III. People who have a lot of religious knowledge and zeal but no love are very unpleasant and dangerous people.
They are always critical of others, proud, stubborn, and arrogant.
They may impress people a lot, but they do not produce real religion.
They work hard to win you over, but not in a good way.
IV. What a person’s zeal is aimed at shows what kind of religion he has.
It will show whether the knowledge in his mind comes with love.
If it does, his zeal will not be about his own group or church party.
Show me a man who is full of jealousy toward everyone who is not part of his group or party, and that man is very far from perfect love.
True love never attacks people or is harsh.
If it needs to talk about other people’s faults, it does so kindly and with sadness.
Perfect love cannot speak in a rough or insulting way, either to people or about them.
It will not make a big deal of the small side issues in religion, or fight over particular methods or forms.
Many people will argue fiercely for or against certain things, like for or against new methods. But if they were full of love, they would not do it.
Zeal that is ruled by perfect love will not wear itself out arguing for or against forms of religion, or attacking small errors and wrongs.
Love leads us to put the weight on the basic truths of religion.
It holds on to warm-hearted Christians, no matter what church group they belong to. It loves them and enjoys spending time with them.
This kind of zeal never loves to argue, and it is never full of fighting over ideas.
Find a man who loves going to church business meetings and jumps into every argument of the day, and that man is not full of love.
For a mind filled with holy love, it is very painful to go to such meetings and watch ministers split into sides, scheme, make secret deals, argue over tiny points, and fight to win.
Find someone who loves arguing in the newspapers, and he is not full of love.
If he were, he would rather be insulted, mocked, and lied about, either face to face or in the papers, than stop to defend himself or answer back.
He would never answer insults with insults. Instead, he would bless.
And as much as he could, he would keep peace with everyone.
V. So much of what people call religion has no love in it!
So many things that look like religious works are pushed along by outside pressures and influences, not by the power of love inside!

People should understand this better than they do: unless love is the main driving force, it does not matter what the outward action is—praying, praising, giving, or anything else—there is no religion in it. So much excitement that people call religion has no love in it!
So much zeal has no real religion in it!
Look at that man who is always full of bitter zeal. When someone corrects him, he runs to Paul’s example, when Paul said, “You child of the devil!”
If perfect love were ruling him, he would see that his situation is so different that it does not give him the right to act in that spirit.
VI. Religious excitement that is not made up of the spirit of love is not a revival of religion.
The church may be very stirred up. It may rush around with a big show of zeal and loud noise, but have no tenderness of spirit.
Those who go around visiting may show a proud, rude spirit and start a fight with every family they visit.
I once knew a young man who admitted that he tried to make people angry. The reason he gave was that it often made them feel their guilt, and that led to their conversion.
Well, the same thing might happen if he went in and said horrible, blasphemous things in front of them until they were scared into thinking about their own lives.
But who would defend acting like that just because it sometimes turned out well?
And if this is what the excitement is like, it may be a revival of anger, spite, and every kind of unloving spirit, but it is not a revival of religion.
I do not mean that when some people, or even many, are “filled with anger,” it proves for sure that there is no revival of religion.
I mean that when this is the main character of the excitement, it is not a true revival of religion.
Some of them may have the spirit of love. But those who are filled with bitter, argumentative zeal are certainly not truly religious.
Religion may come alive again in some people. But mostly, in cases like this, it is a revival of ungodliness.
VII. When people say they have been converted, but love is not the main thing in their character, they are not truly converted.
They may look good in other ways. Their ideas may be clear and their feelings deep. But if they do not have the spirit of love for God and love for people, they are fooling themselves.
Do not trust converts like that.
VIII. Think about what the world will be like when everyone is moved by a spirit of love.
We learn that a time is coming when nothing will hurt or destroy, and the Spirit of love will rule everywhere.
What a change that will be in society!
What a change in the way business is done, and in the way people treat each other, when everyone loves his neighbor as himself and seeks the good of others as much as his own!
If one of the saints living now could come back to earth in that day, he would not recognize the world he lived in. Everything will be so different.
“Can this really be the earth?” he would cry out. “Is this the same earth that used to be so full of quarreling, cruelty, and cheating?”
IX. What the Lord Jesus Christ is set on doing is bringing all people under the power of love.
Isn’t that a worthy goal?
He came to destroy the devil’s work.
And this is how to do it.
Imagine the world full of people like Jesus Christ was as a human being.
Compare that with the world as it is now.
Wouldn’t a change like that be worthy of the Son of God?
What a glorious goal—to fill the earth with love!
X. It is easy to see what makes heaven what it is.
It is love—perfect love.
And it is easy to see what makes heaven begin here on earth in people who are full of love.

How sweet their nature is! What wonderful friends they are! What a blessing it is to live near them and spend time with them! They are so open and fair, so kind, so gentle, so careful not to offend, so lovable in everything, like God himself!
Can people really reach this?
Can we love God, here in this world, with all our heart, soul, strength, and mind?
Is it our privilege and our duty to have the Spirit of Christ? Then should we show the spirit of the devil?

Dear friends, let us set our hearts on perfect love. Let us give God no rest until we feel our hearts full of love, and until all our thoughts and our whole lives are full of love for God and love for people.
Oh, when will the church rise to this level?

If the church will only be full of love, she will be as beautiful as the moon and as bright as the sun. She will be as frightening to all evil, among the powerful and the lowly, as an army marching with its flags flying.
“Tell one another the wrong things you have done, and pray for one another, so that you can be healed.” — James 5:16
In this message we need to look at the following points.
I. What does the command “Confess your faults to one another” mean?
II. What does it take to obey it?
III. Why were we given this command?
IV. What does the command “Pray for one another” mean?

blocks.x: I. What does the command “Confess your faults to one another” mean?

s: 1. There is no reason to think that this verse supports the Roman Catholic teaching that people must confess their sins to priests.
You know the teaching that has been common in that church for so long. It is called “auricular confession,” because it was spoken privately into the priest’s ear.
This teaching says that everyone must privately confess every action and every thought that troubles their conscience at all.
So this system turns the priest into a storehouse for all the sins of the church. He holds all the most private sins of every member, man or woman. And they must confess them, or else face damnation.
Anyone who knows what this system has led to knows that it has naturally done great harm to the purity and morals of both the priests and the people.
It is very clear that the apostle did not have such a system in mind and could never approve of it.
Confessing faults to one another is not the same as confessing all your faults to the priest alone.

2. The verse does not say exactly which sins it means. But we can be sure that the apostle is mainly talking about wrongs done against other people. He is telling us to confess our wrongs to the people we have hurt.
The Bible teaches this kind of confession, and takes it for granted, in many places. So we can take it that this is what is meant here.
But the idea behind this may reach a bit further. (1) It may include telling others about the sins we keep falling into, and about our own special temptations and weaknesses.

Clearly, if we let trusted Christian friends know about these temptations and struggles, we can win their care and their prayers for us. That way we get real help to resist and overcome these temptations.

(2) The idea in this verse may also include sins that are not really done against one certain person, but that are done in front of other people. Because of that, they bring shame on our faith and make the people around us stumble.

Take a short temper, for example. It often makes others stumble, and it can become a sin we keep falling into. Or take the habit of speaking harshly about others. This often deeply hurts not only the people we speak badly about, but also every kind-hearted person who hears us.
Clearly, these sins and others like them should be confessed.
Please notice what I am not saying. I am not saying that people must reveal everything they know—every sin they think they are guilty of—even sins that no one knows about except themselves and God.
The Bible does not seem to make confessing to people a duty that covers everything like that.

blocks.x: II. What does it take to obey this command?

s: 1. First, we must be fully convinced of our sin. We must admit not only that we did it, but also how wicked it was, as a sin against God and against our neighbor.
It is one thing for a person to confess a fault as a real fault and a sin. It is something quite different to admit what happened without seeing how terribly guilty it was.
So our verse must mean that we truly understand the real guilt of our sin and honestly confess it.
2. We must be sorry for our sin, turn away from it, and give it up.
If confession does not come with repentance and giving up the sin we confess, it is nothing but an insult to God and to people.
3. Obeying this command also takes humility.

By humility I mean an attitude that is happy to take its proper place, even if it is a very low place. It does not try to make excuses. Instead, it honestly takes off its own mask and naturally looks for the place that really belongs to us.
Usually the big thing that makes confessing hard is that people are too proud.
They do not like to lower themselves in other people’s eyes as much as they should.
Humility is the exact opposite of this pride. It means being willing to come down to your own low place.
The verse is not talking about a confession that is forced or dragged out of someone.

Sometimes a man confesses only because his conscience stings him like a scorpion. Or he confesses because things have come out in public, and shocking facts have left him cornered, so he has no other way to keep up any appearance of being a Christian. A proud man may have a huge struggle to make that kind of confession. Even so, it is worth very little.
4. True confession means being ready to make up for the wrong we have done.
In fact, confession is in one way a piece of making things right. For example, if you have harmed your neighbor’s property or his good name, admitting what you did is one step in making it right.
But it is far from the whole thing.
If it is about property, you must pay back what was lost. If it is about someone’s good name, you must repair it as much as you can.
This is really part of the spirit of this command.
No one in his right mind would think that if he had stolen something, his confession would be worth anything at all unless he paid it back in full.
And surely the same rule should apply whenever it is possible to make things right.
5. The confession must be full and freely given, not skimpy or forced.
Make it with a free, complete, and honest heart. Make it with an attitude and in a way that will satisfy what the hurt person can fairly expect.
How can we think God will be happy with anything less?
Imagine you have wronged a man, and he knows it and feels it.
You come to him and sort of confess. But instead of making a full confession that settles things, you only hint at the wrong things you did.
He knows you are not an honest man. He knows you have not even done what your own conscience demands.
A confession like that cannot do you or your neighbor any good.
So confession should pour out freely like water, full and complete.
6. Real confession means throwing yourself on someone’s mercy.
When people fully confess their sins to God, they stop defending themselves before Him. They throw themselves completely on His mercy.
They rely on His kindness alone and leave themselves entirely in God’s hands.
In the same way, when you confess to a person, you throw yourself on his kindness. You admit your wrong and give up every excuse.
7. When people confess the sins they keep falling into, it shows that they truly want to be holy. It shows they have honestly decided to give up sin and be free of it forever.
I have often been struck by how differently people react when they hear the teaching about being made holy.
Tell a group of people who say they are Christians that, by God’s grace, they can be set free from all sin in this life. The way they react will often say a lot about what they are really like.
It shows exactly how they feel about sin.
For example, I once preached on this subject in Rochester. As soon as the crowd had left, one man came up to me and said very seriously, “Mr. Finney, that news is too good to be true.”
But there was a minister in that crowd who did not think it was good news at all.
He did not act as if he had any wish for the teaching to be true.
Who has not noticed this very difference?
Preach about being saved from sin right now to a man who is really longing to be set free from sin. He will greet it with deep interest, and maybe even welcome it with an open heart right away.
He will accept it very gladly if he thinks it might be true.
He will long for it to turn out true. His heart will not put up any roadblocks when he honestly looks into the evidence. And he will warmly accept everything the evidence can be shown to support.

But if he does not want it to be true, he will bitterly pick at it and find fault with it. He will stubbornly push away the evidence. And of course he will likely show, without realizing it, that he is an enemy of all that is right.
He will show that he has no interest in being set free from sin now—and no real interest in ever being free from sin.
These things show what a person is really like inside much better than anything else can.
No one who truly longed in his heart to become holy has ever picked at this teaching and found fault with it.
Even if he does not believe the teaching is true, and so feels he has to oppose it, he will not have a fault-finding spirit.
When you see people nitpicking at any teaching, you can be sure they do not want it to be true.
Their hearts do not like it.

Lately the teaching that we can be made completely holy has faced a lot of opposition. People claimed they were only being zealous for the truth and fighting against error. But in the end, before God and the whole world, it has been nothing more or less than a fault-finding spirit. It has plainly been opposition to the truth and an unwillingness to see that teaching proved true. Who does not know this?
It has been sad and shocking to see how much real opposition to holiness has shown up in many places over the last few years.
I am sure I am not saying this in a harsh, judging spirit.

Everyone who has kept his eyes open knows it is true. They have seen the real attacks on the teaching of holiness in this life—from pulpits and in the press, through church organizations, and in many other ways.

But back to the point. When Christians tell their fellow believers about their deep sin, it always shows that they are truly longing for holiness. It shows that they hate the sins they confess. And it shows they are ready to do anything, no matter how humbling, to put to death these horrible sins they hate so much.

blocks.x: III. Why are we told, “Confess your faults to one another”?

s: When it comes to harm we have done to others, this command is based on justice.
Confession is a necessary part of making things right.
We cannot be fair to the brother we have hurt without it.
Also, confession is necessary for peace with God.
It is simply impossible for us to have peace with God if we do not confess the wrongs we know we have done to our neighbor.
Who needs to be told that God can have nothing to do with injustice—and of course nothing to do with people who act unjustly!
Doesn’t He see every sin? The neighbor you hurt could come to the Lord and say, “Lord, he has wronged me. You know it. Will You still be close to him now?”
Confession is just as necessary for peace of mind as it is for peace with God.
Suppose the whole world were at peace with us. And suppose, if it were possible, that God were at peace with us too. We still could not convince ourselves that we are in the right.
Our conscience will keep blaming us forever, until we confess and do everything we possibly can in our situation to make up for the wrong things we have done.
Confession is necessary for peace with the people we have hurt.

The person we hurt may hold no grudge against us. He may have no attitude that goes against the gospel and no wish to get back at us. Even so, he cannot feel Christian closeness and harmony with us as long as he knows we are not sorry and will not confess the wrongs we know about.
This is a problem—a wall between us. It cannot be taken down until he is sure that I am honest. And he cannot be sure of that until I confess my fault.
Confession is necessary for peace and closeness with all people who are fair and good.
It is true that neither God nor the person who was hurt can be at peace with the wrongdoer until he confesses. The same is just as true of all holy beings.
Their minds cannot be at peace and in harmony with me while they know I have done wrong and will not confess.
As long as they know I am in this condition, they have to see me as a lawbreaker. And that has to put a wall between me and them that will never go away.
They may have no wish to get back at me or hurt me. In fact, they may be praying very earnestly for me, asking God to humble me and break down my pride.
Their attitude toward me may be nothing but true kindness. Still, until I confess, they cannot share Christian closeness and friendship with me.
It is simply impossible.
The same is true even of wicked people.
They cannot be at peace with me until I confess my wrongs.
It is amazing, but a wicked man condemns wrongdoing just as truly as a good man does—even though he may do the very same thing himself.
His judgments about right and wrong can be fair and true, even though his own character is bad.
Give him a case where his own selfishness does not bribe his conscience and blind his thinking. Then he will decide that wrong is wrong, and that it ought to be confessed and put away.
So you cannot have the respect of even wicked people unless you confess the wrongs you know about.
Even the most wicked people, or the devils in hell, cannot be satisfied that what you are doing is right until you confess.
They might not love you if you became holy. But they certainly can never respect you until you do—never until you confess and give up all the wrong things you know you have done.
They can never excuse and approve of your sins.
Confessing your wrongs is necessary for self-respect.
It is simply impossible for you to respect yourself while you hold back from properly confessing your sins.
The very laws of your moral nature make this impossible.
Who does not know this?
If you do not know it, you certainly can know it. If you pay even a little careful attention to the warnings of your own conscience, you certainly can know it.

Surely fighting against the demands of a conscience that knows the truth will do you no good. Even if the whole universe left you alone in your sin, your conscience would not and could not leave you alone.
Its voice would still ring in your ears, and you could not silence its scolding.
Haven’t you sometimes been ashamed of yourself because you were too proud to confess?
This very shame about confessing has filled your soul with bitter pain and the sharpest self-blame. Sometimes you have felt that it is a bigger shame and a deeper guilt than the first wrong itself.
Imagine you happen to meet the very man you have wronged.
You have the perfect chance to make the confession you know you owe him—but shame and pride keep your mouth shut.
You do not whisper a single word of confession.
You walk away full of regret and guilty shame. You can hardly help feeling that this last sin is worse than the first one.
A doctor in this kind of situation once cried out, “Oh, how full of hell I am!” And perhaps you sometimes feel you have to say the same thing.
You know that what you feel in your soul is a foretaste of hell. For you are all too sure that you deserve the deepest, darkest place in the home of the damned.
No one else can trust you or respect you as long as people know you will not confess the wrongs you know about.
You may work hard to win back their trust—but all your work will be wasted.
You may hope to live it down. You may try to wash away, with good deeds, the ugly stain that sticks to you because of bad deeds you have not confessed. But you will surely work for nothing.
Who can think you are an honest man?
The truth is, they know better. You have given them the clearest possible proof that you are extremely proud and selfish.
Act as saintly as you like. You still cannot make them trust you as an honest Christian man until you confess your sins wherever the situation calls for confession.
Think about this too: you can never win back the trust of wise, observant people until you are willing to go further in confessing than you are absolutely forced to go.
People often go as far as they have to, but not one step further.
They make it very clear that they only keep going on the path of confession because they are pushed so hard they cannot avoid it.
Step by step—one step at a time, only as fast as they have to and no faster—they move along.
I have often stood and watched this strange process in amazement.
The guilty man finds that one thing has come out too clearly to deny any longer. So he confesses that—but nothing more.
“No,” he says, “that’s all.”
Soon another part of the same business comes out, and it is even darker than the first.
“Sir, you are guilty of this too!”
“No, I’m not.
You can’t prove it.”
“Yes, my friend, it has been proved beyond any doubt.”
“Oh, well then, I confess that. I am very sorry. But that’s all.
There is nothing more.”
Then by the next day some new fact comes up, and he goes down the same road all over again.
First he denies it, then it is proved, then he confesses. And then, to save what is left of his good name, he begs you to accept his solemn promise that there is nothing more like it to come out.
A man like that often uses up his good name faster than he realizes.
He hardly stops to think how worthless his forced confessions become. Nor does he see how little anyone trusts his most solemn promises that he has confessed everything.
It is much better to go all the way to the bottom right at the start.
Yes, go to the bottom—pour it all out—all of it. Do it so completely that neither people nor God can find anything more to do with that matter.
Do this, and there is hope for you.
People will say about you, “Now we know his heart is honest. Even though he has done wrong, he opens his heart completely, and we can trust him again.”
It is not in human nature to resist the pull that sincere, honest-hearted confession has on the human heart.
Also, confessing the wrongs we have done to others is very helpful to both people involved.
It brings great relief to the guilty person. It rolls a weight as heavy as a mountain off his soul, and it brings back sweet peace and joy.
On the other side, the person who was wronged often seems to need it.
You may remember a story I told not long ago about Dr. Hopkins. His deep and wholehearted confessions led to the conversion of his wicked brother-in-law.
Confessions will often do what nothing else can do.
They often show wicked people that Christians are completely different from them in spirit.
Wicked people know they do not confess their faults like that. They know nothing about that kind of broken spirit.
That is why the confessions of a humble Christian reach their conscience like nothing else can.
I have often seen people spread conviction of sin like fire through a whole congregation just by simply confessing their own sins.
I remember right now the story of a minister whose confession to his church started a wonderful revival.
