He had been to Rome during the great revival there. There he became deeply convinced of how guilty he was for caring so little about whether his people were saved.
He went back home and wrote a sermon for his church. But when he stood up in the pulpit the next Sunday, he could not preach it.
His heart was so full it felt ready to burst, and he told the people he could not preach a single word.
“Oh,” he said, “I have been with you for so many years, and how little I have cared about your souls!
I have tried to please you. I have done my regular duties, but with far too little heart. Oh, how guilty I am for ignoring whether your dying souls were saved!”
He had hardly started confessing like this when the deacon wanted to confess too, and then other church members. That church building became another Bochim.
The Lord was there, and His work moved forward with power.
You can easily see what effect that minister’s confession had.
Everyone said, “If our minister has sins to confess, so do we!
If he has reason to confess with such sorrow and bitter tears, we have so much more reason!”
So his confessions did what none of his sermons had ever done.
Also, honest confessions bring great honor to the person who makes them.
There may be no other way that people show more strongly how sincerely they love what is right.

It surely says a lot about a man’s honesty when he shows he loves what is right so fully and strongly that he does not hold back for a moment from condemning himself for any wrong he knows he has done.
His love of what is right wins out over his pride in his reputation.
This man’s confessions are a noble proof that his heart is deeply sincere.
How strange that people should be ashamed to confess their sins!
They could not make this big mistake unless they were “treating darkness as light and light as darkness.”
Isn’t it very honorable for a man who has done wrong to make it right—for a man who has sinned to make a full and free confession?
How strange that people should be afraid to confess!

They might as well be ashamed to show that they are honest. They might as well be ashamed to let the world see that they care more about what is right than about a reputation they do not deserve—a reputation for being something they are not.
Confessions help take the weight off the mind of the person who was hurt, and they lead him to forgive.
Wrongs done to people, especially by those who say they are Christians, often become big traps and temptations for them.
Many people are overcome by them. They fall into a bad state of mind, where God’s truth and grace seem to do their hearts no good.

Maybe they know it is wrong to hold on to such feelings. But, they say, they have been treated very badly—and by someone who claims to be a Christian, too! And they find it hard to get what happened out of their minds.
In cases like this, an honest confession by the one who did the wrong is the natural cure.
It usually does more than anything else—more than everything else put together—to remove that terrible stumbling block.
Christian reader, is any sinner stumbling like this because of some sin of yours?
Be careful that you do not trap his soul and bring him to ruin.
Be careful that the blood of his murdered soul is not found on your clothes!
I have sometimes seen one man keep provoking another until he made him angry, and then scold him for that very anger, instead of blaming himself for causing it.
This is cruel and wicked.

The man who has made another person angry like this ought to humble himself and confess completely. He should say, “I have acted in a very low and mean way. I tempted you to sin, and then I scolded you for giving in to my temptation—when I should have scolded myself most of all.
I am sorry. I am grieved by my own wickedness, and I condemn it.”

You may remember a story that is told about a man who was against Wesley’s teaching about being made holy. He wanted to prove that a certain person who believed that teaching was not completely holy. So he took a washbowl full of dirty water and threw it in that person’s face.
Now let’s suppose the man who was wronged got offended and angry. Seeing this, the one who did the wrong gloats and says, “Some holiness this is—getting angry over such a small thing!”
But notice how unbelievably low and wicked it is for this man to tempt someone to sin like that.
He should break down and confess his own sin with shame.
He should say, “I am the guilty wretch in all this!”
If he did this, repentance would pour freely from both of their hearts.
Also, confessing is a strong way to win the prayers of the people you have sinned against and to whom you confess.
Nothing works better to make them want to pray for you right away.
How naturally they cry out, “O Lord, forgive this man, because he admits his wrong. Forgive all his sins and show him the light of Your face.”
It is also very helpful to confess the sins we keep falling into to people we have not hurt, so that we can get help to overcome those sins.
It usually makes our fellow Christians care a great deal about us.
Who does not know how strongly the heart is moved to pray for people who confess the sins they keep falling into like this?
Haven’t you experienced this yourself?
IV. In this setting, it is easy to understand what it means to pray for one another.
It means that we care deeply about the spiritual well-being of those who confess their faults. It means we use our influence with God to win their pardon.
It is like signing a petition asking that they be set free from the punishment for breaking the law.

Imagine that your neighbor has broken the law of the state. He is found guilty and sent to the state prison for life. But he is deeply sorry and shows that he is a changed man. Now someone brings you a petition asking for his pardon, and they ask you to sign it.
Will you join in the request?
Will you say, “Does he confess his sin?
If he does, I can pray for his pardon.”
In the same way, when people confess their sins to God and to others, you should pray for God to forgive them.
God commands you to do it.
V. Obeying this command means having a real spirit of forgiveness. It means wanting God to forgive, and showing that wish through real prayer to God.
This is too obvious to need an example.
When people confess the sins they keep falling into, it means we should care about their becoming holy and pray hard to God for this great result.

blocks.x: Remarks.

s: 1. Wrongs done against the public should be confessed in public.
No one can have any doubt about this.
If a confession should be made at all, it should be made to the people who were sinned against.
2. Wrongs against individuals may be done either in public or in private. Either way, the confession should match how the wrong was done and how public it was.
Suppose a man hurts another man’s reputation in public by writing lies about him or preaching lies about him. Then the sin is public. Clearly the confession should reach as far as the wrong did.
If you can, you must take back your words just as widely as you spread the wrong.
3. You can see why many people never overcome the sins they keep falling into.
They are never humble and honest enough to confess them. They never pour out their hearts to their fellow believers so as to win their care and prayers for themselves.
They never use the great moral lever that confession gives. Confession slides under a person’s giant sins like a lever, to dig them up and roll them out and away forever.
4. You can see how wrong it is to think that confessing to God is enough, and that confessing to people is useless and not required.
The Catholic teaching about confession has pushed many Protestants to the opposite extreme. So many churches are against having anyone confess anything at all in front of others.
But just because Catholics have misused the teaching about confession, it does not at all mean we should throw it all away.
It does not mean we have no duty to confess to the people we have hurt.
Not at all! If that way of thinking were right, we would soon lose all our Bibles.
5. I have often seen people suffer for a long time under a load of sins that no one else knew about. These were sins they might not have needed to confess at all, except for their great pride.
But God saw that their pride had to be humbled, and He could not give their souls peace until it was.

So let a man like that go to the people whose good opinion he cares about most and confess his sins. Let him really take up his cross in this, and not go easy on his proud heart at all. He will find it is an excellent cure.
I have often seen this done.
A man goes to someone he respects very much and says, “My pride has trapped me. It is dragging me away from God and down to hell, and I am determined to defeat it.”
Then he pours out his confession of sin.
This is like grabbing a big club to crush the snake’s head—the head of wicked pride. And it usually works.
People in this situation will often find that confession is absolutely necessary.
6. When both people are to blame for a personal fault, neither one should ever wait for the other to confess first.
Let each one hurry to confess as warmly and fully as he can. Then the right spirit will win out, and each will encourage the other to do good.
Often one person holds back because he is afraid the other will use his confession against him.
It does not matter if he does.
I mean that, compared with everything else, it does not matter enough to think about for a moment.
It is far, far more important that you do what is right before God, the world, and the man you have hurt, than that you hold back your confession to keep him from misusing it.
Besides, there is not much danger that he will.
And if he does, he alone is responsible.
I once knew a man in a situation like this who said, “I will confess my wrong. If my neighbor does not want to confess his, or if he chooses to misuse what I confess, he alone must carry the blame.”

He poured out his confessions like water and found sweet relief and peace in his soul. Soon after that he died. That neighbor, and every enemy he had, grieved bitterly over his grave. They admitted that at least one good man had lived.

I once knew a church that was in serious trouble. Its members were set against each other, with strong prejudices, and they had taken sides. But in the end, the spirit of confession began to win out. Each man felt he was more to blame than his neighbor. Now the only contest was to see who could confess first and confess the most.

The argument now was not about each one proving that his neighbor was at fault. Instead, each one argued that he himself had been the worst sinner, and the main cause of both his own sins and his neighbor’s.
Every man was ready to take his hand off his neighbor and lay it on himself.
This was good. If you could have seen those humbled Christians confessing their sins, you would have said, “It is good to come down low and get the spirit of confession.”
In situations like this, confessing to each other seems to be the only thing that can save the good name of Christians and save the church.
When people have done wrong, they must humble themselves and confess their faults to one another.
It is a beautiful sight to see two believers meet each other in a spirit of confessing, forgiving, and praying for each other.
God is glad about it, and every holy angel in heaven sings a new note of joy and praise.
It is one of the loveliest scenes ever seen on earth.
Prayer offered in situations like this is especially powerful.

Imagine you had been wronged. The person who wronged you is taken to court, found guilty, and sentenced. But over time he becomes truly sorry. You are ready to forgive him, so you send a request to the governor asking him to pardon the man.
Who does not know that your name will count ten times more, because of your special connection to that crime?
That is how it was with Job and his three friends.
They had spoken unkindly about him, and they had good reason to ask him to forgive them.
God was angry with them. What did He say?
“Go to My servant Job,” He said. “My servant Job will pray for you, because I will accept him.”
They had accused Job of being a hypocrite.
Now let them make things right with Job and get him to pray to the Lord for them. Then they can be forgiven.
He, more than anyone else, is the right man to pray for them.
God can hear him.
Have you wronged a brother in the faith?
Go and confess to him, and beg him to pray for you.
He is the right person to pray for you.
God can hear him.
Humble yourself at his feet until he can feel enough faith to pray for you. Then you can hope for a prayer that will make a difference with the Lord.
“Oh,” said a slave owner who was dying, “how can I die here in my bed with no one praying for my guilty soul?”
His caring wife said, “What should I do? Should I send for the minister?”
“No, no,” said the dying man. “Send for my slave Tom.
I have heard him pray in my barn many times. Send for him.”
Tom came in quietly, tucked his hat under his arm, and walked over to the bed. “What does Master want?”

“Tom, I want you to pray for your dying master. I have wronged you and robbed you of your freedom for all these years. I am sorry. Oh, if only I could live to make it up to you! But if you can pray for a poor lost sinner, please pray!”
And who would not rather have the prayers of the man he had enslaved and wronged than the prayers of everyone else on earth?
A prayer like that is worth more than a whole world of other prayers!
But how can you have it without confessing?
“God loved the world so much that he gave his only Son. Whoever believes in him will not perish but will have everlasting life.” — John 3:16
The word “world” here does not mean the planet we live on. It means the human race.
The word is often used this way.
“The world” and “the whole world” are phrases often used to mean the people who live in the world—the human race as a whole.
In this verse, the word “perish” does not mean being wiped out of existence. It is clearly set against “everlasting life” as its opposite.

As it is used here, “everlasting life” does not simply mean existing forever. I do not know of any other part of the Bible where the term is used in that sense. Whether existing forever is a blessing or not depends on the state people are in—whether they are happy or miserable.
In some situations, existing forever could be anything but a blessing.

The everlasting life spoken of here is surely living forever with God in heaven. It is existing forever and being happy forever. This is the eternal life the Scriptures speak of so often, and surely it is what is meant here.

To perish is the opposite of this. It does not mean being wiped out or simply ceasing to exist. For the person sentenced, being wiped out would often be no harm at all. For someone who is miserable, it would not be a harm but a great favor.
In short, it is very clear that to perish is the exact opposite of everlasting life. It means everlasting death—a state of punishment that never ends.
As I speak about these words, I plan to look at—
I. Who this love is for.
II. What kind of love it is.
III. Why this love went so far as to give God’s only Son for people.
IV. What the faith is that can win this great goal—the salvation of the soul—and why that faith is needed.
I. Who this love is for.
This love is for the world. Not for part of it, but for the world.

There is no reason, in the nature of things, why one part of humanity should be loved more than another. Notice this: God did not show this love to saints as saints. It had nothing to do with the character of the people of the world. It was shown to a world of sinners.
God loved people as a race—as sinners, as God’s enemies.

So there was no reason to love one part of this race of sinners and not all of them. The kind of love that could love some people must, by its very nature, love them all. This is the only love a good being could have shown toward people—a love for everyone.
But this leads me next to ask about—

blocks.x: II. What kind of love this is.

s: First, I point out that this could not have been a love that takes pleasure in people’s character. There was nothing in the character of the human race that would allow God to love them or take any delight in their character. That is completely certain.
God could not possibly have loved humanity with a love that approves of them. That would have made him infinitely more wicked than they were.
What does loving a wicked person involve?

Why, it involves being in sympathy with his character. God could not have loved them with an approving love without being infinitely more wicked than they were. For an infinite being to be in sympathy with wicked natures, he would have to be infinitely wicked himself.
It is certain that this love could not have been based on people’s character. They were not loved for their character. That is impossible.

Again, this love could not have been just an emotion. Emotion does not affect how we live unless the will is involved. Emotion does not cause anything. It cannot bring anything into being—not even strong emotion can. It is only a state of mind we do not choose, something that belongs to our feelings. It often moves us to act and can push the will. But feeling alone never caused anything. The power to cause things lives in the will of every moral being, and it is very different from emotion.
Again, it was not a fondness for certain people.
There was no reason in God’s nature, and no reason in people, for God to feel any such fondness.
I also point out that it was not a love he could not help. What it did makes this clear.
It must have been a love he chose, because the proof of its power is right here in front of us. And it was a love that got things done because it was a chosen love.
Again, it was not an unreasonable state of mind.
Of course, there was nothing in human character that would allow for an approving love. Still, this love was not unreasonable at all. Reason did not forbid it.
Sometimes we see people have feelings that are completely unreasonable.
Sometimes we see deep affection—what we call love—among people in a way that goes completely against reason.
But God had a good reason for this love. It was something his own understanding and conscience approved.
There was something about people that made it reasonable for God to love them with a certain kind of love.
I also point out that the love God actually showed was the only kind of love that could have mattered to people.
If God’s love had been only emotion, or pity, it would have done people no good.
So this love must have been a reasonable affection. It must have been a reasonable love.
When we look at the nature of this love simply and reasonably, there can be no doubt about what it really is.
I point out that it was good will, or benevolence.
This is clear from the fact that it worked for the good of those it loved, in a most striking and wonderful way.
It was clearly good will, because it led to good actions.
Again, it was an unselfish kind of love.
God did not love people because they deserved to have him do them good. All they deserved from him was evil.

Notice, there was a good reason for him to love them. But they had no right to demand his love as a matter of justice. They had lost every claim to his affection or protection. So of course justice did not require God to do them good.

But let me say again: the human soul was of great worth. Its happiness would matter infinitely, and its misery would be a terrible evil. Looking at the true worth of their souls, God saw good reason to love people and do them good. In other words, God did good for the sake of the good itself. He wanted good for them because that good was so valuable to them in itself—infinitely valuable—and not because they deserved it at all.

They had no claim on him for this love. In fact, there were strong reasons for him to destroy them. Even so, their souls were so valuable, he pitied them so much as he saw their coming and certain destruction, and he loved and wanted their happiness so greatly, that he overcame every obstacle. He rose above any desire to punish them or pay them back for their wickedness, and he sought only to do them good.
As I have said, there was good reason for this. It was not because of what people had done, but because of how valuable their souls were.

I point out once more that this love was a selfless love. By this I mean that he did not have his own interest in view as the reason for doing this. It was love for the world. It was a desire to do them good. It was love for their good that led him to do it.
He did not plan to help them so that he could gain some great good for himself in a selfish way. It was a completely selfless love.
In fact, he did find joy in it himself. Yet it was a completely selfless love, and so it will bring him all the more glory.
The more single-mindedly he aimed to secure their good, the more he gained his own approval and the admiration and praise of all holy beings.

When I say selfless love, I do not mean that he had no interest in it. He had an infinite interest in what he did. But I mean that his love was completely unselfish. He tried to do good because the good itself is so valuable.
But let me say again: this must have been an amazingly strong love. It could not have been a weak state of mind. It must have been infinitely intense!
Just think about it!
“God loved the world so much that he gave his only Son!”
What a wonder this was!
On one side was a world of enemies at war with him. On the other side stood his beloved Son—his only Son, the Son he loved so dearly.

Just look at this. Imagine a state of mind that would choose to give that Son—that only Son, that dearly loved Son—to die for those rebels who stood there with the weapons of rebellion in their hands.

They had rebelled against his government. They deserved his frown and his anger, and his own conscience clearly declared that they deserved to be sent away from his presence. Yet he valued their souls so highly, and he weighed so seriously the terrible suffering they would face if the law’s penalty fell on them, that he gave his Son. He would rather do that than send that world of rebels away from the glory of his power to die in their guilt.
No one will understand how strong this love must have been to lead to such a decision—unless he thinks deeply about these things.

Let a parent imagine this, if he can. He has an only child who has never offended him. This child is the darling of his heart. He loves this child as much as he loves himself, and he has reason to. Could he give up that child for the good of his enemies?

Suppose people abuse him and do everything they can to hurt him. They make themselves as hateful as possible, so that they deserve his anger and condemnation, and his total rejection and disgust with them forever.
Now imagine a state of mind that could deliberately make a choice like the one God made.

It was not a matter of sacrificing an innocent person in place of the guilty. It was not a matter of punishing Christ—agreeing that Christ should suffer instead of sinners being punished. No, there was no such idea in God’s mind.
But later on we will look more fully at why God gave his Son to die for the good of the world.
Right now I am talking about how intense this love was.

Now imagine, if you can, your son on one side and your enemies on the other. Think what struggles you would feel as you realized that either these enemies must perish forever or you must give up your son!

You see that he is willing. He is ready to take on the task of rescuing them from death. He is willing to accept everything involved in being their Savior. But it requires your consent. You must enter into it with your heart and say to him, “Go.”

When we realize what God must have felt in such a situation, it is easy to understand how intense his love was. It was a love that could overcome the feelings that would naturally cling to his Son, and give him up for the good of the world.
Just think how many things there must have been against this.
God knew what it would cost him. He knew his Son must go through trials, suffering, persecution, poverty, and agony.

The Father saw every trial and every pain his Son would have to go through. He saw him weighed down with sorrow and despised. He saw him in the garden, too, when he sweated what looked like great drops of blood, because his agony was so great. All this was before God’s mind when he gave up his Son to be the Savior of the world.
The Father saw his Son so weary that he was ready to faint as he carried his cross up the hill of Calvary. His cruel persecutors had to put the load on someone else.
He saw him mocked and pierced on the cross. He saw him in the agonies of death and heard his pitiful cry, “My God, my God, why have you deserted me?”
How many scenes must have crowded into God’s mind, all urging him not to give his Son to save a guilty world!
Yet his love was so great that he overcame all these obstacles. He freely gave him up for us all, so that we would not perish but have everlasting life.
Dear listeners, let this truth take hold of your minds.

I must not say more about this. But I must go on to say something that must never be forgotten or overlooked: it was love for enemies, not for friends. Notice that the whole world was in view. It was as sinners that God gave Christ to die for them. They were a race of sinners.
Notice, God did not give his Son for a single Christian as a Christian. He gave him for sinners as sinners, for rebels as rebels. It was with their sinfulness in full view that God gave his Son.
It is very important always to keep this in mind: God gave his Son not for good people but for bad people, not for the righteous but for the wicked.
Again, it was a patient love.
Some people seem to think that when we speak of God denying himself, we are suggesting that he is sometimes selfish.
But let me say this: in any being, self-denial always means the very opposite of selfishness. It means agreeing to give up some good, or to suffer some evil, for the benefit of others.
Of course, no one who is living selfishly can practice self-denial.
It was self-denial for God to agree to deny himself by giving up his Son. It must have been very hard on his feelings to agree to give up his Son to die for the world.
But I must not say more about this.
Let me say again: of course it was a universal love.
It was not love for human beings only. It reached to other worlds.
No doubt it was largely with other worlds in view that he chose the course he took in forgiving sin in this world.
It was the good of his whole kingdom, everywhere, that led him to take this particular step.
Again, his love was a holy love. It hated sin.

This love was shown to sinners. So it was very important that something be done to make the whole universe understand one thing. Although it was love for sinners as sinners, it did not mean he was turning a blind eye to their sin.

In fact, as anyone can see, this was the main and most important point. Since his love was shown to sinners, how could he fully guard against the impression that he was turning a blind eye to their sins? For notice, he was going to show great love for sinners by giving himself fully to doing them good.
Now pay attention: how would people know that he was as much against their sin as he had said he was, and as the conscience of all beings required him to be?
It is often a delicate matter for human rulers to show love and kindness to people who are rebels against the government.
It is a very delicate matter for the governments of great and wide empires to show deep and anxious love for people who are enemies of the law and who defy it.
There is also a great danger that the justice of the law will be pushed into the shadows. Respect for the law may be lost, and the sin of the rebellion may be forgotten.

In God’s government the danger of this was infinite. So while he pardoned the sinner, he needed to show as strongly as possible that he was against sin. In this way he would make it plain to the world that he was not turning a blind eye to their sin.
But again, this love was just as truly as it was merciful. That is, it was just toward the universe.
In his government there were other interests besides the interests of sinners.
There were reasons why he must not put his authority at risk or weaken respect for his law.
It is easy to see that justice to the universe required him to be careful about how he showed the great and infinite love he had in his heart for sinners.
This leads me to look at—
III. The reasons for this wonderful step in God’s government.

Notice that his love aimed to bring about the world’s salvation. He wanted to save those who deserved to die. And we are told that he took this step of giving his only Son for sinners—a wonderful step indeed!
It is clear that the reason for this was anything but ill will on God’s part.
Again, what led him to do it was anything but anger at them.
Of course, in one sense he felt a holy anger at their sins. But it was not this anger that led him to give his Son. He gave him in spite of his just and holy anger at their sins.
So it was not God’s anger but his wish to be merciful that led God to require Christ to die for sinners.

God wanted to be merciful. This was the secret of the whole thing. This was the great foundation of the whole plan. The very reason God took on the task of saving them was that he loved them and wanted to show them favor.
So I say it was not a lack of mercy, and it was not hatred. It was love for sinners—the one great reason that led God to show mercy to people.
There was one great reason in God’s mind, the most basic reason of all: his love for sinners.
Now notice: we are told that God took this step of giving his Son to secure the good of the world. For several reasons, which I will name, he did not pay them back for all their opposition to him.
Notice that there must have been some very serious reasons. There must also have been reasons that had to be overcome, and they could not be overcome by any step other than the one he actually took.
We should always understand that God acts reasonably, for wise and good reasons.
So no one should think that he used any harsh measure that was not needed.
No one can reasonably think that God used any means that could have been avoided in that situation.
He had set his heart on the means—wise means, means that the circumstances and the occasion called for.
Who can believe that he used any other means?
But let us look at the reasons for the particular step he took.
It is very important to understand them.

We have seen that God had a good reason for the step he took. It was a sufficient reason, a reason that could not have been set aside or overcome. But now let us find out, if we can, what these reasons were.
Whatever they were, the law of good will must have approved them, or they could not have been virtuous.
If the step had not been approved by the eternal laws of God’s own reason, he could never have taken it.
But in fact it is simple enough. It does not take great learning to understand it. You only need to look at it, and everyone can see right away that such circumstances called for such a step.

Look at the situation. The human race had resisted God’s government. They had denied that his law was just—the law that even the angels obey, and that is absolutely necessary for the well-being of the universe and for their own salvation.
If God had seemed to turn a blind eye to people disobeying his law—the law of the whole universe—all other beings might have denied that the law was just, and disobeyed it too.
So notice: the whole universe, everyone who lives in heaven, had a strong interest in upholding this law.
Now pay attention! This law had been disobeyed. A public lie had been told, and people kept on telling it. They had denied that the law was just, and they did it very deliberately.
So what was to be done?
Clearly, something had to be done that could not be taken to mean he was turning a blind eye to this rebellion.
Now look at how man and God were related.
God’s law had been trampled down, and the whole universe was watching God to see what he would do. The well-being of all depended on it.

Because of his relation to the universe, he had to either carry out the law or give a demonstration of his own, from his own heart. For what the universe needed was to see how highly he valued the law.
It was up to him to act, and everything depended on the path he chose.

It is easy to see that God himself could fully uphold the honor of the law. He could do this by showing the whole universe that he approved of the law and of the public good. Such a demonstration would serve the same purpose as carrying out the law on the offenders.

Suppose God took on human nature. Suppose that in this nature—both God and man—he stood out in plain view before the whole universe and obeyed the law’s commands. This would be the highest proof he could possibly give, in any way at all, of his respect for the law.

He would take on the nature of those who broke the law. In that nature he would obey its command and suffer its penalty. Then the demonstration would be complete, and the law would be perfectly honored.

Now suppose that Christ, his eternal Son, stood forward in this way as the representative of the race of rebels. He had no sin in himself. Yet he stood in a position as if the sin of the whole race were summed up in him, and the whole rebellion were centered in him. It is easy to see that God could then pardon sinners and still honor the law.

Pay attention! He stands as the representative of the world, as the representative of sin. And it is easy to see that this plan made a far deeper impression than carrying out the law on the rebels themselves would have made.
The Lawgiver himself steps forward to show the beauty of his own law and to defend its honor.
But I must not say more about this.

Under this point, I only need to say that it is perfectly easy to see how this step affected the universe itself. It perfectly met the urgent need of God’s government and made it completely safe for God to pardon the guilty.
Next, I will make a few remarks about—
IV. The nature of faith.
Now notice the motive that led God to do this.

I have sometimes heard people talk about Christ’s atonement and God’s motive in a certain way. It showed that if they really believed God had the kind of motive they gave him, they could not possibly respect him.

They speak of the atonement as if it did not come from a merciful heart in God. They speak of it as collecting a debt, as if God required a certain amount of payment for every sinner before he would forgive. They say it did not come from a merciful heart.
I say that if anyone believes this, he cannot even respect God’s character.
But we are taught that God gave his Son to die for people as sinners, out of love for them. And we are taught that they receive the blessing by putting their faith in Christ.
That is what gives it all its power.
Just let a sinner understand that God loves him as a sinner. If anything can break his heart, that will.
I do not mean that knowing this will always do it. But I do say that if this does not, nothing will.
In short, sinners must truly grasp and believe this declaration of love for them if they are to be saved.
A few remarks must close what I have to say.
First, many people miss the nature of this love because they cannot imagine how God can love sinners.
I know this from my own life, because I stumbled over this point for a long time.
I had not experienced a love of good will at all.
I had loved. I knew what the word meant in some of its senses.

I knew what it was to take delight in people whose character I admired. And I knew what fond affection is like among selfish people. But notice, this was the only kind of love I had known. So I could not understand how God could love a wicked man. It seemed impossible to me that God should love a sinner.
I said to myself, “If God can love a sinner, he must be a sinner himself.” And do you think God can be a sinner?
You see, I was judging God by my own selfish love.
The love I had known involved some fellowship and sympathy with the one I loved.
At last I was able to understand that God could love people without a selfish love.
Many people speak very carelessly about this subject. They do not understand the nature of God’s love for sinners—a selfish mind cannot.
When a sinner first becomes convinced of his sin, he thinks it is completely impossible for God to love him. He is ready to cry out, “He can no more love me than he can love the devil.”
And that is partly true.
God can no more love the sinner with a love that approves of him and is in sympathy with him than he can love the devil that way—not one bit more.
But sinner, there is another way of looking at this that is very important for you to see. There is a kind of love you know nothing about—love for your enemies.
“Oh,” you say, “what reason do I have to love them?”
Why, you have the same reason to love them that God has—exactly the same!
God does not love with an approving love, which means being in sympathy with people’s character. But make no mistake, sinner: he can love you with a love you cannot even imagine.

The kind of love God will show is exactly the kind you ought to show your enemies. To receive this love, you must rise completely above your selfishness and give yourselves wholeheartedly to seeking their good.
The fact is, you have never shown this love, so you cannot understand what it is.
But God can rise above—oh, he was never in the selfish mud your soul is stuck in.
He is not filled with the spirit of revenge that you feel. So even though he sees and knows all the sinner’s guilt, he can still look at him with compassion and give his whole heart to saving him.
But let me say once more: the fact is, sinners misunderstand the nature of God’s love, and so they try to make themselves happy.

They always think they must do something to deserve his love. You ask them to come to Christ, and they say, “I must do more. I must become better. I must pray. I must do this or that to deserve his love.”
You see, they have the idea of an approving love. They think they must deserve it before they can have it. They want to feel that they deserve it.
The sinner will never believe that God loves him as a sinner.
But let me tell you, sinner, this is all wrong. You can never deserve God’s love in the way you hope to have it. And if you try to deserve it that way, you will never be saved.
But remember, it was as a sinner that Christ died for you!
It was as a rebel that God gave his Son to die for you!
Just as you are, in your sins, God loves you. For you, just as you are, he gave his Son to die.
This is what you must believe.
You will find it hard to believe, but you absolutely must believe it.
I beg you, let this idea fill your minds completely. Say to yourself, “Why should I try to make myself deserving, if God loves me now just as I am?”

“It was as I am that Christ died for me. It was as a sinner that God loved me, and he loves me still. So I will go to Jesus as a sinner, just as I am—as a humble, repentant sinner—seeking, but not deserving.”
Will you come? Will you come now?
Will you believe now? Or will you make God a liar?
“So repent of this wickedness of yours, and pray to God. Perhaps he will forgive you for what you had in your heart.
For I can see that you are full of bitter poison and chained up by sin.” Acts 8:22–23
These words were spoken to Simon Magus.
A revival was going on in Samaria while Peter and Philip were working there. Many people turned to God. Simon Magus was one of the people who said they had been converted.
He had been an important man in that town. He had fooled many people with his magic.

Then he saw these Christian apostles do greater wonders than he could. He was amazed. He was an ambitious man, and he grabbed at the idea of getting this new secret so he could have even more power over people.
So he offers the apostles money to buy this new power.
Peter saw right away what was in his heart, and he gave a noble answer: “May your money be destroyed with you! You have no part or share in this, because your heart is not right in God’s sight.”
Then he tells him what to do, in the words of our text: “So repent of this wickedness of yours, and pray to God. Perhaps he will forgive you for what you had in your heart.”
I will follow the order of thought in the text. I will
I. Look at the principle shown here, which helped Peter see that this man was still in his sins;
II. Show what repentance is;
III. Show what repentance includes;
IV. Show why sinners are told to repent first, and then to pray for forgiveness;
V. Explain why it is so important to follow this example whenever we deal with people.
I. Peter did not claim that God had told him what kind of man Simon Magus was.
Peter did not know everything the way God does.
He surely was inspired by God. But inspiration taught him truths that apply to everyone, not what each person is like inside.
Peter could see that Simon’s heart was selfish. It did not fit with the spirit of the gospel at all.
Simon still had the same old attitude. He wanted the power to give the Holy Spirit to anyone he chose. He wanted it for the same reason he had once wanted and valued his magic powers.
That is why he offered money. He acted as if the apostles were as greedy as he was.
Peter saw that he was selfish and therefore blind. He was very far from understanding what Christianity is about.

blocks.x: II. So Peter told him to repent. What is repentance?

s: We must always tell the difference between repentance and being convicted of sin.
Conviction is something that happens in your mind whether you want it or not. So of course there is nothing good or praiseworthy about it.
A person could feel as much conviction as there is in hell itself, and still have nothing good in him.
There is terrible conviction in hell. But there is no real repentance there.
Repentance is also not just feeling sorry.
In fact, strictly speaking, sorrow is not part of repentance at all. Sorrow does not belong to the thinking part of the mind. It belongs even less to the will—the part of us that makes choices.
Repentance is also not the same thing as remorse.
Remorse can be the sharpest and most painful blaming of yourself. But it does not have to mean that you have repented.
A person can feel remorse without changing his mind at all.
Repentance is simply and exactly a change of mind.
The original word means thinking again, or turning the mind around. It is like when someone realizes he is going the wrong way and turns around to go in the opposite direction.

When the word is used for the repentance the gospel calls for, it means more than just a turning of the mind. It means a change in all of a person’s goals. It is a change in the whole direction of the will.
So repentance is not remorse. It is not sorrow. It is nothing like that. It is the mind turning away from selfishness to goodwill—from living for yourself to truly wanting what is good for others.

blocks.x: III. What does repentance include?

s: 1. It includes being convinced that sin is a wrong done against God.
Without this, repentance cannot make any sense.
2. It includes the sinner becoming truly honest with God.
He must honestly admit the truths his reason tells him and his conscience presses on his soul.
Most of all, he must recognize God’s rights. He must see that he himself is God’s property and truly belongs to God.
3. It includes becoming fair and just toward other people—becoming a truly honest person.
Selfishness is the greatest dishonesty in the world.
No selfish person is honest deep down. He could only be honest if a person could be honest while ignoring everyone’s rights but his own.
No! Selfishness is dishonesty in its most complete form.
It is ridiculous for a wicked person to pretend to be honest.
He does not have one bit of real honesty, any more than Satan does!
What is honesty? It is respecting the rights of all other people, and especially God’s rights, as much as they truly deserve.
But the sinner calls himself an honest man while he completely denies God’s rights.
How false their claims are!

They only respect their neighbor’s rights for their own benefit. They do it only because they expect to get something good for themselves out of the respect they pretend to show for their neighbor’s interests.
The truth is, people are completely fooled if they think they are honest with others while they are not really honest with God.
Honesty is not in their hearts.
If they do not love their neighbor as they love themselves, they are not honest.
No one has the right to live as if his own rights and interests matter more than his neighbor’s.
Living that way is both false and dishonest.
4. No one has truly repented unless he is honest in this way: he gives God what belongs to God, and he gives people what belongs to people.
He must start by giving back to God the self he has stolen from him.
God created him. God has kept him alive. God has redeemed him. So God has a claim on him for three reasons. And yet he sets himself up against God and does not share God’s heart at all.
So no one is honest until he repents and turns to God.
The first step is to give himself back to God. Along with himself, he must give whatever is left of his time, his talents, his property, and his influence.
True repentance always means giving back everything you can. The only exception is what you have wasted so completely that you honestly cannot give it back.
5. Repentance includes confessing sin to God and to everyone you have hurt.
No one should think he has truly repented until he has confessed wherever confession is owed.
Some sins are known only to God. Some are committed only against God.
These should be confessed to God.
In a few special cases, God does require people to confess secret sins.
But this is the exception, not the rule.
I cannot go into all the careful distinctions on this subject right now.
But clearly, sometimes you cannot make things right without confessing. For example, you may have damaged someone’s reputation. In that case, you keep on doing wrong unless you confess.
You have misled many people about your neighbor, and it has hurt him. You must undo the wrong you did to him. Otherwise you cannot think you have really repented.
6. Besides confession, repentance always includes restitution—paying back and making things right.
Each person should do this as far as he is able.
This is always part of repentance, because a person who repents also has goodwill toward others.
He loves his neighbor as himself. So, like Zacchaeus, he hurries to pay back what he took. He does not even think it is too hard to pay back four times as much.
7. Repentance means completely giving up every way of life and every kind of business that does not fit with being a Christian.
Do you think a man who truly has goodwill toward others could run a business that ruins people instead of saving them?
Of course not! Would a man who cares about the good of others as much as his own spend his life buying and selling human beings?
He would sooner sell his own flesh and blood! He would sooner sell himself into slavery, or sell the bodies and souls of his own wife and children!
8. Repentance also means giving up not only every selfish kind of business, but every selfish way of doing business—even business that is good in itself.
Selfish people often run a good business in a bad way. They run it on very selfish rules and plans.
Repentance rules this out too. That is because repentance is a change of heart and life, from selfishness to real goodwill.
It means giving up all selfishness.
9. Repentance means a complete change of life. This change reaches every kind of sin.
People who repent turn away from all sin because it is sin. They see it as sin, so they want nothing to do with it.
So they give up every sin they know about right away.
And for them, nothing counts as sin unless they know it is sin. So giving up all known sin really means giving up all sin.
No one has truly repented if he lets himself keep on in some sin he has chosen, and picks and chooses which sins he will enjoy.
That is not repentance at all.

When I talk about giving up sin, I do not mean that a person who repents will never fall back into it, not even for a moment. But I do mean that he sets himself against sin with real honesty and seriousness.
10. Finally, true repentance includes trusting in God and in Jesus Christ.
If a person truly repents of sin, he will of course believe in Jesus Christ.

blocks.x: IV. Peter put these duties in a certain order—repentance first, and then prayer for forgiveness. What does that order show?

s: 1. Peter took it for granted that Simon Magus was completely sinful. He was completely turned away from God, and so he did not want to give up his sins.
That is why Peter could not tell him to pray for forgiveness while he was still in his sins.
Peter knew very well that Simon would jump at the idea of being forgiven before he repented. But Peter wanted to warn him as strongly as he could against this false hope.
He knew that Simon’s sin was that he was clinging to his selfishness. So he told him to give up his sins first and then ask for forgiveness.
Peter assumed that Simon’s great sin was that he did not want to give up his selfishness. This was the sin he had to repent of and get rid of first of all.
2. Peter took it for granted that God could not forgive Simon until he got rid of his sin.
Peter knew what Simon’s big problem was. He knew Simon was holding on to his ambitious, selfish way of life. So he told him plainly that mercy could come to him only after he had fully repented.
3. Peter did not think Simon had any right to ask for forgiveness, or even to want it, until he had repented.
Notice that Peter saw that Simon was unrepentant and selfish.
So Peter assumed that Simon had no right to ask for forgiveness or expect it while his mind was in this state.
He did not tell him to pray for repentance. He knew Simon did not want to repent, so a prayer like that would only be mocking God.
And yet many people tell the sinner to pray for repentance!
Oh, do you want the sinner to mock God?
Peter did not tell Simon to pray for repentance. He knew that until Simon himself was willing to repent, this would only be mocking God. And Peter could not invite him to insult Jehovah.
4. Peter also took it for granted that Simon was fully able to repent.

Some people teach sinners to pray that God would make them able to repent. Many even suggest that the sinner is trying as hard as he can to repent. They say all he needs to do is cry out to God to help him repent. They talk as if the only problem were that God does not give him enough strength!
“Trying to repent” always means two things. It means you are willing to repent, and it means you do not have the power to do it.
Trying means making an effort to do something your mind is set on. If you fail, it means you failed because you did not have enough power.
Now Peter understood this whole subject.
Peter knew that this man had enough free will and enough ability to repent if he wanted to.
So he tells him to repent first, and then to ask for forgiveness.
Asking for forgiveness before repenting would only be blasphemy against God. Peter could not advise him to do that.
5. Peter shows that Simon already had enough conviction, so he did not need to wait for more.
That is why he did not tell him to wait for it. He told him to repent right away.
Of course this means Peter believed he had enough conviction.
Many people tell sinners to pray for conviction, as if they needed more and wanted more. Usually neither of these is true.
6. Peter took it for granted that the sinner has no excuse—no excuse for his sin, and no excuse for refusing to repent.
He insisted that repenting was that man’s duty right then. Of course, that means that as God sees it, every sinner has the duty to repent.
Now it must be extremely important for us to know how God judges this.
Here is a remarkable fact. Peter and all the other teachers inspired by God agree: they all show God requiring sinners to repent right away.

blocks.x: V. It is extremely important to follow this example that God inspired. Here is why:

s: 1. Telling people to repent before they ask for forgiveness—and only this—fits the facts.
So what are the facts?
Just these. The sinner is free and makes his own choices.
He uses that freedom to set himself selfishly against what God’s law of love requires.
So what should God require him to do?
Change his course, of course! In other words, repent.
Nothing could be clearer. If someone is choosing to do wrong, he should turn around and choose to do right.
This, and only this, fits the facts and what is right.
But suppose you try to guide a sinner who is still selfish—someone who lives to please himself.
The first thing you do is tell him to pray.
Pray for what? That God would give him what his heart wants?
Of course, if he prays without first changing what his heart is set on, he will pray for what he wants. That means he will pray for God to give him the selfish things his heart desires.
His prayer would be, “O Lord, let me have heaven without being holy. Lord, forgive my sins, but let me keep on living in sin, because I don’t want to repent!”
Can mocking God like this do any good?
Would you expect the Bible to tell awakened sinners to do something like that?

If people are truly willing to repent and give up all sin, God asks nothing more of them. Being willing is really the same as doing it. But there is no bigger mistake in the world than to assume that sinners are willing to repent and want to repent before they actually do it.

2. People who are seeking God are usually told to do things in the opposite order from what the Bible commands. It is as if the sinner were ready and God were not. It is as if the sinner had to do things to get God ready and push him to do his duty.
3. Telling the sinner to pray for repentance assumes that he wants to repent but cannot. It assumes he needs God’s power to help him.
The truth is, no one can choose to give up sin without actually giving it up. Choosing it is doing it.
4. Telling sinners anything different from what God tells them in the Bible deceives them.
Thousands have been fooled this way, and their souls have been ruined forever.

If you tell them to pray for forgiveness before they repent, you leave them with a false idea. They think they are doing something they ought to do—doing their duty. But they are not doing their duty until they repent!
What a horrible teaching this is!
Imagine teaching a sinner who has not repented, and who is still holding on to his sins, to pray for forgiveness!
This would ruin a whole world of sinners.
It would leave all of them fooled and deceived in their sins, and under God’s anger forever!
5. Telling the sinner to pray for the Holy Spirit is really the same thing in a slightly different form.
Nothing could be more misleading than telling the sinner to pray for the Holy Spirit when you know he is only resisting the Holy Spirit—and when you let him keep on resisting.
“You always resist the Holy Spirit,” says God’s word, through one of its most faithful and truthful preachers.
What does the Holy Spirit do?
He takes the truth and shows it to the sinner in powerful ways.
This is his job when it comes to the sinner.
As soon as the sinner gives in to the truth that the Holy Spirit shows him and presses on him, he is converted.
Until he repents, all he does is resist the Spirit.
So what good does it do to tell him to pray for the Spirit, as long as he is resisting the Spirit?
While he keeps doing this, what can his prayer be except mocking God?
What he should do is not pray for the Holy Spirit. He should give in to the influence the Spirit is already having on his mind.
The first thing, and the only right thing, for the awakened sinner to do about the Spirit is to give his heart to what God’s revealed truth requires.
If he did this, he would be converted in a moment.
He should be told that he does not really feel his need of the Spirit. So he cannot pray with understanding for the Spirit to work more strongly on his mind.
He should also be told that the only honest thing he can do first is to stop resisting the Spirit.

Peter did not say to Simon, “Pray for the Holy Spirit to work on you, or to repent for you, or to make you repent, or even to help you repent.” He simply said, “Repent yourself. Repent first of all, and then ask for forgiveness.”
6. Suppose you tell a sinner who is still in his sins to pray instead of repenting. Then you leave him thinking that once he has prayed, he has done his duty.
You tell him to pray. He prays, and then he says, “Now I have done my duty. So why am I not converted?”
But suppose you tell him what Peter told Simon—to repent first and then pray. If he follows your advice, he is converted. And then his prayer can be pleasing to God.
The opposite way—the backward order that puts prayer before repentance—really puts the blame on God when the sinner stays unrepentant.

If you tell the sinner to pray first instead of repenting first, you are really suggesting that the problem in the sinner’s way is one that God has to remove. You are suggesting that the reason he has not repented is in God, not in himself.
If the sinner follows your advice, he prays before he repents. Then, after he has prayed, he says, “Why am I not converted and saved?”
“I have prayed. God does not convert me. So the blame is on God, not on me!” What a horrible effect this way of doing things must have on the sinner’s mind!
7. No writer inspired by God supports any other way than the one in this text.
Search the Scriptures from beginning to end. You will not find any instructions to sinners that are different from this.

If you did find any, you would have good reason to be amazed. Telling the sinner to go and pray before he repents ignores what repentance really is. It also ignores what the mind of a person who is sinning is really like.
8. Every teaching of the Bible agrees with the instructions given in this text, and with no other instructions.
Every teaching of Scripture leaves the sinner with only one choice: to do his duty now.
The whole Bible urges him to do what he should do now. If he has sin he has not repented of, the Bible tells him that his first duty is to repent.

People have made up a strange method of their own. They tell sinners to do something other than repent. But the Bible holds firmly to the only way that makes sense. Again and again it urges every sinner to repent first of all.
John came preaching in the wilderness of Judea, “Repent!” Jesus Christ came after him preaching the same thing, and nothing different. “Repent,” he says, “for the kingdom of the gospel is near.”
In the same way, every prophet and every apostle, each in his own time, cried out, “Repent, REPENT!” It was as if they did not dare to say anything else until this first duty was done.
This is the only reasonable way. It is the only way based on Scripture, on reason, and on a true understanding of how the mind works.
Every sinner knows that he is a sinner.
You do not need the Holy Spirit to show you that you are a sinner, any more than you need him to show you that you exist.
This is why the Bible always confronts the sinner head-on. It simply assumes, “You are a sinner, and that needs no proof.”
Every sinner knows it.
9. Sinners are often very willing to pray, but not willing to repent.
Just let the sinner skip the heart-work of repenting, and he will gladly do lots of other things.
A young man once told me, “I would travel anywhere in the world if it would get me saved.”
“Yes,” I told him, “but there is one thing you will not do. You will not give up trusting in your own goodness and be saved by Christ alone, without doing anything to earn it yourself.”
Every sinner is like that.
Tell him to pray for conviction.
Oh yes, he will pray for conviction! But he will fight against conviction until he repents.
Tell him to pray for the Holy Spirit.
Oh yes, he will pray for the Holy Spirit! But he may still keep resisting the Holy Spirit all the time.

He is ready to do the outside work, but not the heart-work. He will gladly clean the outside of the cup and the plate. But turning his own heart away from his sins and selfishness—that is the hard thing. That is the one thing he least wants to do.
Sinners like to defend themselves by claiming that they cannot control their own hearts.
They admit they can control their muscles. If Jesus were on earth, they say, they could come to him and kneel in front of him. But they cannot come with their hearts and bow their hearts to him.
But what is the heart, that you cannot control it?

You are controlling your hearts all the time! The very thing God complains about is that you control them too stubbornly. His truth and his Spirit cannot move you. You control your heart the wrong way, and so stubbornly that you block all his efforts to save you.
That is why he cries out, “Turn around, turn around! Why will you die?”

blocks.x: Closing remarks.

s: 1. But you ask, “Shouldn’t a sinner pray?”
The answer depends on what the question means and what it assumes.
Does it mean, “Should a sinner mock God?”
Then I answer, No. Do you mean, “Should he truly pray, sincerely and honestly?”
Yes. “Should he lie to the Holy Spirit?”
No. “Should he turn to God?” Yes.
But here is all that needs to be said about this. The sinner should be told to repent and pray—not to pray and repent.
He should follow the Bible’s order. That order is based on reason and on the way things really are.
2. This order of duties makes perfect sense.
Suppose a sinner had stolen some money.
He knows that God is very displeased with him for this. He is also afraid of being caught and shamed.
Now he says, “What should I do?”
“Should I repent and then pray for God to forgive me? Or should I pray first?”
He really does not want to confess, repent, and give the money back. So he says, “I will do the other thing. I will pray.”
“I will go off by myself and pray about it. And then maybe I will repent.”
Look at him. He takes out the stolen money.
He passes it from one hand to the other. “I am so upset,” he says. “What should I do?”
“Should I put it in my pocket and go pray?”
No, sinner, no! Take it back. Repent first, and then go and pray.
Don’t go and pray for the Holy Spirit first. There is no need for that. The Holy Spirit is already convicting you of your great sin.
Don’t insult him by refusing to give in to his urging, and by pretending to pray for his guidance and help!
Let this stand for all sin.
Stealing money is only one kind of sin. Let it stand for every kind of sin.
You, sinner, are completely set on living for yourself.
You have robbed God by tearing yourself away from serving him.
God says, “Give it back. Give yourself back to me and to my service.”
But you answer, “What should I do?”
“Shouldn’t I go and pray?”
God says, “Give it back first. Return the stolen goods first. Then you may pray.”
What would you even pray for, until you have given back what you stole?
Surely you will not insult God by praying for forgiveness before you have given back what you stole.
There is no point in praying for the Holy Spirit unless you give it back. Praying without giving it back is just resisting and mocking God’s Spirit.
But the sinner says, “You talk as if I could repent.”
Yes, and so does God.
In his word, God always speaks as if you can repent, and as if you should know that you can.
What if Simon Magus had said, “But you don’t really expect me to repent, do you?”
Notice that he did not say anything like that.
His own conscience did not give him that excuse or let him use it. And the apostles’ preaching did not encourage it either.
But you say, “Does the Bible always assume that I can repent?”

Yes, everywhere! It does so in all its commands. It does so through every prophet and every apostle. It does so through the lips of everyone who came before Christ to prepare his way, and through the lips of Christ himself.
Every command and every instruction God inspired speaks the same way and means the same thing.
You can repent, and you should do it right now!
3. When the sinner says, “I can’t repent,” he is really accusing God of being a tyrant.
If saying that God requires you to do impossible things is not calling him a tyrant, what is?
4. But doesn’t the Bible teach that God gives people repentance?
Yes. And he gives it in the same way he gives you your daily bread—bread that you still have to get and eat for yourself.
God does not give you your daily bread as long as you insist on starving yourself.
In the same way, God gives you repentance by persuading you to repent. He draws you. He presses the truth on your heart and conscience.
In fact, there is no other possible way he can give you repentance.
He does it only by bringing the truth before your mind. He presses it on your heart and conscience in a thousand ways.
That is because repentance is a thoughtful choice. The sinner makes it himself, because he sees that truth and reason require it.
5. Every sinner should see and feel that God requires him to repent right now.
He should see that this is exactly what he must do, and nothing else.
There is nothing strange or foolish about this.
Suppose a man had committed murder, and you told him to repent of this terrible sin.
Is there anything mysterious about that?
Or suppose you see a man doing some particular wrong, and you urge him to stop and repent. Is there anything strange or unreasonable about that?
Then how can it be unreasonable to require a sinner to repent of all his sins? Or to repent of the one thing that includes all wickedness?

6. Some of you are so afraid you might repent that you pick up a book, even during the most serious preaching. You try to keep from thinking about your own sins. And even then you pretend that you cannot repent. You would love to make it sound as if you would repent if you could!
How beautifully consistent that is!
7. Many people who claim to be Christians have drifted far away from God. They still go through the motions of praying, but they don’t repent.
Many talk about prayer as if praying could make up for the ways their sinning fails to please God.
I once asked a young woman, “Do you pray?”
“Yes, sir.” “When?” “When I go to bed at night.”
“What do you pray for?” “That God would take me to heaven if I die before morning.”
“Do you expect God to do that?”
“No.” “So you plan to keep on sinning.”
Now be honest enough to tell God the plain truth.

Say to him, “Lord, forgive my sins. Give me strength through sleep and food so that I can sin a little more. I have sinned all day today. I don’t plan to repent. I just want to be taken to heaven if I die, because I can’t stand the thought of sinking into hell. Lord, help me keep sinning against you as long as I live, and then take me up to heaven!!”
You are shocked. But what is it that shocks you?
The way you live, or the words I use?
Look—there is the sinner.
He gets on his knees to tell God that he wants to repent. But he is lying when he says it, every moment, until he actually repents.
And you who claim to be Christians but have drifted away—you lie to God in every word of your pretend prayer.
Do you say, “I will not repent—I don’t plan to repent”?
If you say anything other than this, you are lying to God. Nothing else is true until you actually repent.
The truth is, as long as you stay selfish and unrepentant, you do not mean to repent.
So no matter how he prays, what he really means is, “I have no plan to repent of my sins.”
This is always true, until he does repent.
Oh, how sinners pray while they hold on to their sins and do not mean to repent!
Listen to him: “O Lord, I beg you to search my heart.”
No, you don’t mean that at all. You are hiding your heart the whole time.
“O God, come close to me.”
But you are pushing away from God every moment. And while you are trying to get away, you just look back over your shoulder and cry out for God to show his face and come close to your soul!
Listen! Hear what the Bible says.
“If someone turns his ear away so he will not hear the law, even his prayer will be something God finds disgusting.”
And isn’t that exactly what you are doing?
8. Let me tell you: God is more ready than you can imagine to meet you and bless you.
He comes with forgiveness in his hands—forgiveness all sealed with blood.
All you have to do is give up your sins and come to him. Then everything will be all right.
The very first moment you come to God with a heart that has repented, he will meet you with smiles of love and kindness.
His parable of the prodigal son shows this and proves it.
Look—the son who wandered away comes to his senses.
He does not stay away and try to live on pig food. He turns toward home. He comes with a confession on his lips and tears of sorrow for his sin on his cheeks.
He is coming! And now look at the old father.
He sees him far away. He recognizes the son he lost so long ago.
See how he jumps up from his doorway and runs to hug his son who has come back.
Oh, how ready he is! Oh, how much more than just READY!!
Oh, how ready God is to meet you, too, with complete forgiveness! He is ready to wipe away all your tears and to comfort your aching heart!
Now, dear listener, don’t go away and say I told you not to pray.
Suppose I told you not to go into your private room, get on your knees, and curse and blaspheme God. Could you honestly say I told you not to pray?
In the same way, I am not teaching you not to pray. But I am teaching you to be honest.
I warn you: when you pray, do not mock God.
I beg you: when you pray, give your heart to God and repent of all your sin.
When I first repented, I did it on my knees while I was praying.
I knelt down as a sinner who had not repented, and I got up as someone who had.
Right while I was speaking to God, my heart broke. I gave myself to God.
This is the way.
Are you asking, “Can I believe God?”
Yes. “Can I pray with faith?”
Yes. “Can I turn my heart over to God in repentance?”
Yes. Why not you, as well as Paul—as well as Peter—as well as any of the countless people who have done this very thing and found mercy by doing it?
“God loved the world so much that he gave his only Son. Whoever believes in him will not be lost but will have life that lasts forever.” — John 3:16
Sin is the most costly thing in the whole universe.
Nothing else costs so much.
Whether it is forgiven or not, its cost is endlessly great.
When sin is forgiven, the cost falls mainly on the great one who took our place to pay for it. When it is not forgiven, the cost must fall on the guilty sinner himself.
Sin is real. People everywhere experience it, and people everywhere see it.
There is sin in the human race everywhere, and it is terribly bad.
Sin means breaking a law that is endlessly important. This law was designed and fitted to bring about the greatest good for the whole universe.
By its very nature, obeying this law is necessary for the good of every creature.
Without obedience, there could be no happiness even in heaven.
Since sin breaks such an important law, it cannot be taken lightly.
No government can afford to treat disobedience as a small thing. Everything depends on obedience—the whole well-being of the government and of everyone it rules.
The more valuable the things at stake, the more necessary it is to protect the law and to punish disobedience.
God must not do anything that dishonors his law.
People have already dishonored it by disobeying it. So God has all the more reason to stand by his law and win back its honor.
The worst dishonor you can do to a law is to reject it, disobey it, and look down on it.
Sinful people have done all of this.

This law is not only good. It is truly needed for the happiness of everyone who lives under it. So the most necessary thing of all is that the Lawgiver should defend his law and show that it is right.
He absolutely must do it.
That is why sin has cost God’s government so much.

There are only two choices. Either the law’s punishment must be carried out, and that would cost the well-being of the whole human race. Or God must put up with the worst results of people disrespecting his law—and in some form, those results would also cost a huge amount.
Take any human government as an example.
Suppose people reject and dishonor the fair and necessary laws it makes.
Then the broken law must be honored by carrying out its punishment. If not, something else must be suffered that costs just as much, and probably much more.
Breaking the law must cost happiness somewhere, and a great deal of it.
In God’s government, it was judged wise to provide a substitute—someone to take the sinner’s place. This substitute would save the sinner and still honor the law.
Once this was decided, the next big question was: How will the cost be paid?
The Bible tells us how this question was actually answered.
It was done by a kind of volunteer sign-up—should I call it that? Or should I call it a gift?
Whatever we call it, it was an offering given freely.
Who will put his name at the top of the list of givers?
Who will start, when so much has to be raised?
Who will make the first sacrifice?
Who will take the first step in such a huge project?
The Bible tells us.
It began with the Father, who is infinite.
He made the first great gift.
To begin with, he gave his only Son. And after giving him first, he freely gives everything else the situation needs.
First he gave his Son to make the payment for sin that the law required. Then he gave and sent his Holy Spirit to take charge of this work.
The Son, for his part, agreed to stand in for sinners. He did this so he could honor the law by suffering in their place.

He poured out his blood. He freely offered a whole life of suffering on the altar. He did not hide his face when people spat on him, or his back when they whipped him. He did not pull back from the worst insults that wicked people could pile on him.
In the same way, the Holy Spirit gives himself without stopping to the most self-sacrificing efforts, to reach this great goal.

It would have been very quick and simple for God just to turn his hand against the wicked people of our race and send them all straight down to hell. He did that once with certain angels who “did not keep their first place.”
A rebellion broke out in heaven.
God did not put up with it for long around his high throne.

But with human beings he took a different path. He did not send them all to hell. Instead, he planned a huge set of steps to win people’s souls back to obedience and to heaven. This plan involved the most amazing self-denial and self-sacrifice.
Who was this great gift for?
“God so loved the world.” This means the whole human race.
Here, “the world” cannot mean just one part of it. It means the whole race.
The Bible shows it, and so does the very nature of the matter: the atonement—Christ’s payment for sin—must have been made for the whole world.

Here is why. If it had not been made for the whole race, no person could ever know that it was made for him. Then no one could believe in Christ in the sense of receiving the blessings of the atonement by faith. Suppose the gift were only for some people, and no one knew who they were. Then the whole gift would fail, because no one could have a sensible faith to receive it.
Imagine a rich man writes a will. He leaves certain property to certain people no one knows. The only description he gives of them is the name “the elect.”

That is the only way they are described. Everyone agrees that the man who wrote the will had exact people in mind. But he left no description of them that anyone could understand—not the people themselves, not the courts, not anyone alive.
A will like that is completely worthless. It cannot be used at all.
No one alive could claim anything under such a will. It would not help even if these chosen people were described as people who live in Oberlin.
The will does not include everyone who lives in Oberlin, and it does not say which ones. So everything is lost.
Everyone has an equal claim, but no one has a clear claim. So no one can inherit anything.
If the atonement were made like that, no one alive would have any good reason to believe he was one of the chosen before he received the gospel.
So he would have no right to believe and to receive its blessings by faith.
In fact, if that were true, the atonement would be completely useless—unless God gave a special message to each person it was meant for.
But here is how it really is. The simple fact that a person belongs to Adam’s race—that he is human, born of a woman—is all that is needed.
That puts him inside the circle.
He is part of the world that God gave his Son for, so that whoever would believe in him would not be lost but would have life that lasts forever.
What moved God’s heart to give this great gift was love—love for the world.
God loved the world so much that he gave his Son to die for it.
God loved the rest of the universe too. But this gift of his Son came from his love for our world.
It is true that in this great act God also took care of the interests of the whole universe.
He was careful not to do anything that would make his law seem even a little less sacred.

He very carefully made sure that no one would misunderstand how much he values his law. He also wanted no one to misunderstand how much he cares about obedience and happiness among all the thinking creatures of his universe.
He meant, once and for all, to remove the danger that any thinking, choosing creature would be tempted to think little of the moral law.
There is more. God gave up his Son to die not only because he loved souls. He also did it out of respect for the spirit of the law that comes from his own eternal reason.
This is where his plan to give up his Son began.
The law of his own reason must be honored and kept sacred.
He may not do anything that goes against its spirit.
He must do everything possible to keep people from sinning and to win the trust and love of those he rules.
He held these great goals so sacred that he would rather bathe his Son in his own blood than put the good of the universe in danger.
Without any doubt, it was love and concern for the highest good of the universe that led him to sacrifice his own dear Son.
Next, let us think carefully about what kind of love this is.
The verse puts special weight on this: “God so loved.” His love was of such a kind—so wonderful and so special—that it led him to give up his only Son to die.
Clearly, these words mean more than just that his love was great.
His love is very special in its character.

If we do not understand this, we may fall into the strange mistake of the Universalists. They are always talking about God’s love for sinners. But their ideas about what this love is like never lead anyone to repent or to become holy.

They seem to think of this love as simple niceness. They think of God only as a very kind, easygoing being whom nobody needs to fear. Ideas like that do not help anyone become holy at all. In fact, they do the very opposite.
Only when we understand what kind of love this is do we feel its moral power pushing us toward holiness.
Someone could fairly ask this: If God loved the world with a love that was simply great, and nothing more, why didn’t he just save the whole world without sacrificing his Son?
