That question is enough to show that the little word “so” has a deep meaning. It should lead us to study that meaning carefully.
1. This love is not the kind that takes pleasure in how good someone is. It was not delight in the character of the human race.
That could not be, because there was nothing lovable in their character.
If God had loved such a race by taking pleasure in them, it would have been an endless disgrace to him.
2. It was not just an emotion or a feeling.
It was not a blind urge, even though many people seem to think it was.
People often seem to think God acted the way people do when strong feelings carry them away.
But there would be nothing good or right in that.
A man might give away everything he owns because of a blind rush of feeling, and not be any better a person because of it.
But saying this does not mean there is no emotion at all in the love that wants good for others, or in God’s love for a lost world.
He did have emotion, but not only emotion.

In fact, the Bible teaches everywhere that God’s love for people lost in their sins was a father’s love—the love of a father for his children. In this case, they were rebellious, stubborn children who had run away and wasted everything.
Of course, the deepest compassion must be mixed into this love.
3. On Christ’s side, as the one who stands between God and people, this love was a father’s love.
“He is not ashamed to call them his brothers.”
In one way he is acting for his brothers, and in another way for his children.
The Father gave him up for this work. So of course the Father shares in the love that fits these relationships.
4. This love must be completely unselfish. God had nothing to hope for and nothing to fear. He had nothing to gain from his children if they were saved.
In fact, it is impossible to think of God as selfish. His love includes all creatures and all interests, each according to its true value.
No doubt he was glad to save our race. Why shouldn’t he be?
It is a great salvation in every way. It adds greatly to the joy of heaven. And it will greatly add to the glory and happiness of the infinite God.
He will respect himself forever for such unselfish love.
He also knows that all his holy creatures will respect him forever for this work and for the love that gave rise to it.
But we must also say this: he knew they would not respect him for this great work unless they saw that he did it for the good of sinners.

5. This love was full of passion. It was not the cold-hearted attitude some people imagine. It was not just an idea. It was a deep, eager, earnest love, burning in his soul like a fire nothing can put out.
6. The sacrifice was one of the greatest acts of self-denial.
Did it cost the Father nothing to give up his own dear Son to suffer and to die such a death?
If this is not self-denial, what is?
To give up his Son to so much suffering like this—isn’t this the noblest self-denial there is?
The universe could never have understood what great self-denial is without an example like this.
7. This love was for each person because it was for everyone. And it was for everyone because it was for each person.
God loved each sinner one by one, and so he loved them all.
He loved everyone equally, without favorites. That is why he loved each one personally.
8. This was a very patient love.
How rare it is to find a parent who loves his child so much that he is never impatient!

Let me go around the room and ask you parents. How many of you can say that you love all your children so well, so much, and so wisely that you have never felt impatient with any of them? Can you take them in your arms even when they provoke you the most? Can you love them until they soften—love them out of their sins, love them into being sorry, and into the heart of a loving child?

Which of your children could you say this about: “Thank God, I never got irritated with that child”? Which of them, if you met him in heaven, could you say this about: “I never caused that child to get irritated”?
I have often heard parents say, “I love my children, but oh, how I lose my patience!”
And after their dear children have died, you may hear them groan bitterly: “Oh, how could I have made my child stumble so much and sin so much!”
But God never gets irritated. He is never impatient.
His love is so deep and so great that he is always patient.

Sometimes parents have children who are unfortunate—poor children who deserve pity. Parents can put up with anything from them. But when their children are very wicked, parents seem to feel it is quite all right to be impatient.
In God’s case, these are not unfortunate children. They are extremely wicked, and they know exactly what they are doing.

But oh, how amazing his patience is! He is so set on their good and wants their highest well-being so much. No matter how they mistreat him, he keeps working to bless them. He sets out to win them over by his tears, by his blood, and by his death—the death of his Son in their place!
9. This is a jealous love. Not in a bad way, but in a good way. It means he is extremely careful that nothing happens to harm the ones he loves.
It is like a husband and wife who truly love each other. They watch over each other’s well-being with a jealous care that never sleeps. They always try to do all they can for each other’s true good.
This gift has already been given. It was given sincerely. It was not only promised; it was actually given.
The promise made long ago has come true.
The Son has come. He has died. He has paid the ransom, and he lives to offer it. Salvation is ready for everyone who will accept it.
The Son of God did not die to calm down a desire for revenge, as some people seem to think. He died because the law demanded it.
The law had been dishonored by being broken.
So Christ took on the job of honoring it. To meet the law’s demands, he gave his life of suffering and his death that paid for sin.
It was not to satisfy a spiteful spirit in God. It was to bring about the highest good of the universe through a plan of mercy.
Now that this atonement has been made, every person in the human race has a right to it.
It is open to anyone who will accept it.

Jesus is still the Father’s Son. But by a right that comes from grace, he also belongs in an important way to the human race—to every single person. So every sinner has a share in his blood, if he will only come forward humbly and claim it.
God sent his Son to be the Savior of the world—of anyone who would believe and accept this great salvation.
God gives his Spirit to bring this salvation to people.
The Spirit comes to each person’s door and knocks. He wants to get in if he can, so he can show each sinner that salvation can be his right now.
Oh, what a work of love this is!
If this salvation is received at all, it must be received by faith.
This is the only possible way.
God rules over sinners in a moral way, not by physical force. That is because the sinner is a moral being who makes choices, not a physical object.
So God cannot influence us at all unless we give him our trust.
He can never save us just by moving us to some place called heaven. That would be like thinking that a change of place could change a heart that makes its own choices.
So there can be no other way to be saved except by simple faith.
Now don’t make a mistake here. Don’t think that accepting the gospel just means believing these facts of history, without truly receiving Christ as your Savior.
If that were the plan, Christ would only have needed to come down and die. Then he could go back to heaven and quietly wait to see who would believe the facts.
But the real situation is very different!
Christ comes down to fill the soul with his own life and love.
Sinners who are sorry for their sins hear and believe the truth about Jesus. Then they receive Christ into their souls, so he can live there and rule there above everything, forever.
Many people get this wrong. They say, “If I believe the facts as history, that is enough.”
No! No! That is not it at all.
“It is with the heart that a person believes and is made right with God.”

Yes, the atonement was made to open the way. It made it possible for Jesus to come down into human hearts and draw them close to himself, so they are united with him and feel as he feels. It made it possible for God to reach down with his arms of love and hold sinners close. And it made sure that God’s law and government would not be dishonored when God showed such friendship to sinners.
But the atonement will not save sinners at all, except by opening the way for them to come close to God in heart and friendship.
Now Jesus comes to each sinner’s door and knocks. Listen! What’s that? What’s that?

Why is he knocking? If the plan were only to believe facts, why didn’t he go away and stay in heaven? He could have waited there until people simply believed the facts of history and got baptized to be saved, as some people think.

But look how he comes down! He tells the sinner what he has done. He shows him all his love. He tells him how holy and sacred it is—so sacred that he can never act without thinking of the holiness of his law and the purity of his government.
In this way he presses deep and big ideas of his holiness and purity into the heart. He makes it clear that we need to repent deeply, and that we have a sacred duty to give up all sin.

blocks.x: SOME REMARKS.

s: 1. The Bible teaches that sinners can lose their birthright. They can put themselves where mercy can no longer reach them.
Not long ago I talked to you about how clearly necessary it is for God to protect himself against people abusing his love.
The situation makes it very likely that people will abuse it. So God must make sinners understand that they may not abuse his love, and that they cannot do it without being punished.
2. Under the gospel, sinners carry the greatest responsibility possible.
They are in the greatest danger of trampling the very Son of God under their feet.
They say, “Come on, let’s kill him, and then the inheritance will be ours.”
When God finally sends his own dear Son, last of all, what do they do?
On top of all their other sins and rebellions, they add the worst insult of all to this glorious Son!
Imagine something like this happening under a human government.
A rebellion breaks out in some parts of the kingdom.

The king sends his own son. He does not send him with an army to cut the rebels down quickly. Instead, the son goes among them gently, humbly, and patiently. He explains the laws of the kingdom and urges them to obey.
What do they do?
All together they agree to grab him and kill him!
But you say this does not apply to you. You ask me, “Who murdered the Son of God?”
“Wasn’t it the Jews?”
Yes, but sinners, have you had no part in this murder?
Hasn’t the way you have treated Jesus Christ shown that you fully agree with the Jews of long ago who murdered the Son of God?
If you had been there, would anyone have shouted louder than you, “Take him away! Crucify him! Crucify him!”?
Haven’t you always said, “Go away from us! We don’t care to know your ways”?
3. It was said about Christ that he was rich, but he became poor, so that because he became poor, we could become rich.
How amazingly true this is!
Our rescue cost Christ his life. It found him rich, but it made him poor. It found us endlessly poor, but it made us rich—rich with all the wealth of heaven.
But no one can share in these riches until each person accepts them for himself in the right way.
They must be received on the terms God offers. If not, the offer disappears completely. Then you are left even poorer than if these treasures had never been placed at your feet.
Many people seem to completely misunderstand this.
They don’t seem to believe what God says. They keep saying, “If, if, if only there were some salvation for me! If only there were an atonement to pay for the forgiveness of my sins!”
This was one of the last things that became clear to me before I fully gave my soul over to trust God.

I had been studying the atonement. I saw how it all fit together logically. I saw what it demanded of the sinner. But it annoyed me, and I said, “If I became a Christian, how could I know what God would do with me?”

Because I was annoyed, I said foolish and bitter things against Christ. Finally my own soul was horrified at how wicked it was. Then I said, “I will make all this right with Christ, if that is possible.”
Many people move toward the encouraging promises of the gospel in this way, as if it were only a “maybe”—just an experiment.
They take every step forward very carefully, with fear and trembling. They act as if it were very doubtful whether there could be any mercy for them.
That is how it was with me. I was on my way to my office when this question came into my mind: “What are you waiting for?”
“You don’t need to make such a fuss.”
“Everything is already done.”
“All you have to do is agree to the offer. Give your heart to it completely, right now. That is all.”
That is exactly how it is.

All Christians and sinners should understand that the whole plan is complete. All of Christ belongs to each and every person—his character, his work, his death that paid for sin, and his prayers for us that never stop because he lives forever. It only needs to be accepted.
There is a whole ocean of it.
There it is. You might just as well take it.

It is as if you were standing on the shore of an ocean of soft, pure water, dying of thirst. You are welcome to drink. You don’t need to worry that you will use up the ocean, or that someone else will go without because you drink.
You don’t need to feel that you are not allowed to drink from that ocean. You are invited—even urged—to drink. Yes, to drink as much as you want!
This ocean supplies everything you need.
You don’t need to have the qualities of Jesus Christ in yourself. His qualities become yours to use in every possible way.
The Scripture says it like this: God has made him our wisdom, our being right with God, our holiness, and our rescue.
What do you need?
Wisdom? Here it is.
Being right with God? Here it is.
Holiness? Here you have it.
Everything is in Christ.
Can you think of even one thing you need to be morally pure or useful that is not here in Christ?
Nothing. Everything is provided here.
So you don’t need to say, “I will go and pray and try,” like the hymn says—
There is no need for any “maybe.”
The doors are always open.

They are like the doors of the Broadway Tabernacle in New York. Those doors were made to swing open and lock themselves open. That way they could not swing back and shut on the crowds of people pushing to get through.
When they were being made, I went to the workmen myself. I told them they absolutely must build them to swing open and lock themselves in that position.
In the same way, the door of salvation is always open. It is locked open, and no one can shut it—not even the Pope, not the devil, not any angel from heaven or from hell.
There it stands, swung all the way back. The way is wide open for every sinner in our race to come in, if he wants to.
Again, sin is the most costly thing in the universe.
Sinner, do you really know what a price has been paid for you? It was paid so that you could be rescued and become an heir of God and of heaven.
Oh, what an expensive business it is for you to keep enjoying sin!
And what a huge tax God’s government has paid to rescue this part of his kingdom from ruin!

People talk about the tax Great Britain collects to help the poor. But add in the taxes of all the other nations too, and it is still nothing next to the sin-tax of Jehovah’s government—that terrible sin-tax!
Think how much machinery is kept running to save sinners!

The Son of God was sent down. Angels are sent as helpers to serve those who will receive salvation. Missionaries are sent. Christians work, pray, and weep with deep and anxious concern. All of this is to look for the lost and save them.
What a wonderful, enormous tax is placed on the goodness of the whole universe to get rid of sin and save the sinner!
If the cost could be counted in solid gold, there would be a whole world of it—a solid globe all by itself!
Look at all the hard work and cost that has come from angels, from Jesus Christ, from the Holy Spirit, and from living people!
Shame on sinners who hang on to sin in spite of all these loving efforts to save them! Instead of being shamed into leaving sin, they say, “Let God pay this tax. Who cares!”
“Let the missionaries work. Let godly women work their fingers to the bone to raise money to keep all this human machinery running. It doesn’t matter. What is all this to me?”
“I have loved my pleasures, and I will go after them!”
What a cold, uncaring heart that is!
Sinners can easily afford to make sacrifices to save other sinners.
Paul could do it for other sinners.
He felt that he had done his part in making people sinners. So now it was right for him to do his part in turning them back to God.
But look over there. That young man thinks he cannot afford to be a minister, because he is afraid no one will support him well.
Doesn’t he owe something to the grace that saved his soul from hell?

Jesus made so many sacrifices for him. So did the Christians who belonged to Christ before him—didn’t they pray and suffer and work hard for his soul to be saved? So doesn’t he have some sacrifices to make too?
As for his fear of not having enough to eat while doing the Lord’s work, let him trust his great Master.
But let me also say this: churches may be very much to blame for not supporting their pastors well.
They should know that God will surely let them starve if they let their ministers starve.
The people God sends to feed them with the bread of life—if they greedily let them starve, then their own souls and their children’s souls will be as barren as death.
Think how much it costs to get certain kinds of sin out of society—slavery, for example.
How much has already been spent! And how much more must still be spent before this terrible evil, this curse and sin, is pulled up by the roots from our land!
This is part of God’s great work, and he will push it forward until it is finished.
But what an amazing cost!
How many lives and how much agony it takes to get rid of this one sin!
How terrible it will be for those who make money from people’s sins!
Just think of the man who sells liquor. He tempts people while God is trying to persuade them not to rush on down the road of sin and death!
Think how guilty people are who line up like this to fight against God!
So Christ has to fight against liquor sellers, who are doing everything they can to block his work.
This subject shows clearly that sin is simply selfishness.

Sin does not care how much it costs Jesus Christ. It does not care how much it costs the church, or how much it drains the loving care and self-sacrificing work of all good people on earth and in heaven. It doesn’t matter. The sinner loves to please himself, and he will do it while he can.
How many of you have cost your friends endless tears and trouble as they tried to bring you back from your sinful ways?
So much has been done for you. Aren’t you ashamed that no one can persuade you to give up your sins and turn to God and to holiness?
Everything God does for people is a work of suffering and self-denial.
It started with the sacrifice of his own dear Son. It keeps going with sacrifice after sacrifice and hard work, at a great and amazing cost.

Just think how long these efforts have already gone on! Think how many tears, poured out like water, it has cost. Think how much pain of many kinds this work has caused and cost. And all because of that very sin you enjoy like a sweet treat you roll around under your tongue!
No wonder God hates sin when he sees how much it costs! No wonder he says, “Oh, do not do this disgusting thing that I hate!”
But God is not unhappy in giving up so much.
His joy in the results is so great that he thinks of all the suffering as small by comparison. It is like earthly parents who enjoy the hard work they do to bless their children.

Look at them! They will almost work their hands off. Mothers stay up at night sewing until they stagger from tiredness and can barely see. But if you watched them work, you would often see their joy too, because they love their children so much.
That is what the work, the joy, and the self-denial of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit are like in their great work of saving people.
They are often grieved that so many people refuse to be saved.
They keep working together with one shared heart. Within reasonable limits, there is nothing they will not do or suffer to finish their great work.
It is wonderful to think how all of creation also feels for this work and for the suffering it requires.
Go back to the scene where Christ suffered.
Could the sun in the sky look down on that scene and not be moved?
Oh no! He could not even look at it. He covered his face so he would not see it!
All of nature seemed to dress in her darkest clothes of mourning.
The scene was too much even for nature, which has no life, to bear.
The sun turned his back. He could not look down on such a sight!
This subject shows powerfully how much a soul is worth.
Do you think God would have done all this if he thought as little of the soul as sinners usually do?

Martyrs and saints enjoy their sufferings. In their own lives they fill up what is still lacking in the sufferings of Christ. This is not in the atonement itself, but in the smaller parts of the work that still need to be done.
True religion by its very nature loves self-denial.
The results will completely prove that the cost was worth it.
God had carefully counted the cost before he began.
Long before he made a universe of moral beings, he knew exactly what it would cost him to rescue sinners. And he knew the result would be more than worth the cost.
He knew that a wonder of mercy would be done. He knew that the suffering required of Christ, as great as it was, would be endured. And he knew that endlessly glorious results would come from it.

He looked down the path of time into the far-off ages. There, as the ages rolled on, he could see the joy of the rescued saints. They are singing their songs and playing their harps again and again with the song that never ends, through the long, long, LONG eternity of their happiness. Wasn’t that enough for a heart of endless love to enjoy?
And what do you think about it, Christian?
Will you now say, “I am ashamed to ask to be forgiven”?
“How can I stand to receive such mercy!”
“It was paid for with blood. How can I accept it?”
“How can I cost Jesus so much?”

You are right to say that you have cost him a great deal. But the cost has been paid gladly. The pain has all been suffered, and it will never need to be suffered again. It will not cost any more if you accept than if you refuse. And there is more to think about. Jesus Christ did not act foolishly. He did not pay too much to rescue the soul. He did not suffer one pain more than God’s government required and the worth of the soul made worthwhile.

Oh, when you see him face to face and tell him what you think about it—when you are some thousands of years older than you are now—won’t you worship the wisdom that runs this plan, and the endless love it was born from?
Oh, what will you say then about the amazing humility that brought Jesus down to rescue you!

Tell me, Christian, haven’t you often poured out your soul to your Savior, admitting what you have cost him? Didn’t it seem as if something was lifting up inside you, as if the very bottom of your soul were rising, and you wanted to pour out your whole heart?
If anyone had seen you, they would have wondered what had happened to you to melt your soul like that with thankfulness and love.
Now tell me, sinners, will you sell your birthright?
How much do you want for it?
How much do you want for your share in Christ?
What price will you sell your soul for?
Sell your Christ! Long ago they sold him for thirty pieces of silver. And ever since, the heavens have been raining tears of blood on our guilty world.
If the devil asked you to set the price for your soul, what price would you name?
Lorenzo Dow was once riding along a lonely road on his way to an appointment. He met a man and said to him, “Friend, have you ever prayed?”
“No.” “How much money will you take never to pray again?”
“One dollar.” Dow paid him and rode on.
The man put the money in his pocket and went on his way, thinking.
The more he thought, the worse he felt.
“There,” he said, “I have sold my soul for one dollar!”
“I must have met the devil!”
“No one else would tempt me like that.”
“I must repent with all my soul, or I will be damned forever!”
How often have you made a deal to sell your Savior for less than thirty pieces of silver!
No, for almost nothing at all!
Finally, God wants volunteers to help with this great work.
God has given himself. He has given his Son and sent his Spirit. But more workers are still needed. What will you give?
Paul said, “I carry on my body the marks of the Lord Jesus.”
Do you want that kind of honor?
What will you do? What will you suffer?
Don’t say, “I have nothing to give.”
You can give yourself—your eyes, your ears, your hands, your mind, your heart, everything. Surely nothing you have is too sacred or too good to give to such a work when God calls like this!
How many young men are ready to go? And how many young women?
Whose heart jumps up and cries, “Here I am! Send me”?
“Blessed are the merciful, for they will receive mercy.” Matthew 5:7
What is mercy? And who are the merciful?
These are the first questions we should look at.
Mercy is not the same thing as goodness. It is only one quality of goodness.
Justice is another. But in some ways justice stands opposite to mercy.
Goodness is the bigger word. It includes both mercy and justice.
Justice treats people as their character deserves. Mercy treats them better than that. It wants to do them all the good it can, even though they deserve punishment.
That is why God sends rain on the unjust as well as on the just. He does good even to people who deserve none.
Justice wants to carry out the law. But mercy sets that aside wherever it can do so with reasonable safety.
Justice seems strict. It makes no effort to bless the guilty. Instead, it sacrifices them for the good of the public. In these ways it is quite different from mercy, even opposite to it.
Mercy keeps on trying to do the sinner good. It is patient even with enemies.
Christ praises the practice of mercy.
He says, “If you love only those who love you, why should you be thanked?
And if you do good to those who do good to you, why should you be thanked?
Don’t even the tax collectors do the same?
What are you doing here that is more than others do?”
Mercy and justice look a little different in someone who acts as a ruler.
For him, justice becomes more urgent. He may not be free to show mercy whenever he would like.
His job requires him to care deeply for the good of the whole community.
This is also true of God in his role as the moral Ruler of the human race.
In that role he must watch over his kingdom with endless care. He must make sure people properly respect the law and the great Lawgiver.
But God does not make it hard for us to show mercy. He does not give us the job of carrying out his punishments under his government.
He knows we are not able to handle that responsibility.
It is good that we do not have to carry it.
So we are free to forgive our enemies. We can show them almost unlimited mercy.
“Vengeance belongs to God.” He knows how and when to carry it out.
We are completely free to seek our enemies’ good, and only their good. The only exceptions are when God or the needs of society require otherwise.
You know that in a few very unusual situations, God has told his people not to seek the good of the wicked.
About the Ammonites and Moabites God said (Deuteronomy 23:6), “You must not seek their peace or their prosperity all your days, forever.”
When God comes to carry out his law against nations, they are put beyond the reach of our mercy.
In the same way, when he sends sinners to hell under the full working of his justice, we can no longer pray for them. We may no longer seek their peace.
But in every other case, unless God forbids it, we should work hard for their good.
We should always have a merciful attitude.
God always does. We can truly say that mercy is always alive in his heart. It is always welling up from its deep, eternal spring.
He is never spiteful, not even toward his worst enemies in hell.
He would speak as kindly as Abraham does in the parable: “Son, remember that during your lifetime you received your good things.” Every word there is spoken as kindly as the situation allows.
In the same way, human judges often hold back their tender feelings.
Their hearts are full of love. But their duties force them to carry out justice. Under God they are “ministers of wrath,” appointed to carry out his sentence against those who do evil.
Notice here a very clear difference between a person’s office and the person himself.
As a man, in his personal dealings, the judge may treat the prisoner with the tenderest compassion. Yet as a judge he firmly sentences him to a shameful death.

The sheriff may, with a steady hand, strike the fatal blow that drops the trapdoor of the gallows. Yet afterward he may suddenly faint. Sending a guilty man so suddenly into eternity is a terrible shock to his nerves.
As a man, he is merciful. As an officer, he must be just.
When we read the New Testament, we are struck by how widely it commands us to be merciful.
In the Lord’s Prayer we are taught to pray, “Forgive us our debts, as we forgive our debtors.” It is as if we should not expect more mercy from God than we show to other people.
Someone asked, “If my brother sins against me, how often should I forgive him?
Up to seven times?” “No,” Jesus answered, “up to seventy times seven.”
It is your duty always to seek the good of your enemies. Treat every one of them with loving kindness.
Our Lord puts great weight on this. He always uses strong examples. He requires this attitude toward everyone, friends and enemies alike.
What does forgiveness involve?
When God forgives, he sets aside the penalty of the law.
But forgiveness cannot mean that for us, because that is not our responsibility.
Under any government, a pardon removes the legal penalties that the crime brought on.
But for us as private people, forgiving means having a loving spirit. It means gladly showing favor and goodwill.
Suppose someone has wronged you.
What does mercy mean for you then?
It means you try to help the offender change. It means you try to save him from the penalty of God’s law. Unless he repents, that penalty will sink him into hell.
The true idea of mercy is to keep on trying to do him good.
This is what we owe our personal enemies.
That is why Christ teaches us to bless those who curse us, and to do good to those who do us harm.
Mercy means doing this, and never giving up in loving efforts to save them.
Our Lord urges his people to show mercy in many ways. He does so with amazing force and fullness.
“You have heard that it was said, ‘An eye for an eye and a tooth for a tooth.’
But I tell you, do not resist evil. If anyone strikes you on the right cheek, turn the other cheek to him too.”
He insists that we must not take revenge or pay people back. We must go all the way with mercy.
In these beatitudes, Christ commanded kinds of goodness that are among the hardest for our sinful human nature.
We can see this if we compare them with other things we call virtues.
For example, we think of hating sin, having a sense of justice, and approving of punishment as virtues.
But even sinful hearts have these almost naturally.
It is natural to hate sin—all sin except our own, and maybe even our own. We certainly cannot approve of it.
People can never love sin just for itself.
They love it for the good they hope to get from it, even though that good does not last.
Who can be pleased with the character of the devil?
No one can approve of real malice.
That is why you see outbursts of violence and quick punishment by lynch mobs.
A striking example happened a few years ago. A steamboat captain sexually assaulted a young woman who had been placed in his care.

When his trial began in Buffalo, his lawyers seemed set on treating his crime as a small thing. People even thought the judge was going along with this. The public became so angry that the people threatened to tear down the judge’s office. They did force him to carry out justice in the case.
You could hardly find anyone who would put up with that kind of crime.
It is fairly easy to have the kind of virtue that shows itself in anger against sin.
But the virtues praised in Matthew 5 are real and difficult.
They may be the only sure tests of a heart that has been born again.
If these are missing, the evidence is lacking.
There is a kind of pity for the offender that makes excuses for sin. It tries to protect the criminal from punishment. It does not try to protect society from harm.
It cares a lot about shielding the guilty. It cares little about peace and purity.
We often see this attitude among Universalists.
All their sympathy usually goes to the sinner.
They use their influence to get in the way of justice.
Where Universalism is strong, you often cannot get a jury to convict someone of a crime that carries the death penalty.
Clearly, this attitude is against God’s law, not for it.
People who plan and hope to escape all punishment themselves find it easy and natural to side with criminals.
A merciful attitude never takes the side of sin and the sinner against what is right.
You see this in the attitude that moved God to send Jesus Christ to die for sinners. He did this to uphold the law and honor his throne.
You see the same thing in the attitude Jesus himself showed.
Both of them always defended God’s law. They fully honored it and upheld it.
Christ came to condemn the world’s sin, not to excuse it or justify it.
Because he condemned it, he gave his life for it.
He would not ask for sinners to be forgiven until he had fully honored and satisfied the law. He did that by dying in the sinner’s place.
Here is a strange fact. The Universalists, the very people who use their influence against punishing criminals, also set aside the atonement made by Christ’s death.
They do not accept the principle it is based on.
They do not believe in sacrificing anyone’s happiness in order to uphold law and government.
What if Christ had thought like them and acted on their principle?
Then there would have been no salvation for the human race.
Mercy has no sympathy for sin. It never hides sin from view.
Guilt has to be there before mercy can be shown.
The very idea of mercy assumes that someone is guilty.
No one can receive mercy unless he deserves punishment.
If someone deserves only a little punishment, there is room for only a little mercy.
If a man deserves three years in the state prison, mercy can pardon him for only three years.
The greater the virtue of mercy, the richer its reward.
When mercy is shown in the right situation, it surely brings deep happiness. But if we use justice where the situation calls for mercy, we miss the reward.
Using justice where it is called for also brings real happiness. But mercy in its proper place brings much more.
We all know that when we show mercy in the right way, it gives us special joy. That joy is far greater than what we feel when we carry out justice.
If the public good requires justice to be done, we are glad of it. But wherever mercy can be shown, there is great luxury in it.

blocks.x: REMARKS.

s: How great and wonderful God’s mercy is!
Just think of the moral greatness he shows in his mercy toward our world!
Our sins are great, yet he is patient and holds back. More than that, he loads us down with kindness.
Then think also of what it cost him.
Suppose a man hurt you and kept piling wrongs on you for a long time. But you freely pardon him, even though it costs you a great deal.
You give your money, your time, and your work to provide what is needed to win his pardon. In the end you even give your life for him.
Wouldn’t you call that an amazing example of love?
But God showed his love in a most amazing way. He gave his Son to die for sinners. This showed how much he delights in mercy, and that judgment is his “strange work.”
Showing such rich mercy must have given Jesus Christ great joy.
Those of us who have shown mercy to people who mistreated us can understand this.
We can see that Jesus must find the deepest and richest satisfaction in showing his great mercy to sinners.
God wins over the hearts of his enemies by showing his love.

He reveals his great love, and this conquers their hearts. It brings them under the power of his love. They deserve to be sent away forever. Yet he rejoices over them like someone who has found great treasure.
It is like when the prodigal son came home starving and filthy, but sorry for his sin. We see the father rushing out to meet him, his heart overflowing with joy.
If we may judge the happiness of heaven by what we ourselves experience, we must conclude this: God’s deepest happiness is found in showing mercy. This is his highest form of virtue.
Showing mercy has always been his present purpose. In that sense, it has always been a present reality.
God’s mercy must greatly strengthen his influence and power as moral Ruler.
Angels long to look into this plan of saving mercy.

They were watching from its very first hints. As soon as it began to unfold, they seized the glorious idea. All the armies of heaven took flight and rushed down to earth. They joined in the rising music of the first great song of praise: “Glory to God in the highest, and on earth peace and goodwill toward men!”
Who can doubt that this greatly increased their happiness and their holiness—their love for God and their joy in his rule?
This display of God’s mercy must baffle Satan and all hell.
What can they say when they see what it costs God to show mercy?
How baffled they must be! Their plan was to overthrow God’s kingdom by bringing sin into our world. But through God’s glorious displays of mercy, it has mostly made his kingdom stronger!
Some have wondered why God did not wipe out Adam and Eve as soon as they fell into sin.
The truth is, he could not afford to.
That event gave him the opportunity to do a great work for his kingdom.
It was a glorious opportunity, and he could not afford to lose it.
Mercy was a rich and glorious part of his nature. Now the time had come to show it on an amazing scale.
With the fallen angels, he had shown his justice in its terrible forms. But an ocean of mercy was welling up from deep in his heart. How could he hold it back any longer?
Why should he go on giving up the luxury of showing it?
Did I say luxury?
Yes, I did. His mercy is so great that no luxury compares with it.
Do you think it feels like a sacrifice to him, or makes him unhappy, to show mercy to lost people?
Not at all! It is just as true of him as it is of us: “Blessed is the merciful!”
Those who have not forgiven everyone from their hearts are not forgiven themselves.
Sometimes I have seen people in great distress of mind for a long time. I have asked them, “Are there people you think of as your enemies, people you will not forgive?”
In many cases, this was clearly why they could not find mercy.
It is very common for people to stay a long time under conviction of sin and in deep anxiety. They cannot find peace at all, because they will not forgive those they think are their enemies.
Some years ago there was a poor Black man among us. As he came near death, he was very troubled about whether he was ready.
I asked him, “Do you forgive all your enemies?”
“No,” he said, “not at all! Almost my whole life I have been robbed of my freedom, my work, and my very life. How can I ever forgive the men who did all this?
If I cannot be saved without forgiving my enemies, then I must be lost!”
I found him like this several times, and I worked hard to show him his duty.
At last, one time as I came into his room, I saw his face glowing with joy and peace.
As soon as he saw me, he cried out, “I’ve gotten over it! God has helped me over it! I love my enemies now!”
He truly was a new man. He died in the blessed peace of the gospel.
Some people say, “I can forgive, but I can’t forget.”
They probably have not really forgiven.
Many people gain a hope of salvation and fool themselves.
They do not fully forgive their enemies from the heart. And God does not forgive them either.
Sometimes people say, “If those who hurt me have repented, I can forgive them. Otherwise I can’t.”
That is the wrong basis.
God will deal with their repentance before him. He can judge whether it is sincere far better than you can.
He does not give you the job of finding out whether your enemy is truly sorry.
All he asks is that you have a merciful spirit toward him.
That is your part.
The gospel shows us the spirit of the law. The law requires mercy, because it requires perfect goodwill toward all, and that of course includes mercy.
When Christ died for sinners, he showed us the true, spiritual meaning of God’s law.
So the gospel does not go against the law. It shows the law truly and beautifully.
God’s character as we see it in the gospel is like his character as we see it in the law. The only difference is that the law leaves out some things the gospel shows.
As far as they can be compared, what they show is alike.
You find more in the gospel than in the law, but nothing that contradicts it. Nothing in one clashes with the other.
The Jews in Christ’s time had a very low view of the law.
So Christ had to work hard to raise the law above their standard.
We see this all through most of his sermons on the mount.
His whole teaching on forgiveness and loving enemies set a higher standard.
Christ taught people not to resist evil. Instead they were to be as patient and merciful as they could possibly be.
Again and again Christ said, in effect: You teach a virtue that both saints and sinners have—doing good only to those who do good to you.
I have come to give you new and higher ideas of virtue.
There is a feeling that looks like mercy and is often mistaken for it. But it falls short.
Christ refers to it when he says, “If you love those who love you, what reward do you have?”
It is a partial mercy. It is patient with those we love, who are perhaps tied to us in special ways.
But this is not real mercy.
True goodwill means loving everybody. It reaches to all.
You are not showing mercy if you love only certain people, while there are others you have no desire to forgive.
As long as there is even one person you cannot pray for, it is clear that there is one person you do not truly love.
If your attitude is such that you cannot work lovingly for his salvation, you prove that something is deeply wrong with you.
For you are required to forgive everyone.
Otherwise, how can you honestly pray the Lord’s Prayer: “Forgive us as we forgive”?
Luke puts it this way: “Forgive us, for we forgive.”
How can you dare to say this before God when you do not forgive?
It is not enough to pray, “Lord, help us to forgive others.”
That is not what the Lord’s Prayer says at all.
Reformers are very likely to be fooled by a partial kind of goodwill.
They mistake hatred of sin for love of souls and love for all that exists. They can condemn slavery and slaveholding fiercely. But so could the devil.
No doubt he hates it as one of the lowest sins in his kingdom.
He cannot help hating sin and wickedness.
He cannot love it for itself, because there is nothing lovely about it.
He must treat sin and sinners with the deepest contempt, because he is a moral being.
No moral being can honestly say, “Evil, be my good.”
It is striking that some who claim to be reformers show no mercy to sinners. Instead of blessings, they seem to want to call down curses and vengeance on them.
They will do little good for the world until they get the right spirit themselves and truly try to improve the moral condition of people’s hearts.
The Temperance movement did very little until it took on the Washingtonian style. Then it gave its warm right hand to the drunkard to help him up.
Then it took a huge step forward.

The temperance men lifted their fallen neighbors out of the gutter. They washed them and clothed them. They kindly led them forward to take the pledge. They went to their empty, broken homes and brought joy to the sad hearts there. They supplied needs that had long gone unmet. It was then that people turned away in crowds from the path of the destroyer.
I knew of a case in Boston.
One cold winter evening at a Methodist meeting, my friend saw a man slip in late. He leaned over the stove, shivering with cold.
After the service my friend spoke kindly to the poor man. The man humbly apologized for coming in and said he hoped he had not done any harm.
When my friend asked him questions, he told a sad story of poverty and sorrow. He admitted that he had been living as a miserable drunkard and that his family was suffering terribly.
My friend said, “I will go home with you.” He took the man’s arm and walked on with him. On the way he stopped at a grocery store to have some food sent, and at a coal yard to order some coal.
So when he arrived, these welcome and badly needed supplies arrived too.
To the poor, suffering people in that sad home, his visit seemed like a visit from an angel of mercy.
His words and his whole manner were kind too.
He said to the father of the family, “I can’t stand to see you drunk ever again.
You must not drink anymore.
I would rather be whipped until I bleed than see you go back to the path of death.”
I tell you this story to show the difference between hunting a man down with justice and following him with mercy.
I have talked about how a judge’s relations and duties in his office differ from those he has as a man.
The same difference exists between a person as a citizen and as a private person.
As a citizen, you may be required to report a crime. But as a private person, you have no right to take revenge.
The purpose of enforcing the law is to protect the public.
For the public’s sake, we have no right to refuse to report those who destroy property and disturb the peace.
Suppose a wicked man came into your house and committed murder there.
You would be required to arrest him and report him to the proper authorities.
The safety of other families demands it, since they are in danger from such a murderous man.
But at the same time, you must pray for him. You must do all you can to bring him to true repentance before God.
You should say to him, “Listen. You have committed a terrible crime. I have reported you, as I had to do. But I still love you. I beg you to repent of your sin and give yourself to Christ.”
As a private person, no one may give in to revenge.
No matter how badly you have been wronged, if you cannot pray and work for that person to change and be saved, you are not right with God.
Maybe you cannot be glad when any human being at all does well. Maybe it spoils your happiness to see anyone happy. If so, your heart is badly wrong.
This shows that if you were in heaven, you could not possibly enjoy its joy.
Many people have a spiteful nature. They seem to love to store up their grievances and brood over them with spiteful feelings.
Falling away from God often begins with grievances that are held on to and not forgiven.
You will find that people who have fallen away are almost always critical of others.
They hold on to a quarrelsome spirit. They go through life elbowing their way along, always at odds with someone, and often with many.
Suppose you die like this. You will surely go to hell!
How can anyone dare to live without mercy toward another person?
It is a horrible way to live!
You may die suddenly. You certainly cannot die in peace while that evil spirit of hatred hides in your heart.
Maybe you have had a quarrel with a neighbor. Now you are saying, “If he goes to heaven, I don’t want to meet him there.”
If he does go to heaven, you will not meet him there with the attitude you have now. That much is certain.
But if he goes to hell, you will meet him there!
You cannot go to heaven unless you can forgive everyone, and do it freely from the heart.
A woman who had a bitter quarrel with another woman was asked, “What if you met her in eternity?”
She answered, “I would hunt her down in hell.”
“Do you expect to go to hell?”
“I have nothing in me but the spirit of hell!
It burns and boils in my soul all the time.”
One evening two men who claimed to be Christians had a quarrel.

The next morning one of them said to the other, “We’ll love each other better after we’ve had a ground-sweat.” He talked as if lying in the grave until the resurrection would sweat such bitterness out of them!
Not at all! The grave has no such power.
The “ground-sweat” never does that.
Only the mercy of Jesus and his dying love can reach this hateful spirit and cure it. And this cure must happen here on earth.
Are you going to your deathbed with an unforgiving spirit?
Do you say to your enemy, “He has wronged me; I cannot forgive him”?
What a terrible state! Suppose I have to preach at your funeral.
Should I say, “This man has gone to heaven”?
God forbid that I should speak dishonestly and deceive the living!
But you say, “I have been hurt and wronged so badly!”
Have you? Wasn’t Christ hurt too?
Yet didn’t he cry out, “Father, forgive them, for they don’t know what they are doing”?
Wasn’t Stephen hurt?
Yet listen to him pray: “Lord, don’t hold this sin against them!”
This is how people die who are going to heaven.
But you who have no forgiveness in your souls, do not sleep on with your unforgiving spirit.

Go to Jesus. Wash your soul in tears of repentance. Keep on until you can pray the Lord’s Prayer without fear that you will bring nothing but curses down on your soul. For you are forgiven only as you forgive others!
“And the second is like it: You must love your neighbor as yourself.” Matthew 22:39
I will speak about this part of our Lord’s summary of God’s law. First, I will ask what KIND of love is required here.
Second, I will name some of the things this love includes.
Third, I will show that nothing less than this love is true humanity.
Last, I will show that nothing less is true morality.
I. The love we must have for our neighbor is certainly not being pleased with his character.
Being pleased with someone’s character means approving of it and delighting in it. But our Lord makes no difference between good people and bad people. So he requires us to love them all.
But he cannot be asking us to approve of bad people’s character and delight in it. So we must conclude that he does not have this kind of love in mind. It is not what he requires.
To be pleased with the character of wicked people because they are wicked is to be as bad as they are.
No sensible person can think that this is what the Savior requires. No one can think that this is what he says God’s law requires.
Also, it is not the fond affection we sometimes feel for certain people.
Some people are naturally pleasing to certain others. Some are pleasing to everyone. They are naturally likable and stir up pleasant feelings.
But this is not the love the text is talking about.
Also, this love cannot be something that happens to us apart from our will.

Earlier I spoke about the love we must have for God. I said it must be a free choice. It cannot happen apart from our will. If it did, God could not fairly demand it. I say the same about this love for our neighbor.
It cannot happen apart from our will. If it did, no fair and just being could require it.
To put it positively, this love for our neighbor is goodwill. It must be goodwill.
God’s love for people is goodwill. It is a pure and strong concern for their welfare. It is a desire for their happiness. He actively wills their happiness as the thing dearest to his heart.
The way his great love has shown itself proves this.
Our own reason tells us that this is the love God has had for our race, and still has.
So we must conclude that this is the love he requires people to show to each other.
Notice also that this love requires us to value our neighbor’s interests as our own.
This rule applies to all our neighbors. It applies to our enemies as well as to our friends.
Also, it is a steady love. It does not come and go, and it does not fade away. It does not act on sudden impulse. It flows from a spring of goodwill that lasts forever.
It is a state of mind. It is a settled state that treats our neighbor’s interests as our own.

blocks.x: II. Now I will name some things this love includes.

s: (1.) It does not mean we must divide our energy and resources equally among all people. It does not even mean we must divide them equally among everyone near enough for us to know.
It cannot mean this. If it did, no one could obey it.
There is no doubt that God’s law demands goodwill toward all people, always and in every situation. But some situations rule out ways of showing it that would be right at other times.

Think of a criminal who is serving a just sentence under human law. We must not do the same kind things for him that would be fitting after he has served his sentence, or if he were not under sentence at all.
Sinners come to stand under the sentence of God’s law. Their relationship to God is then such that he cannot bless them.

It is not that he has stopped loving them. He still has a deep, intense concern for their happiness. But he loves all the rest of his thinking creatures just as much. And their interests demand that he carry out his righteous law against the wicked.
So he cannot give them even as much good as a cup of cold water.
Sometimes the same kind of situation may require us, too, to hold back from active efforts to do good to the wicked.
Also, this law requires each person to love his neighbor. So it is clear that God means these kindnesses to go both ways.
If God does good to us, we should gratefully try to do good to him.
If he advances our interests, we should work hard to advance his.
The same is true of children toward their parents.
Children should not always receive and never give. They should count it a great privilege to repay their parents for all the work and care given to them.
Parents may live long enough to become old and helpless. Then their children should be glad for the chance to repay the kindness shown to them when they too were helpless.
The same is true of citizens and rulers.
In the same way, students and teachers have interests that go both ways.
Neither side should do all the receiving and none of the giving. Both sides should give and receive.
In the same way, this school, with its teachers and students, has a close relationship with the people who founded it and support it.
Others have done the work, and we have come in to enjoy the results of their work.
Others have given their money, and we are enjoying the benefit.
Every building here owes something to donors from other places.
Others have prayed, and God has blessed us because of those prayers.
So we should try to repay those kindnesses. We should do all we can to advance the very goals to which these Christian friends have given so much of their wealth and prayers.
In the same way, ministers who preach and the people who listen should give good to each other and receive good from each other.
All of us should do more than just receive good from others. We should work hard to do good to others as well, and give back to them generously.
Why shouldn’t this principle apply to all people in their relationship with God?
Some of you have never cared about God. Is it right for you to receive everything from God and give him nothing back? Is it right to give him no love and no obedience?
Do you have no zeal for his honor? Are you not devoted to his interests at all?
He has fed you and raised you like a child, and you have done nothing but rebel against him.
Is that right? Why don’t you say instead, “God has given me talents. I must give them back to him by using them whenever I have the chance”?
Surely you must see God as your neighbor in this sense: He has interests and rights. And you have the highest duty to repay Him for countless kindnesses.
The same is also true of how you relate to the church of Jesus Christ.
How much do you owe Him?
After all this, do you have any right to say, “He will never get one word of thanks from me! He will never get one thank offering from me!”?
What don’t you owe him!
Have you ever realized that you really owe him your very life? Without his mission of mercy, you would never have lived.
Without that offering and sacrifice on Calvary, none of us could have existed at all.
Without it, Adam and Eve would have been cut down at once in their sin. The law would have carried out its righteous judgment: “On the day you eat of it, you will surely die.”
So you are alive only because God has had mercy on our race.
Come now, step up right away and face what this great truth demands of you.
Don’t you owe God everything?
And will you pay back nothing at all?
Here you are in God’s house, surrounded by prayer. You could be in hell instead, screaming and wailing in the depths of despair!
Do you say, “I don’t owe Christ anything”?
But you claim to be a respectable person.
Yet who can respect you if you treat Jesus Christ like this?
Don’t you feel anything for the great sacrifices he made and the suffering he went through to save you?
Would you leave all the work and sacrifice to him, and give nothing back in love or thanks?
Will you flatly refuse to love him?
Do you say, “He is welcome to love me and die for me. But I have nothing to give him in return.
I leave it to him to do everything and suffer everything. He will not get a single word of thanks from me”?
Do you think this is right?
Is it generous? Should it be called respectable?
III. Nothing less than the love required here is true humanity.
It is not true humanity to do good only to your own children.
People think of their children as part of themselves. So doing good only to them is nothing more than selfishness stretched a little wider.
Only one kind of love is truly love for people. Only one kind is true humanity. It is the love that values human well-being for its own worth, and loves people simply because they are human.
IV. Nothing less than this is true morality.
Our reason and our conscience require nothing less.
It is not true morality to put special weight on our own interests just because they are ours.
It is still not true morality, even if we try to be honest in seeking the good of certain people.
If we love only certain people, that is favoritism.
Also, no one loves his friends in the way that pleases God unless he also truly loves his enemies.
Suppose someone does love his friends.
Listen to what Jesus Christ says about exactly this case: “If you love those who love you, what reward do you get?”
“Don’t even tax collectors [notorious sinners] do the same?”
Jesus Christ says, “Love your enemies.”
No one can ever be thought to do right unless he loves his enemies.
Someone says, “There are certain people I never wrong.”
What is your reason for doing them good and not harm?
If you truly loved your neighbor for the right reasons, you would love every neighbor. You would see every living person as your neighbor, in the sense this law means.

You would love every being you know of. That is because you would love to increase the happiness of every living, feeling being. You would try to love each one according to how much his well-being is worth.
Real goodwill would try just as hard to do good to enemies as to friends, if it could reach them. It would do them just as much good.
Understand this: to love your friend in the right way, you must love him as God does, and for the same reasons.
You cannot love him in the right way unless you also love your enemies, and for a similar reason.
Nothing a person does for his friend is acceptable to God unless he would do just as much for his enemies if he could.
God cannot give him any credit for doing good to his friends unless he does it on a principle that would lead him to do just as much for his enemies if he could.

No one does any duty for one person in a way that pleases God while he refuses or deliberately neglects to do the same for another. I say this because God’s law requires you to love all your neighbors, every single one. And if you have a spirit of obedience to God, you will.
No one does right in any true sense unless he acts from a love that is for everyone and is not self-seeking.
On any other basis it cannot be acceptable for even a moment.
Think of a mother nursing her baby. God gives her no credit for this if she does it for no higher reason than an animal does.
She has a duty to love her own children, because God has placed her in exactly that relationship.
But she must never think that God gives her credit for simply following her animal instincts.
Her soul should rise higher than a mere animal.
She has a duty to make it her aim to please God.
Nothing less than this can be the condition for being saved.
No one can be free from sin and living in grace unless he has been brought into a state of true love for his neighbor.
Imagine a man who comes to heaven’s gate and asks to be let in. What would happen to him if he met an enemy there? Suppose it was a man he had never loved, a man he had hated and never prayed for.
Could he walk past such a man into heaven?
How could you enjoy heaven without a holy heart?
Some of you would hurry out. You would be like the rude, bad-mannered boys we have sometimes seen rushing out of church before the worship service was even over.
A person who loves his neighbor will understand this: his neighbor has a right to enjoy the public worship of God without being disturbed.
Without this love, salvation is impossible by its very nature.
It is also impossible because of how God governs. It cannot happen as long as God rules and cares for the interests of his great kingdom.
The entrance to heaven is guarded on every side. Nothing that does what is detestable will ever get in. Nothing unholy will enter.
Imagine a man going there in his selfishness!
Not if God can keep him out!

blocks.x: REMARKS.

s: If everyone obeyed God’s laws, society would be perfect.
I do not mean there would be no more progress, no more advances, no more improvements. No, not that. There is still much to be done.
But this much is true: morality would be perfect. There would be no more war and fighting.
Every family would be a little picture of heaven.
Every community would look like heaven.
Angels would come down so close that their wings would fan such loving hearts. And heaven’s doors would stand open all day long for such a people.
We can see how we should treat people who are oppressed and enslaved.
We must put ourselves in their place. We must ask what we would ask them to do for us if we were in their situation.
Suppose that my family and I are slaves.
An election is coming up.
Do I have a right to expect my friends in Ohio to vote in the way that will most directly help set me free?
I would be very likely to think that no one should vote against my freedom just for money or a government post.
Even politicians can see how shameful and how terribly wrong it is to own a human being as property.
And that this should be called an institution of the Bible! Of all monstrous things, that is the most monstrous!
It is so disgusting that I can hardly imagine how anyone can honestly hold this opinion.
Still, let us be fair. I can easily see that the merely legal relationship could exist without breaking the law of love.
This golden rule works equally well everywhere and in every situation.
It is good to use when we ask for favors.
We should not ask anyone for a favor if knowing his situation and properly caring about his welfare would rule it out. That is the kind of care we would want him to have for ours.
The same is true of receiving favors.
If we apply this law honestly, it will show us which favors we should let others do for us.
Sometimes it is not right for us to let others do us favors.
Suppose a poor man has worked for me for a month and refuses to take any pay. Then I too must by all means refuse to accept his work as a gift.
If I think properly about his situation, I must refuse such a large gift from him.
He cannot afford to give it. So I cannot afford to receive it.
From this subject you can see what the morality of unconverted people really is.
It is not morality at all, in any true sense.
All their morality is nothing but sin.
You can also see how God personally relates to selfishness.
Every bit of selfishness is personally hostile to God and hateful to him.
It is so completely unlike his heart. It is so totally against all his principles and all his actions. He can have nothing to do with it.
He must hate it completely forever.
You can also see how God, as ruler, relates to sin.
He can put up with the personal insult, and he does. He does for now. If it were not for the needs of his government, he might overlook it forever.
He is patient with sinners now. He does not fret. He does not show angry passion as people do when they are insulted. But he cannot overlook what sin does to his government.
He must see how selfish people are toward him and toward each other.
He is a judge and ruler with the highest responsibilities in the universe.
All eyes are on him.
He must take note of the evil done among his subjects and his creatures.
He must see all their wickedness as they bite and devour one another and trample each other down.
All eyes look up to him.
What does the Judge of all the earth say to this!
Oh, this must be answered!
God’s role as ruler over his government makes it a terrible thing for people to love selfishness.
Every selfish sinner is in sure danger of eternal death.
People know this. They cannot help knowing it.
God’s mercy flows at your feet like a deep, wide, glorious river. Yet you pay no attention to it!
Yet you push Jesus away!
You have done this often and for a long time.
Can you keep doing it even longer?
Jesus comes close to save you, with a bleeding heart and a loving hand. But you are saying: Go away from me! Leave me alone in my sins a while longer!
I will not let this man rule over me, or save me, on such terms of salvation!
O sinner! Will you keep going down a path that is so ruinous and so outrageously insulting to Jesus Christ?
